When I use the term “inherently,” I mean that we ignore the real-world welfare benefits of larger populations, including but not limited to: economies of scale, network effects, and urbanization. In the field, philosophers distinguish between intrinsic value and instrumental value. The former is the notion of the “inherent” value of individuals. The latter refers to the practical benefits of individuals.

7

If this seems unpersuasive to you consider the following transformation to any arbitrary population: an individual of welfare 10 is born and dies instantaneously. This transformation is effectively identical to no transformation at all. Keep in mind that this happens in a vacuum, meaning no other individuals are meaningfully affected by this.

8

Technically speaking, transformations are just stochastic transformations of degenerate probability.

9

If you’re risk-averse, one approach is to apply a concave monotonic transformation to the value of each possible outcome under a given theory of population ethics. You can then compute the expected value of the population after applying this transformation.

10

It’s possible to model time as continuous, though this requires calculus.

11

If you apply an infinite time horizon, the average would converge to zero. Infinite time horizons kind of complicate the process of averaging and have weird implications that I’d like to avoid.

12

It’s a modification of the Taylor series sum for Euler’s number.

13

Suppose you want to apply meta-total utilitarianism under total utilitarianism given a stochastic transformation. Simply calculate the expected value of the population over the years (or use an alternative method for evaluating stochastic transformations). This can get kind of complicated as the possibilities branch off. I’d be interested to see a computer program visualize such a process.

14

Discounting can be done in continuous time.

15

I imagine that in the real world, people who decide how many animals to breed inside of factory farms use sales figures to inform these decisions. For example, a factory farmers might see that 5 more chicken breasts were purchased in the last quarter. Humans have a tendency to “bunch” numbers, meaning we treat arbitrarily close numbers as the effectively identical. For example, at the scale of an entire factory farm, an increase in quarterly chicken breasts sold from 1,000,000 to 1,000,005 might not “feel” like a sufficient increase to justify breeding an additional chicken. Perhaps a more realistic assumption, therefore, is that every 100 additional chicken breasts sold leads to an additional 50 chickens bred. You can assign a random probability to the event that your purchase of a single pack of chicken breasts is the “tipping point.” Similar expected utility reasoning extends to democratic processes and other collective action problems.

16

You could theoretically incorporate the real-world benefits of larger populations into the model. For example, you could design a transformation that simultaneously grows/shrinks the population and increases/decreases individual welfare.

17

Essentially you represent the value of the populations under each counterfactual as an infinite geometric series with the discount factor as the common ratio. It’s similar to a discounted cash flow analysis or a repeated prisoner’s dilemma. If this article is received well enough, I’ll transcribe the calculations.

18

Meta-average utilitarianism requires us to take the expected value of the population and average it across every year. Discounting causes this average to equal zero for mathematical reasons. Thus, meta-average utilitarianism paired with discounting encounters some problems.

19

I acknowledge that this is a pretty bold statement. I don’t even agree with it. But it’s cool.

20

Please excuse me for not presenting a more comprehensive argument against the notions of welfare and utility. It’s somewhat beyond the scope of this article. I touch on a few of these arguments here and here.

21

This is a calculus concept.

item.title: Shonenism
item.description: my favorite moral philosophy
item.content:encoded:
Note: When I say that Shonenism is my favorite moral philosophy I’m not asserting that it’s the “best” moral philosophy or that it’s my primary moral philosophy.

What if I told you that the moral philosophy that has had the greatest continued influence on my life doesn’t even have a name? This article is my effort to fix that.

What is Shonenism?

Shonen manga is manga targeted at a demographic of adolescent boys1. The term shonen literally means “boy” in Japanese and has become colloquially associated with anime and manga (animanga) targeted at this demographic. It’s also used as a pejorative for anime and manga with an emphasis on battles and action; the insinuation is that fans who prefer shonen to more “cinephilic”2 animanga are juvenile or Philistines. Those who would use the term “shonen” as a pejorative often forget one of the reasons shone is so broadly appealing: the moral themes.

For the rest of the article, when I say “shonen,” I’m primarily referring to animanga targeted at adolescent boys that place a strong emphasis on battles and action. Indeed, shonen preaches the value of optimism, probity, friendship, and determination, among other things. These values are often epitomized in shonen protagonists—most notably Goku, Naruto, Luffy, and Ichigo. These characters are persistent cultural icons, perhaps primarily because they’re morally inspiring. Goku’s compassion, hard work, and selflessness served as a role model for many milennial and early Gen Z men across North America. Luffy’s conviction in fighting for the freedom of others was brandished on his pirate crew’s flag in major protests in Nepal, Indonesia, and the United States.

As a big animanga fan, the lessons these characters embody have become so natural to me that it’s hard to begin to outline them. Nevertheless, here is my definition of Shonenism, the moral philosophy of shonen protagonists. Shonenism believes the following:

  1. Have moral conviction. You must adhere to your morals absolutely. If you believe that you shouldn’t fight with your fists3, for instance, then you shouldn’t use your fists even when on the verge of death in a fight.

  2. Be optimistic. Maintain the hope of victory even when on the precipice of defeat.

  3. Be empathetic. See the good in everyone. Believe in redemption. Be receptive to befriending the enemy.

  4. Have deontological beliefs. That is, have beliefs about morally permissible and impermissible actions.4 For example, you you might believe that you shouldn’t kill anyone.

  5. Cherish interpersonal bonds. Be willing to befriend or reject anyone on the basis of their character. Be willing to make major sacrifices for your friends and family. Remain loyal to your friends and family.

  6. Be amenable to iconoclasm. Rebel against social norms, institutions, and more broadly “the establishment” when they oppose your moral beliefs. For example, if the world is ruled by a despotic government, you might declare war against it.

Note that there’s room for variation within this moral framework (e.g. people can vary in their moral convictions and deontological beliefs). These six principles are the quintessence of shonen protagonists, some individual differences notwithstanding.5 I would add that many characters outside of shonen that embody Shonenism, such as Amarendra Baahubali (from Baahubali), many protagonists of Indian cinema, many video game characters, Aang (from Avatar: The Last Airbender), Thorfinn (from Vinland Saga, a non-shonen manga), and many superheroes.

The flaws of Shonenism

I find it quite inspiring and formative, even though I don’t entirely agree with this philosophy. First, moral conviction can come with severe drawbacks. Morals can be difficult to define, nebulous, and flawed. For example, some male shonen characters refuse to hit women, even women who are evil and severely harm innocent people. Second, there are limits to empathy. It can be argued that some people are beyond redemption or that any possibility of redemption would likely be a Pyrrhic victory. There are also cases where befriending one’s enemy, or more broadly pursuing a diplomatic solution, is exceedingly impractical. Third, deontological beliefs suffer from the same flaws as moral conviction. Fourth, excessive alacrity in befriending others can leave one susceptible to betrayals. Sometimes loyalty is not well-defined.6 And this definition of friends and family is also quite nebulous. Shonen protagonists tend to err on the side of classifying someone as their friend or family, though I question this heuristic. Finally, while iconoclasm is noble and consistent with deontological beliefs and moral conviction, it’s highly impractical. Would you declare war against your government because it treated your friend unjustly? Luffy would. I’m not certain I would. All in all, the principles of Shonenism are highly flawed.

Shonenism also fails to account for utilitarianism.7 For example, suppose a superhero is given a choice between saving a civilian from death and capturing a villain. In most mainstream superhero media, there’s no meaningful tradeoff between these decisions; the superhero saves the civilian and the villain doesn’t kill more people counter-factually. A lot of mainstream media, including shonen, insulates the audience from the painful possibility that a small sacrifice might actually make the world better off. It’s easy to parade virtues when they aren’t put to the test.

There are a number of other edge cases—some I’ve seen properly explored in shonen—that expose gaps in Shonenism. For example, how should one morally prioritize their friends over strangers? In wars, soldiers can rationalize their participation by weighing the welfare of “their people” above that of “the enemy.” Shonenism both endorses this (principle 5) and discourages this (principle 3). Shonen often glosses over the moral implications of tribalism by pitting the protagonist and their allies against characters so morally reprehensible that violence is (ostensibly) justified.8 But what happens when the protagonist is pitted against people who are also fighting for their comrades?

I particularly love Naruto for how it handles this dilemma. Without spoiling the story, in one of its story arcs, the titular protagonist Naruto is pitted against a villain who harmed his village. Naruto and his comrades are shinobi (effectively soldiers) of a military nation called the Hidden Leaf Village, while the villain is an expat of the Hidden Rain Village. The Hidden Leaf Village historically committed many civilian casualties against the Hidden Rain Village. Naruto argues to the villain that his actions are wrong because he harmed the Hidden Leaf Village. The villain then asks Naruto the following (not verbatim): “What about my village? What about my friends? You fight for a village that committed atrocities just as you claim that I’m committing atrocities now.” Without spoiling how Naruto resolves this apparent hypocrisy, I can say that his resolution is actually consistent with Shonenism. Indeed, most of the flaws of Shonenism are really just ambiguities. Unfortunately, shonen don’t ask a very important question: what happens when two “good guys” are pitted against each other?

A more inadequately explored edge case in shonen is the idea that a friend could betray you. Shonen protagonists are often so quick to befriend people on the basis of their ostensible character that they leave themselves susceptible to betrayal. In one shonen manga (I’m withholding the title to avoid spoilers), the protagonist’s friend is revealed to be a spy. Surely the protagonist was punished for their alacrity in befriending strangers, right? Wrong. It turned out that the spy betrayed the protagonist out of coercion. This is often how the trope plays out in shonen; betrayals are rarely genuine, as the traitor is typically still on the protagonist’s side.

My relationship with Shonenism

Shonenism, despite its shortcomings, played an essential role in sculpting my moral character. Almost all of my values can be traced back to scenes where some character with a ridiculous outfit said that he would never go back on his word, or he had no enemies, or that he would never give up. I still get goosebumps when I see virtuous characters crusade against the injustices of their world.

I think the tendency for older animanga fans to spurn shonen is emblematic of something more tragic than elitism. As we get older, it’s easy to reject the teachings of Shonenism as naive ideals. Life can be hard enough. Why should we care about others? Why should we stay optimistic and determined? With age, people use the cracks in Shonenism as justification for looser morals. Suppose you believe as a kid that everyone is redeemable. After trying to help an incorrigibly toxic friend in adolescence, you update this belief to say that some people are irredeemable. You become overwhelmed with college and then your job. Adult life is too much. This belief that some people are irredeemable becomes an excuse not to see good in anyone. You live a cynical, miserable existence. That child in you who extended a hand to others is dead. Long gone.

The moral ambition and resulting impracticalities of Shonenism are precisely why I have more respect for it as an adult. Of course it can be easier to see good in people when you’re a kid. That’s why it’s so valuable for this the teachings of Shonenism to persist into adulthood. And it’s for this reason that I continue to ask one simple question when faced with moral uncertainty in my personal life: What would a shonen protagonist do?

Thank you for reading! Subscribe to support my work and receive new publications.

1

The other three major demographics are shojo (young girls), seinen (adult men), and josei (adult women). You can easily infer the sensibilities of the four demographics.

2

Commonly, these “cinephilic” animanga fall under one of the following categories: 1) deliberately obtuse/complex animanga (e.g. Neon Genesis Evangelion, Serial Experiments Lain, Ergo Proxy) 2) seinen animanga (targeted at an adult male demographic) (e.g. Berserk, Vagabond, Vinland Saga) 3) animanga without an emphasis on action (e.g. Ghibli films, Legend of the Galactic Heroes, Monster). There’s nothing wrong with liking any of these, of course.

3

For those who didn’t catch the reference, there’s a character in One Piece named Sanji who is a chef. Sanji fights using kicks because he believes that his hands should only be used for cooking.

4

This is different from the first point. This point is basically saying that you should draw moral lines. The first point is saying that your moral beliefs, including these moral lines, should be firm.

5

Naruto believes in redemption much more than Luffy, for example. In Naruto, villains are typically written as tragedies who reflect the flaws of their society. Naruto sees the empathy in these villains where no one else would. In One Piece, on the other hand, villains are typically written as irredeemable tyrants who oppress the friends Luffy makes along his journey. Accordingly, Luffy defeats them, restoring freedom to the newly liberated peoples.

6

For example, say that your friend is about to make a terrible decision and refuses to heed your warnings. You can either stop your friend against their will or respect your friend’s agency. What’s the loyal thing to do here? For me it’s not so clear-cut.

7

There’s a trend in media of deontological heroes and utilitarian villains. I use the word utilitarian with acquiescence because often the schemes of these villains aren’t truly utilitarian. Unless you buy Malthusianism, Thanos’ plan to erase half the population of the universe would likely decrease welfare, at least on Earth. Deontology is a much more feel-good philosophy than utilitarianism. It’s more marketable. Also, the average person is rarely explicitly confronted with a tradeoff between deontology and utilitarianism. Often, the deontological decision is also utilitarian. Dilemmas between deontology and utilitarianism are more commonly faced (at least explicitly) in the military, politics, positions of power, and Effective Altruism.

8

One Piece is a prime example of this.

item.title: The Loss of Place
item.description: the world around us is dying
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic Status: Much of this is anecdotal.

Imagine that you’re done with an exhausting day of work or school and have some errands to run this bright, sunny evening. You stop by your local library to pick up the latest installment of one of your favorite book series. As you set foot inside, you take in the colorful shelves of books, new decor that the librarians assiduously set up weekly, and flyers of upcoming events. The librarian hands you your book, which she, having already read, assures you is a promising tale; you’re a regular here and she knows you by name. You make a stop at the grocery store to pick up some ingredients for dinner. You eye a fruit you’ve never tried before in the produce aisle—an Asian pear1—and decide to toss one in the shopping cart. You run into your barber and chitchat with him. He invites you to a party he’s throwing this weekend. You head home feeling fulfilled. Your local area feels like a quaint, invigorating community. You feel present in the minutiae of your sense of place: the interiors of buildings, the local people, the town’s cultural history.

This feeling—this sense of place—is empowering, yet elusive in a zeitgeist where other people are mere in an ocean, human connection is increasingly optional, and proximity is little more than a convenience. This isn’t an article about the loneliness epidemic or the adverse effects of social media or the lack of walkability in American localities. At least not directly. It’s about diagnosing our lack of presence in the world around us.

It might still seem unclear what I mean by a “sense of place.” Indeed, this lack of clarity is precisely the issue. I associate a sense of place with the following:

  1. Familiarity: How familiar are you with the places2 around you? Familiarity can include knowing the perceptual details of a place, such as the furniture inside a building’s lobby. It can also include knowing the people there or the place’s history. It’s easy to see how a lack of familiarity with one’s surroundings precludes a sense of place. I for one couldn’t tell you what’s inside many of the buildings in my hometown.3

  2. Uniqueness: What makes a particular place different from comparable places? A good example of this is a local bakery whose owner bakes an original pastry. Another example is an office with avant-garde furniture in its lobby. As you can see, even the most milquetoast of places can have some level of uniqueness. One way of testing your understanding of the uniqueness of a place is to ask the following: how would I feel if this place underwent some kind of renovation? For example, my hometown’s local froyo place used to have a list of ten ostensible benefits of froyo on its wall. The list was scientifically dubious and over half of its items were qualified with high amounts of uncertainty (e.g. some studies suggest that frozen yogurt might have some heart benefits). This list is thus a recurring joke between my brother and me. I was sad to see the list replaced by a new TV when the place was renovated. My attachment to my hometown’s local froyo place, an indicator of uniqueness, is a rare case where I actually did have a sense of place in my hometown.

  3. Interconnection: To what extent do places in your local area feel like an interconnected continuum as opposed to a disparate collection? A good example of interconnection is the ability to recognize people in a wide variety of locations. Seeing your coworker outside of your workplace, for instance, can build a sense of community in your city. Another example of this is living in a town with a rich history. Understanding the context in which various buildings were built can help draw connections between said buildings; maybe all of the town’s oldest buildings were built next to a river. One way in which I lack a feeling of interconnection is how I run errands. I typically treat errand sites (e.g. dry cleaners, the library, the grocery store, etc.) as disparate locations to traverse between by car.4 There are admittedly some benefits to compartmentalizing places. Separating your workplace from a place of relaxation comes to mind. But compartmentalization may come with a cost. What if I explored random places throughout my errand runs? A foray into the nondescript building next to the grocery store may cost little time, while instilling a sense of place.

These three components encompass much of what I term a sense of place. However, this is a concept that is much better experienced than read about. I encourage all of you to be cognizant of your sense of place in some of the pockets of time or mental bandwidth that you have to do so.

I don’t have many prescriptions for how to address the lack of a sense of place. I can’t even say conclusively that this is a modern problem or that it’s worsening with time. Inducing a stronger sense of place is a complex problem at the intersection of urban planning, human culture, the education system, transportation—just to name a few. In other words, I’m both too lazy and too unqualified to offer many suggestions here.

I want to end with a a question I perhaps should have led with: why does a sense of place matter? In short, I don’t know. Maybe it improves individual and/or population-level wellbeing.5 Maybe it’s just aesthetically pleasing. Maybe it’s an antidote to the loneliness epidemic or an escape from the thrall of digital slop. Nevertheless, to me, a sense of place is a wellspring of happiness.6

Thank you for reading! Subscribe to receive new articles and support my work.

1

This is a real fruit that I’ve grown to enjoy. It’s a larger, juicier variety of the ordinary pear.

2

I use the term “place” somewhat vaguely on purpose. You could be familiar with your local grocery store, but unfamiliar with your greater city, for instance. I do think that there are emergent properties to familiarity with larger places, though this is outside the scope of this article.

3

A somewhat recent hobby of mine has been to enter random buildings as a form of observational recreation. It’s especially fun when you can’t guess the purpose of a building from its exterior.

4

This is admittedly symptomatic of the lack of walkability of US cities. However, even if my hometown was highly walkable, I might still feel a lack of interconnection.

5

I caution against spurious correlations between a sense of place and wellbeing. It could be that components of a sense of place, such as efficient transportation infrastructure, are correlated with other determinants of human wellbeing.

6

There’s an episode of Arthur called “Elwood City Turns 100!” I chose a frame of the episode as the image for this article because the episode (and the show in general) is an excellent example of having a sense of place.

item.title: How I Became Baháʼí (sort of)
item.description: on my relationship with religion
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic status: I’m not very knowledgeable about religion. This is more about my personal experience.

I’m agnostic.1 I was an atheist for most of my life, until I realized that my belief in the possibility of the simulation hypothesis should imply belief in the possibility of a supreme creator (see here). I briefly believed in Hinduism—my family’s religion—as a little kid only because I found its mythology appealing. I couldn’t see much reason to believe in religion. This notion that people can have faith in ideas that lack empirical evidence and that are arguably at odds with rigorous science.

But regardless of whether religion was “true,” I found it very unappealing. I didn’t want to label myself as Hindu just because my family did. It didn’t feel right to me to partake in Hindu rituals merely out of filial obligation. The rebellious and inquisitive parts of me also didn’t like the maxim that children adopt their family’s religious beliefs.

Furthermore, I couldn’t accept the notion of “blind faith,” that you shouldn’t need evidence to believe in God (I now believe that faith should be blind). It was nice to think that someone was looking out for me. But if I could believe in God, then I could believe in anything without evidence—at least that’s what I thought. It also didn’t sit right with me that this supposedly nigh-omnipotent figure allowed so much suffering to persist in the world. Why did God seem to treat me so much better than all these other people? There’s another way to think of it: would you stay friends with someone who treats you somewhat respectfully while persecuting other people in the world?

The real nail in the coffin for me was that I could experience most of the benefits of religion without believing in it. The community aspect is relatively easy to obtain; many religious communities I’ve encountered are fairly welcoming to atheists, agnostics, and members of other faiths. Religion is also a form of edification. Fortunately, I can draw on religious texts to form my moral compass without needing to believe in religion. All that I think I’m missing out on is the comfort that comes with believing that a powerful, benevolent entity is watching over you. In fact, as a kid, I found great solace from chanting Hindu slokas in my head when I was scared. Alas, I doubt I could ever regain such solace, whether I want to or not. I’m not sure that I can impose blissful ignorance onto myself. I can’t pretend that I believe in God just to feel some comfort. Think of it like this: could you forget that Santa doesn’t exist, even if it would make Christmas so much more magical for you?

My beliefs about religion, shaped by negative experiences with religious people, turned into prejudice. I still have a slight, reflexive aversion to tradition (religious or otherwise), religious people, and the ubiquity of religion in media. Religion remains such a salient facet of the human experience that I have taken it upon myself to understand it better. It’s a window into empathy and cultural understanding. I knew I had to overcome my prejudices. And so, I joined the Baha’i club at my university.

For those unfamiliar, the Baha'i faith is a niche religion founded by Baháʼu'lláh in Persia (now Iran) in the mid-19th century. It emphasizes the totality of the world’s major religions, as well as the unity of science and religion. I discovered Baha’i through a friend I made at my university’s Effective Altruism group. He invited me to attend the university’s Baha’i club for Friendsgiving. There, I met one of the nicest, most diverse groups of people ever. Many of us weren’t even Baha’i. For context, I grew up primarily surrounded by Hindu Telugu-Americans. It turns out that a lack of exposure to other cultures can limit your growth as a person. Some of the people I knew in my childhood were not the nicest people I’ve ever met, to put it mildly. That is to say, my past experience has taught me not to take the community I’ve found at the Baha’i club for granted.

I just couldn’t get over the fact that I had found a group of intellectual, religious, kind, ethnically diverse people. And this seems commonplace in the Baha’i community, evident in the fact that they have members all across the world. This club provided me with a sanctuary to heal my prejudices against religion and learn about other cultures. Thereafter, I attended almost all of the club’s meetings. Typical meetings consisted of discussions of excerpts from Baha’i texts. Although I didn’t find the teachings of these texts very revolutionary, they emphasize messages that our world would do well to internalize. Like most religious texts, the Baha’i texts speak of universal moral teachings like compassion, acts of service, and detachment from material/earthly desires. Unlike many religious texts, Baha’i texts were very ahead of their time in their attitude towards other cultures.

I’m a big proponent of some level of “impartiality” towards one’s “own” culture.2 It’s fine to celebrate one’s own culture. However, we shouldn’t view our culture as supreme or harbor bigotry. For example, suppose country A and country B begin a war. You are ethnically from country A. You shouldn’t view country A as the “good guy” just because it’s “your country” in an ethnic sense. And I promise this isn’t a dig at any particular international conflict. It extends to our empathy towards different peoples. It’s about doing what’s right, whether it aligns with “your people.” This notion of “my people” is (in some contexts) a blatant indication of selective empathy and a scourge to society. People should view themselves not as beholden to a cultural group but as citizens of the world. This is a pillar of the Baha’i faith.3

This concept of being a citizen of the world seems to have only recently gained traction due to globalization. This is because of something I’m going to call the cultural isolation problem. Most humans who have ever lived have seldom interacted with cultures outside of their own. Immigration, trade, and international politics did exist, though even these points of cultural exchange did not necessarily bridge cultural divides. It’s a tragedy that many of us live in a cultural bubble. In the 21st century, we continue to tackle the multifarious challenges borne from cultural segregation. It’s impressive to me, therefore, that the first Baha’i’s discussed this problem circa the American Civil War. Baha’is championed cultural unity during a time when America allowed race-based slavery.

Another aspect of Baha’i that appeals to me beyond the faith’s “global citizenship” is how well its orthodoxy has held up to modern scrutiny. While I’m not qualified to speak about any religion, I’ve observed that Hinduism and the Abrahamic faiths have had to reconcile unsavory aspects of their orthodoxies with modern norms. For example, some Hindus decry the caste system, and some Christians have found ways to reconcile homosexuality with the Bible (please let me know if I got something wrong). I’m sure Baha’i has also had to evolve. If I remember correctly, some of the older texts do dichotomize male and female gender roles, roles which modern Baha’i seems to have modernized. That said, I found it very difficult for anyone to derive an extremist ideology from Baha’i orthodoxy. To me, this is another sign of how prescient the original Baha’i texts were.

One of the aspects I like most about Baha’i is that the community doesn’t try to convert others. The religion makes clear that its principles are universal and that it’s an ally of other religions. The spiritual aspect of Baha’i and the world’s religions, more generally, more than makes up for their theological components. Baha’i believes in a singular God who, according to my Baha’i friend, is putatively a combination of major deities. I still don’t believe in God, but that didn’t preclude me from making secular interpretations of Baha’i texts.

My time at the Baha’i club accelerated my progress in shedding my prejudices against religion. I’ve learned to embrace the spiritual, non-theological. aspects of religion. I’ve reminded myself that much of what I stand for—kindness, compassion, and service—is fully compatible with religion. It’s for these reasons that I’ll return this August as one of the Baha’i club’s regular non-Baha’i members.

And that's the story of how I “became” Baha’i.

Thank you for reading! Subscribe to receive new articles and support my work.

1

I believe that there may or may not be a creator of the universe. I believe that if such a creator existed, they could not be omniscient or define moral truth.

2

I put the word “own” in quotation marks because it isn’t clear what constitutes “ownership” of a culture. Typically, we consider the culture of our biological family our own. However, this ownership can get very complicated. If you’re adopted by parents of a different ethnicity, is your parents’ culture your own? What if aspects of your culture were imposed on your ancestors (e.g., by colonial powers)?

3

In fact, the Baha’i governing council is called the International House of Justice. Emphasis on international.

item.title: The Ethics of Necromancy
item.description: Why we should resurrect people from the dead
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic Status: This article is almost entirely philosophical and speculative. I’m not a medical professional and have no qualified knowledge about the science of death.

Introduction

Necromancy is the resurrection of dead organisms.1 It’s ubiquitous in pop culture, often decried as a forbidden art. Pop culture and society seem to agree on one belief: death is sacrosanct. In fiction, attempts to obviate death, whether by necromancy, immortality, or other means, are associated with villainy—or at the very least, severe moral irresponsibility. I want to challenge the stigma against necromancy, an issue that may never have any practical relevance.

I’m going to focus this discussion of the ethics of necromancy on the resurrection of dead humans. I’m going to assume that necromancy reverts human corpses to their biological state before the incident that killed them. If the cause of death was more gradual, like a terminal illness, necromancy reverts the corpse to a version of themselves without the symptoms of the cause of death before the time of death.2 For example, suppose an elderly lady developed some terminal illness at age 80 and died at age 81. Necromancy would resurrect her corpse as her 80-year-old self, except without the symptoms of her terminal illness.3 She would still retain any unrelated ailments she had at that age, however (e.g. diabetes). Accordingly, since the lady is biologically 80, she could develop terminal illness again and pass away after only a year. Necromancy doesn’t confer immortality; it merely removes the cause of death and resets the body.

Assume that any human can be resurrected an infinite number of times after death. Assume that the necromancy process produces no sensation (e.g. pain) for both the necromancer and the resurrected person.

If think that this definition is unnecessarily specific, you’ll come to see how relevant the nuances are. If you think that the definition is not specific enough…you’d be right. It’s not hard to come up with edge cases that break this definition, but, as this article is more concerned with the ethical implications of necromancy than a scientific specification, we should be fine.

I acknowledge that the specification of technology that allows necromancy, the ownership of that technology, and the overall circumstances of the kind of world that would have this technology are relevant. What if only powerful individuals could decide who to resurrect? What necromancy was democratized? Let’s brush these questions aside for now.

Preventing death vs. undoing death

The case for necromancy is simple: death is (generally) bad. A central endeavor of humanity has been averting deaths; treating diseases, reducing violent crime, and ending wars are considered morally good chiefly because they mitigate human deaths. How then, is resurrecting the dead any morally different from preventing their death in the first place? Let’s refer to the view that this is a meaningful distinction as Prevention-Necromancy Distinctionism (PND).

One argument for PND is that necromancy necessarily occurs without the consent of the dead. A dead man can’t consent to his resurrection. In contrast, many forms of death prevention are consensual. Hospital patients consent to medical treatment. A driver elects to wear their seat belt and drive cautiously. Even if someone’s death is prevented without their consent/intention, it’s not usually so bad. For example, suppose a man is drowning on a beach and a lifeguard saves him without his consent. The man curses out the lifeguard, screaming that he specifically wanted the lifeguard not to save him. Such cases, often associated with suicide, are in the minority of cases where one person prevents the death of another. Furthermore, the victims in these scenarios may experience a shift in values. Maybe the man decides in retrospect that he’s grateful for the lifeguard.

You might object that a resurrected person could similarly grow to feel grateful for their resurrection. That’s true. However, the man who was against the lifeguard saving his life could decide to drown himself in the beach again—of his own accord—and achieve his desires. If a resurrected person killed themselves, there’s no guarantee that the living will respect their wishes. If you morally prioritize agency, you should believe in PND; necromancers can ignore the wishes of the dead. If you’re morally paternalistic (you do what you think is morally best regardless of the wishes of those affected) you might not believe in PND; the wishes of the dead, one of the main distinctions between death prevention and necromancy, are morally immaterial.

There’s also a utilitarian argument for PND. Some causes of death are painful, like terminal illness. Suppose an individual is presaged to suffer a painful car crash and you have two options:

  1. Prevent the crash. The person dies later of natural causes.

  2. Allow the crash. The person is resurrected afterwards and dies at the same time of the same natural causes.

Clearly, the second option is more painful and otherwise identical. Therefore, according to utilitarianism, the first option is superior.

The scourge of immortality

A strong argument for/against necromancy is that it prolongs the human lifespan. If you believe this is morally consequential, then this is further evidence of PND. To some, it feels wrong that a human could theoretically live forever. Our society teaches us that death is an inevitable aspect of the human condition that forces us to cherish our fleeting lives. Be that as it may, most of us morally value the extension of human life. Some of us would agree that, if we could press a button to increase life expectancy by 10 years, it’s moral to do so. This “button” is really not so proverbial; medical research is but one manifestation of this button.

A simple induction argument arises. If it’s moral to increase human life expectancy by 10 years, why not another 10 years? And another. And another. And another. Endless generations of family and friends would remain connected. Human skill—the ability the improve the prosperity of society—could grow without end. It’s a utilitarian or population ethicist's dream.4 Alternatively, necromancy as a way of extending human life could see diminishing returns. At some point, the gains to human capital and social connectivity could plateau. Simultaneously, a growing lack of urgency and purpose could exceed the welfare gains (and by extension the utilitarian merit) from necromancy.

Alternate specifications

Thus far, our discussion was built upon the definition of necromancy as essentially a resource-free method of enabling the dead to resume their lives before the cause of death. Does tampering with my definition of necromancy have moral ramifications? Kind of.

What if necromancy resurrected the dead as babies who retained none of their memories? Then necromancy is effectively the restoration of specific genetic combination as opposed to a restoration of the person. Unless you’re an absolute hereditarian, the resurrected person will develop into a significantly different individual under their new environment. To the extent that genetics are an adequate signal of human potential, is it ethical to resurrect a promising human corpse in lieu of adoption or conceiving a child?5

What if necromancy could only be performed a limited number of times? If you believe that the world will improve in expectation over time, then you should resurrected someone later rather than sooner, as it gives them a better life (in expectation). If you believe in the hinge of history hypothesis and you believe the person to be net positive value to society, you should resurrect them now, as this allows society to produce more value from the hinge of history. A limited number of “lives” could also imply that only the “final life,” the state where the resurrected individual can never be resurrected again, is of moral relevance.

What if we could resurrect non-human organisms? We would likely morally prioritize the resurrection of humans. The resurrection of animals could be unethical if the animals live net painful lives. We could see bioterrorists resurrect old plagues. We could also see the restoration of blighted crops. Given that non-human organisms are typically afforded less moral patienthood than humans, the possibilities that arise from non-human necromancy are even more expansive.

Conclusion

I’ve focused this discussion on the ethical implications of necromancy without speculating on sociopolitical implications. The potential sociopolitical consequences of necromancy introduce an endless rabbit hole of moral conundrums. I could see someone writing a comprehensive speculative fiction on a version of our world with necromancy.6

Here are just some of the questions we can ask:

  1. What if access to necromancy was unequal?

  2. What kinds of people would humans choose to resurrect?

  3. How would humans treat the resurrected? To what extent could they resume their lives? Would we see an “apartheid” of the resurrected and humans who have never died?

  4. How would the law and/or sociocultural norms influence the wishes of the dead? Could the dead specify in a will that they don’t wish to be resurrected?

Necromancy is a philosophically profound topic that forces us to wrangle with the nature of life and death itself. In the event that we see the dead come back to us, we’ll find ourselves asking: what are the ethics of necromancy?

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

This is a pop cultural definition. In ancient times, necromancy was the practice of attempting to communicate with the spirits of the dead. It was used for divination, among other things.

2

I don’t think organisms have an “exact instant of death” when passing. Just think of the instant of death as some moment in time soon before the cavalcade of biological processes that accompany death, such as cellular death and rigor mortis.

3

I realize that we can’t always delineate an adverse health condition from a cause of death. Comorbidity is a real phenomenon, and so my specification of necromancy isn’t actually that precise.

4

There are plenty of potential adverse consequences to immortality as well. This discussion is limited to the ethics of necromancy, however—not the sociopolitical realities it could induce.

5

Necromancy could be weaponized as a form of eugenics. It feels like all philosophical roads lead back to eugenics.

6

The Scythe trilogy by Neil Shusterman explores a world where humans born after certain technological innovations can effectively be resurrected from any death. However, individuals who died long ago are forever dead. There are so many angles to take in a fictional exploration of necromancy.

item.title: Baahubali: The Retrospective
item.description: a revisitation of the Tollywood icon
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic status: I’m not very knowledgeable about Hinduism. Please let me know if I get something wrong.

Baahubali is a Telugu film duology directed by S. S. Rajamouli that became massively popular in the Indian community. The films, set in ancient India, tell the story of the titular legend Amarendra Baahubali and the kingdom of Mahishmati. Known for its influences from Hindu epics, its breathtaking action scenes, and its palpable drama, it remains a perennial favorite among Indian films.

This is a full retrospective on Baahubali: its cultural significance, its themes, its influence on me, praise, critique, factoids, and anything more I can contribute to the lacking discourse surrounding these films I hold so dear. The beginning of this article contains minor spoilers for the story. I’ll issue a warning for major spoilers partway through the article. Everything that proceeds that warning assumes familiarity with Baahubali: The Beginning and Baahubali 2: The Conclusion. I recommend watching both films after reading the beginning section of this article (if you haven’t already). If you have seen both films, I hope you’ll rewatch them with insights from this article.

I should issue some disclaimers to anyone who isn’t familiar with Tollywood (the Telugu film industry) films.

First, like many Tollywood films (especially older ones), Baahubali: The Beginning depicts the protagonist’s relationship with his love interest problematically; their romance is creepy, perverse, and downright downright undermines the themes of the story. There’s also an item song (a song containing raunchy fanservice). If terribly written romances and/or fanservice ruins films for you, then you’ve been warned. Thankfully, romance is a fairly minor aspect of the original film and is handled far better in the second.

Second, neither film is available in its original language—Telugu—on any popular American streaming services. I begrudgingly rewatched the original movie in Hindi and its sequel in Malayalam when introducing it to a non-Telugu friend a few months ago. It’s sort of like watching an iconic anime in Chinese; someone with no knowledge of Japanese wouldn’t mind, but native speakers will notice the loss of beauty in translation.

Finally, many people (including me) find the sequel much more enjoyable than the first film. If the first film isn’t quite doing it for you, the sequel may change your mind. In fact, much of my praise of Baahubali is directed at the sequel.

The Significance of Baahubali

Baahubali: The Beginning quickly became a cultural sensation within the Telugu community. It grossed about 600 crore INR (about $130 million adjusted for inflation), making it the 23rd highest grossing movie Indian movie.1 It’s the kind of number that you can just feel. For context, films are a major aspect of Indian culture. Especially Telugu culture. I’ve seen some Telugu movies here and there, but it’s not often my parents drag me to the movie theater to see one. And when they do, I know I’m in for either one of the best or worst movies I’ve seen—no in-between. I didn’t even know what Baahubali was when my mom took me to see it in 3rd grade during its debut. But the three hours I spent in that theater showing were more entrancing than most. I left the theater unable to verbalize how exhilarating it was for me. I probably spent the next week agonizing over the prospect of waiting two years for the sequel.

Then, one weekend in 5th grade, the sequel released. Once again, I left the theater mesmerized and speechless. The sequel was everything I could have hoped for and more. It was all any of us could talk about for weeks. When I returned to school on Monday, my friends and I (almost all of us Telugu-American), immediately asked each the same question: “Did you see it?” Once again, you could just feel the commercial success without looking at the numbers. The film grossed about 1800 crore INR (about $372 million in 2026 dollars), making it the 2nd highest grossing Indian film at the time.2 Even today, a mere mention of Baahubali is enough to make many Telugu-Americans ecstatic.

Prior to Baahubali, it was rare for a South Indian film to find popularity outside of its home state. It was primarily Hindi movies that saw nationwide popularity. Baahubali’s success in non-Telugu states (thanks in part to its dub in several Indian languages) proved to South Indian filmmakers that stories are borderless. Perhaps the best example of this is RRR (also directed by Rajamouli), which enjoyed massive popularity not only across India, but worldwide. RRR was the first and only Indian feature film to win an academy award. Baahubali sprinted so RRR could run.

The Themes of Baahubali

Unfortunately, the discourse surrounding Baahubali lacks depth. The films explore their themes with an unacknowledged profoundness. Those who enjoyed the films point to its heart-pounding action scenes and inspirations from Hindu mythology.3 But these aspects of the franchise are only so compelling thanks to deliberate artistic choices and a deep understanding of its themes.

Dharma

The story, like Hindu epics, explores dharma, the Hindu notion of "duty” or “righteousness.” Hinduism reifies dharma in strict moral codes individuals must strive to uphold. Dharma is upheld with extreme austerity in Hindu mythology and those who disobey it, well-intentioned or otherwise, typically face grave repercussions. In Baahubali, Amarendra Baahubali believes that it’s a warrior’s dharma to keep his word. Without getting into spoilers, he honorably upholds his dharma; the antagonists, on the other hand, lack such probity.

It’s important to note that dharma transcends a traditional dichotomy of good and evil; a good person can defy dharma and an evil person can embrace it.4 Ancient conceptions of dharma are also difficult to reconcile with today’s social mores. Indeed, some have argued that the traditional concept of dharma endorses casteism, patriarchy, and/or excessive filial piety. You’ll see throughout this article how Baahubali explores these limitations of dharma as a moral construct.

It’s easy to see how such kinds of moral absolutism, especially within monarchies, beget conflict. Dharma is an ingenious way of imposing unwritten rules on narrative power dynamics. For example, what happens when a character who upholds his dharma is pitted against a scoundrel? What happens when the power structures established under dharma are exploited by such scoundrels? What happens when two characters who each uphold dharma in a different way are in conflict? It’s these kinds of questions that Baahubali portrays with Tollywood’s signature flair. Rajamouli employed dharma to craft a tightly-plotted, dramatically intriguing, and morally complex narrative.

***

THE REST OF THIS ARTICLE CONTAINS MAJOR SPOILERS FOR Baahubali

***

Being A Good Person

The most compelling way that Baahubali explores dharma is by implicitly asking a simple question: what does it mean to be a great person? My answer is Amarendra Baahubali (hereafter, I’ll refer to him as Baahubali and to Mahendra Baahubali as Shiva). Morality is very complex. To some, including me, it lacks any objectivity. Yet there are morals so ecumenical and so commendable that most of us would respect those who exemplify them. Baahubali is such an exemplar. A great person.

He’s kind. He’s so compassionate that he—a member of royalty—socializes with the the common person. He plays with peasant children, brings people flowers, and allows the villagers to feed him meals. He actively improves the lives of his people. For example, when he observes the toil of smashing rocks, he engineers a water wheel that automates the process. Another example is when he saves hostages from the Kalakeya; he refused to let his people die.

It’s no surprise that he was so loved by his people—so loved that they celebrated his exile. Think about that. A guy was so loved that people found happiness in his exile. Usually it’s notorious people whose exile is celebrated. There’s a scene from the first film that sticks with me (as many scenes do). Shiva assists slaves in hoisting up a golden statue of Bhallaladeva. A gust of wind briefly lifts the cloth disguising his face. A slave next to him whispers the name “Baahubali” and the whisper becomes a loud chant. A dead man’s name simultaneously evokes enormous fear into Bhallaladeva and unprecedented hope among the people. Baahubali’s non-diegetic statue is as tall as his character is virtuous—dwarfing Bhallaladeva’s statue.

Baahubali never fails to uplift the people around him. He sees strength in everyone—both literally and figuratively. He taught self-effacing cow herders in Kunthala to steer cows into the invading bandits. And a small kingdom fended off an army of untold size. While in exile, he taught young boys wrestling. And a seemingly weak boy pinned down a kid who previously trounced him. He taught Devasena how to shoot multiple arrows from a bow. He taught Kumara Varma, a spineless coward, remarkable courage in the face of adversity.5

What I respect most about Baahubali is his willingness to challenge social norms. During Devasena’s trial in court, he rebukes Sivagami despite norms of filial piety and laws of subservience to the queen mother. Baahubali also refuses to sacrifice the blood of an innocent buffalo before the battle against the Kalakeyas6, instead sacrificing his own in the ritual. It’s a bold, inauspicious decision.7 A particularly emotional showcase of Baahubali’s moral bravery was how he treated Kattappa. It was beyond taboo for a prince in the ostensibly casteist culture of Mahishmati to socialize with a slave—much less deem him an uncle. Yet Baahubali was willing to see beyond maxims of caste-based discrimination.

Baahubali exudes “aura” in virtually every way a character can: he’s a brilliant strategist, a consummate warrior, and a paragon of virtue. You’d think it would get to his head. But it never does. A humble man, he never demeans others, abuses his power, or thinks too highly of himself. I remember thinking as a kid that Baahubali could only behave be so virtuous because he was such an accomplished person. I was naive. Baahubali would’ve likely been a great person even if he was an incompetent peasant. Although it’s true that our circumstances shape us, Baahubali exemplifies how we can choose to be better people than our circumstances might portend.

Baahubali’s Flaws

I’ve heard a criticism that Baahubali is “too perfect.”8 I disagree. His virtuous character traits backfired numerous times. For instance, he insists on keeping his word (a warrior’s dharma). This radical deontological belief enables Bhallaladeva and Bijaladeva to plot his downfall. Namely, Sivagami forces him to choose between marrying Devasena and becoming king. Baahubali relinquishes his promised throne in order to honor his vow to marry Devasena. I don’t consider Baahubali’s decision (in my view a blunder) a fault of the writing. Rather, it’s a lesson that both moral absolutism and a lack of morals carry flaws.

His excessive trust of Bhallaladeva and Sivagami is another weakness that leads to his demise.9 Sivagami’s pride leaves her susceptible to Bijaladeva’s manipulation, leading to a cascade of unjust decisions in favor of her biological son. For example, she attempts to coerce Devasena into marrying Bhallaladeva. Baahubali could’ve plausibly mounted a coup against Bhallaladeva and Sivagami; his near-unanimous support within the populace allowed him to circumvent the law if he wanted to. His love for his mother and disaffinity for chicanery left Mahishmati in the throes of a tyrant. It’s a tragic paradox that Baahubali’s pure heart—a vulnerability that was heavily exploited—is precisely what makes him a great king.

An Ideal

Despite his flaws, Baahubali is about as great a person as I can ever hope to be. He has continued to serve as my role model. His image has persisted through my extensive personal growth and my ever-accumulating moral uncertainties. He has helped me reinforce life lessons as simple as “be kind to others” in times when I almost strayed from them. I wouldn’t be the person I am today without Baahubali.

And to continue to become a better person, I’ll keep learning from him. That’s because Baahubali (the character and the films) teach timeless lessons.

He teaches us to seek cooperation over competition. A regrettable aspect of Asian culture is that we’re ineluctably conditioned to compare ourselves to each other. We compare grades in school. College applications results in high school. Internship results in college. Jobs, money, and family afterwards. The comparison is endless. It engenders fiercely competitive, envious, selfish, and deceitful behavior. I’ve met no shortage of people who develop an ego as a coping mechanism. Sound familiar? Bhallaladeva personifies the toxicity that stems from an overlay competitive mindset.

In contrast, Baahubali personifies what we can choose to be. We can choose to help others instead of competing with them. We can humbly celebrate the accomplishments of others rather than harboring envy or scorn. We can choose honesty over artifice. Life may incentivize us to defect against such values. But I’ve found that the people who excuse their reprehensible behavior usually have more of a choice than they think.10

The Nature of Power

Power structures are fascinating. Political power does not “exist” in a physical sense. Yet a king’s word could kill thousands. Charisma and political consensus can turn an army against existing rulers. And no individual, no matter how physically powerful, can defeat a major military organization.

Baahubali explores the nature of power compellingly (albeit not in an especially novel way). Namely, it illustrates the unintuitive ramifications of power structures that are not so divorced from those of today.

Kattappa was deemed a slave due to his pedigree as opposed to his behavior. He was a competent leader and likely a more suitable king than Sivagami or Bhallaladeva. He’s nonetheless consigned to the military and impressively rose to the status of general. However, as antiquated power structures would have it, a slave is forbidden the political power of royalty. Kattappa’s influence was fettered. What a shame.

Bijaladeva has few qualities that merit his royal status. Though charismatic, he’s also bitter, resentful, prideful, unscrupulous, etc. This pathetic excuse of a person was at the helm of Mahishmati, manipulating this wife and grooming his son to usurp the throne.11 Unfortunately, he’s easily likened to real world politicians.

Sivagami is not a very meritorious leader. She’s also prideful, gullible, temperamental, and disloyal. Yet her decisions govern so many people. She’s also easily likened to real world politicians.

Mahishmati’s laws—particularly its extreme concentration of power in Sivagami—enable Bhallaladeva to seize the throne from Baahubali. What kind of power structure enables a megalomaniacal, envious, egotistical, vindictive scum to rule a polity instead of a demonstrably superior candidate? It’s easy to laugh at historical power structures, but our modern political institutions are not much less guilty than Mahishmati’s. The kingdom’s power structure is so ludicrous that Bhallaladeva becomes king (and remains so for years) despite the following:

  1. The people of Mahishmati almost unanimously favor Baahubali.

  2. The incumbent ruler, Sivagami, originally declared Baahubali the new king.

  3. Bhallaladeva treats the populace horribly.

It’s so ridiculous that it makes modern democracy look almost picturesque by comparison.

Indeed, the nature of power in Baahubali is rife with contradictions that illuminate those of our own political climate.

Miscellaneous

I wanted to discuss a miscellany of thoughts I had on Baahubali, including but not limited to: praise, criticism, analysis, and factoids.

Praise

The action scenes are highly inventive. Characters wield unorthodox weaponry and tactics. The examples abound:

  • Bhallaladeva’s “lawnmower chariot” that rams through the Kalakeyas

  • The chains Shiva wraps around his fists in the final fight

  • The “flaming tarps” launched on the Kalakeyas

  • The cows with flaming horns that charge against the Pindari bandits

  • Baahubali using the metal lion head from his chariot to bludgeon the Kalakeya chief

  • Kattappa using a large panel as a revolving gateway (can’t remember the context)

  • The trident formation employed against the Kalakeyas’ vastly superior numbers

  • The trees used in the final battle to catapult soldiers, who form their shields into a ring that braces them for impact12

  • Baahubali commanding his battalion to throw bolas at Kalakeya hostages. This caused said hostages to fall to the ground, leaving their captors susceptible to a volley of arrows.

  • Baahubali knocking down a tree in a precise position that crushed Pindari bandits while avoiding Kattappa. This was during their first fight against the Pindaris.

  • Baahubali throwing an entire chariot at Pindaris

  • Bhallaladeva attempting to hang Shiva by the neck using a chain

  • Bhallaladeva’s detachable gada (an Indian mace)

  • Kattappa throwing Shiva a sword while he’s midair. This occurs at the end of the final battle between Shiva and Bhallaladeva.

  • Shiva crafting a makeshift grappling hook from twigs and rope while climbing his childhood mountain

  • Shiva using part of a tree as a sled to help him and Avantika escape from Mahishmati soldiers during an avalanche

  • Kattappa and Baahubali passing a hatchet between each other during their first encounter with the Pindaris

Action scenes this creative—common in anime, manga, and video games—feel rare in the film industry. The expectation of generic action scenes in films presents an opportunity to astound viewers with more inventive action.

The aforementioned examples seldom feel contrived13, despite how brazenly they defy the laws of physics.14 This is because Rajamouli foreshadows and communicates action through simple visual language.15 Let’s examine the scene during the final battle where Shiva uses palm trees to launch rebel forces over Mahishmati’s walls. This could’ve easily felt like a deus ex machina. Instead, it’s an awesome tactic willing a reasonable suspension of disbelief. There are a few reasons for this:

  1. The ability to bend and release palm trees like a spring was foreshadowed during the song Dandaalayya (see here). Baahubali discovers that he can use the trees to catapult water. It tacitly establishes to the viewer a rule that trees (in this universe) can function this way.

  2. The tactic is intuitive. The rationale is as follows: 1) It’s possible to bend objects 2) Some objects are elastic—they recoil when pressure is applied. 3) The more force you apply to an elastic object, the stronger the recoil. 4) Therefore, a bent tree can catapult a group of soldiers. Even though it’s physically impossible for a small group of soldiers to bend a tree like this, let alone sustain the fall with their shields, there’s sufficient intuition behind it.

  3. The tactic isn’t excessively convenient. By this point in the battle, Shiva had faced significant setbacks; Bhallaladeva kidnapped Devasena and greatly outnumbered their forces. Furthermore, the ability to launch the rebel forces over the wall doesn’t trivialize the final battle; Shiva still has to defeat Bhallaladeva. Moreover, it took ingenuity for Shiva to discover the tactic. Thus, the tactic feels earned rather than contrived.

  4. It’s just plain cool.

Even if Baahubali was little more than its fights—a claim I’ve vehemently contested—that’s no pejorative. Visual language, narrative context, coolness, ingenuity, and intuitiveness all play a vital role in its action scenes. Creating good fights is its own form of mastery.

A similar mastery of film is evident in how the sequel builds tension. Once Baahubali and Devasena arrive in Mahishmati—about halfway through the film—a cascade of drama ensues. Something is constantly happening: a consequential dialogue, an emotional scene, a character death, etc. The events naturally lead into each other in the culmination of everything. These scenes were so suspenseful they made me feel like I was standing on a tightrope. They immerse you so heavily that Baahubali’s downfall evokes genuine rage and distress.

I can’t forget to praise the soundtrack. The main songs—the ones in the style of a music video—are iconic, poetic, and magnificent. While I could sing the praises of several of the main songs, I want to focus on a particular line from “Dandaalayya” (see here). The chorus sings:

Nee maate ma maatayya (నీ మాటే మా మాటయ్యా)

Nee choope shaasanamayya (నీ చూపే శాసనమయ్యా)

This roughly translates to:

Your word is my word.

What you show me is law.

In other words, the people of Mahishmati recognize Baahubali as their true ruler even in exile. Their reverence is deep and sincere. During the song, a drum plays in the pause between the two lines, further enhancing dramatic effect.

The background music is as outstanding as the main songs. Its leitmotifs stand out to me in particular. The melody of “Nippule Swasaga” echoes in “Stoned Heart.” The former plays when Kattappa reunites with Shiva in the first film. The old man slides onto his knees in reverence, touching Shiva’s foot to his forehead. In contrast, the latter plays during the second film, when Kattappa backstabs16 Baahubali. You know an OST is good when it immerses you in the tone of its scene. I can’t listen to “Stoned Heart” without suffering the painful sting of Kattappa’s betrayal.

My favorite OST has got to be “The Savior.” It plays at the beginning of the sequel, when Baahubali arrives to subdue an elephant terrorizing the kingdom. The legendary chant “heyssa rudrassa” plays in variations throughout the sequel, inducing goosebumps without fail. But nowhere is it as sublime as in “The Savior.” The way the clarion horns and pounding drums lead up to the chant is intense. More intense is the rawness of the chant, which alternates between an individual singer and a chorus. I’ve come to think of the “heyssa rudrassa” chants as “the aura farming song.” Whenever the chant plays, it’s like the movie is telling you “Baahubali may be a human, but he’s also a force of nature.”

Criticism

Baahubali is not without its flaws. I’ll first address its gravest offense: its depiction of Avantika. The young warrior is introduced as a fierce, independent woman willing to fight for the rebel forces despite gender norms. After meeting Shiva, she’s reduced to his love interest. I’m not even exaggerating. She literally entrusts her dream—her greatest purpose—to Shiva, a man she’s just met. Never mind that Shiva is a predator.

Here are some of Shiva’s questionable behaviors:

  1. He’s unreasonably obsessed with a mask he finds at the peak of his childhood mountain. Shiva is able to sculpt Avantika’s face in sand before ever seeing her. I It’s difficult to take seriously and kind of creepy.

  2. He paints a tattoo on her arm without her consent or awareness. He does so by unleashing an (albeit harmless) snake onto her arm. The rebel forces interpret her tattoo as a focus on her beauty over their own cause.

  3. He forcibly undresses and gropes Avantika while she is trying to kill him.17 She’s visibly uncomfortable and communicates no consent. Somehow, she’s in love with Shiva by the end of the ordeal.

The first film doesn’t portray these behaviors as problematic. It suffers from Tollywood’s perverse view of romance. Baahubali: The Beginning distorts a relationship of a predator and a victim into a romantic one where a warrior teaches a woman to embrace her femininity. I would rather believe that industry standards corrupted Rajamouli’s vision for their relationship than that he was oblivious to the horrors of this “romance.”18

Fortunately, the sequel rectifies its portrayal of romance. Baahubali and Devasena have a much healthier relationship. It’s consensual and doesn’t strip Devasena of her agency as a character. While Devasena does eventually lose agency as a character, this is more to do with the fall of Mahishmati than a fault of the writing.19 Baahubali’s behavior before confessing to Devasena is silly and awkward, but not very creepy.

Another criticism I have of the first film is that its plot is clunky. Events lead into each other haphazardly and in ways inconsistent with character motivations. Let me unpack the main plot of the first movie:

  1. Shiva spends his childhood doggedly attempting to climb a mountain.

  2. Shiva succeeds, discovering a mask that drives his obsession with Avantika.

  3. Shiva saves Avantika. She tells him about her goal of liberating Mahishmati. He undertakes this Herculean task.

  4. Shiva rescues Devasena. Kattappa’s forces pursue him.

  5. Kattappa reveals his connection to Shiva. He begins telling Shiva the story of Amarendra Baahubali.

I’ve already explained how silly the second point is. The third point is especially ridiculous. Shiva takes on the goal of a random woman he’s suddenly infatuated with. He’s willing to risk his life to rescue his biological mother and liberate Mahishmati from Bhallaladeva. Bear in mind that Devasena is effectively a stranger to him and Mahishmati is effectively a foreign kingdom. Shiva’s spontaneous change in motive is a plot contrivance.

I hope by now that I don’t need to elaborate on how lackluster Shiva is as a character. There’s a reason I’ve spent much more of this article extolling his father.

I have a list of other minor criticisms:

  1. Bijaladeva survives the final battle. This undercuts Shiva’s triumph; Bijaladeva can still connive if he’s alive. It also undercuts the theme of good prevailing over evil. Why not have Kattappa kill Bijaladeva during the final battle? This could’ve been a pivotal moment in Kattappa’s character arc of learning where his loyalties truly lie. What makes this choice less egregious is that Bijaladeva is likely stripped of his political power after Shiva’s coronation.

  2. Sometimes the action scenes, particularly in the first movie, require too much suspension of disbelief. Shiva’s makeshift tools, such as the sled he fashions from a tree during the avalanche, feel contrived. We also see Shiva dominate in combat, despite a lack of combat experience. I guess free soloing counts as combat experience?

  3. The Persian sword merchant, Aslam Khan, never reappears. He lost a duel to Kattappa and subsequently offered to buy his freedom. Imagine if the rebel forces in the final battle were joined by Aslam Khan or equipped with Persian weapons. The actor for Aslam Khan is Kannadiga and not Telugu. It seems he was more of a guest appearance than a serious character. Perhaps Rajamouli was unable to hire him for the sequel.

  4. During the song “Pacha Bottasi,” Avantika becomes more fair-skinned and her hair turns brown. It’s a colorist20 implication and perhaps an insinuation that Western women are prettier.

  5. The Kalakeyas have dark skin and use “click” sounds in their language. They have a pre-battle ritual where they offer blood to a monstrous skull that presumably represents their God. Mahishmati offers blood to Kali during their version of the ritual. The Kalakeyas are barbaric and unsophisticated. There are some potentially problematic implications of this: 1) The bad guys have darker skin 2) Deities from “heretic” religions are bad 3) The bad guys are African stereotypes (their unsophistication, their skin, the sound of their language). The second and third implications feel like a bit of a stretch to me, but the first is hard to unsee.

Cool Details

I’m gonna rapid fire some cool details throughout the films:

  • During Baahubali’s childhood, Sivagami bequeaths him and Bhallaladeva each their first sword. Bhallaladeva immediately unsheathes and brandishes the sword. It could be interpreted as foreshadowing of his callousness towards violence, but it’s more likely childlike excitement. In contrast, Baahubali bows and touches his mother’s feet when accepting the sword. It emphasizes not that Bhallaladeva is immature, but that Baahubali displays extraordinary maturity for his age. I’ve not often seen children exhibit such gratitude.21

  • During Baahubali’s childhood, he saves Sivagami from a scorpion, tanking its painful sting. How does his mother repay his loyalty? By exiling him and ordering his assassination. In a sense, Baahubali’s loyalty to his mother led him to get “stung” many times again.

  • Baahubali displays numerous times that he’s able to detect or anticipate attacks from behind; he deflects arrows and stabs warriors behind him without turning around. Yet, Kattappa is able to stab him in the back. I have two theories for this: 1) Baahubali let his guard down because he didn’t register Kattappa as a threat. 2) Baahubali knew Kattappa was about to stab him. He assumed Kattappa had a suitable justification and accepted his death.

  • Shiva’s labor of carrying the Shiva Lingam to a waterfall saves his life in the final battle. Disarmed and bleeding from the chest, he uses the Vibuti (sacred ash) coating a nearby Shiva Lingam as a salve.22 This “second wind” imbues him with the strength to win. I want to believe that Shiva (the Hindu deity) himself helped Mahendra Baahubali in exchange for his religious devotion.

  • Baahubali is a much needed modernization of Hindu mythology. First, Baahubali doesn’t espouse the same questionable beliefs of many of his inspirations (Rama, Krishna, Arjuna, etc.). He would likely decry Agni Pariksha. He lacks the hubris and the casteism of the Pandavas.23 In general, his morals are more progressive. Second, the characters behave much more believably than in Hindu mythology. Mythological characters typically have absolutist motivations and thus behave in radical ways. A soldier might declare fealty to their king by cutting off their finger, for instance. The characters in Baahubali also exhibit extreme behavior, but it feels far more human.

  • During the final battle, Bhallaladeva launches Shiva into the same golden statue that he hoisted up. It’s symbolic of how Bhallaladeva’s own orders (for slaves to hoist up the statue) led his regime to crumble (represented as Shiva’s body destroying the statue).

  • The title of the song “Oka Pranam” translates to "one life.” It putatively refers to Baahubali’s life, though it can also refer to Shiva’s life.

  • Shiva defeats Bhallaladeva by weaponizing chains,24 a symbol of the tyrant’s oppression. It’s symbolic of how Bhallaladeva’s actions come back to bite him.

Reincarnation Theory

It’s implied that Shiva is a reincarnation of Baahubali. Shiva is born almost immediately after Baahubali dies. Although Shiva and Baahubali have vastly different personalities, Shiva is inexplicably skilled in combat and strategy. Shiva is also unreasonably sympathetic to the rebel cause and strangely protective of Devasena. I interpret this as residual qualities from his past life.

The strongest evidence appears in the final battle. After Kattappa implores Shiva to think like his father, his demeanor suddenly shifts. A wayward, intrepid young man becomes a consummate military strategist. He devises the idea to use nearby trees as catapults—the same idea Baahubali once used to launch water.

When Shiva leaps into the air before administering his final blow to Bhallaladeva, lightning illuminates his non-diegetic figure in sky. You can interpret this in one of two ways: 1) Bhallaladeva likens Shiva to Baahubali 2) Bhallaladeva realizes that Shiva is a reincarnation of his father.

The look Shiva and Bhallaladeva give each other at the end of their duel confirms the theory for me. It communicates so much with so little:

  1. Bhallaladeva is grizzled. He’s aged considerably since he usurped the throne. In contrast, Shiva looks just like Baahubali did before his death. Bhallaladeva seems to recognize not only that they look identical, but that Shiva is literally a reincarnation of Baahubali.

  2. The look Shiva gives Bhallaladeva feels very personal. It doesn’t say “you’re an awful person I’ve only known for a few days.” It says: “I know the kind of person you truly are. I know what you’ve done. To me. My wife. My people. You’re done.” It’s a quiet rage that only a deep interpersonal history can produce.

  3. Shiva wears similar earrings to Baahubali and wields his sword.

  4. This detail is unrelated to the theory. The sword hilt, the emblem of Mahishmati, faces Shiva instead of Bhallaladeva. This is indeed the correct orientation of the emblem. It visually reinforces that Shiva (effectively Baahubali) is the rightful king.

  5. Another detail unrelated to the theory: Shiva kills Bhallaladeva himself while looking him in the eyes. In contrast, Bhallaladeva cowardly orders Kattappa to kill Baahubali.

  6. Another detail unrelated to the theory: Shiva’s necklace is a modest thread, while Bhallaladeva’s is a golden necklace.

There’s not enough evidence to conclusively accept or reject the reincarnation theory. However, I still consider it my headcanon because it enhances the final battle and explains Shiva’s strange character motivations.

Kattappa’s Loyalty

Kattappa is simultaneously loyal and treacherous. It’s ironically his conflicting loyalties that lead to his treachery. The man views himself as nothing more than a lowly slave who is therefore obligated to serve the throne obediently. His duties lead him to serve Baahubali, a boy so inspiring that his loyalties begin to shift. The only time Kattappa ever disobeys a royal command, barring the final battle, is when he’s ordered to assassinate Baahubali. The only time. That’s powerful to me.

After refusing to kill Baahubali, he instructs Sivagami to behead him for his disobedience. Sivagami, in turn, warns Kattappa that she’ll assassinate Baahubali herself if he doesn’t follow through. Only then does Kattappa agree. The complexity of Kattappa’s arc is that it’s unclear what his duty truly is. What constitutes loyalty to the throne? Is it merely obedience of the incumbent monarch or service in favor of the “rightful” ruler? Kattappa learns to think of loyalty as the latter kind. In my eyes, he redeems himself via his contributions to the final battle.

Some More Cool Things

  • Kumara Varma is popular in Japan. I’m not entirely sure why. It seems that Japanese audiences preferred the realism in Kumara Varma’s initial cowardice to the large than life qualities of other Baahubali characters. In fact, the Japanese audience supposedly requested Subbaraju (Kumara Varma’s actor) to visit their country (over Prabhas himself). Here's a cool video of the Japanese audience cheering for Kumara Varma.

  • Much like Amarendra Baahubali, the franchise lives on. Baahubali: The Eternal War, two feature-length animated films, were announced to release. The films boast stunning Arcane-esque visuals and follow Baahubali into the afterlife, where he’ll play a role in the conflict between the Devas and the Asuras. Though I’m tempering my expectations, I can see a few reasons to get excited:

    • It’s an opportunity for Indian animation studios to reach the mainstream. Unfortunately, the state of animation in India is lackluster.25 This film, produced in collaboration between Indian and international studios, is hope for Indian animation. Think of all the amazing animated projects that have come out the US, Japan, and (more recently) China. Imagine experiencing such projects through India.

    • The trailer is genuinely some of the most gorgeous animation I’ve ever seen. The fight choreography. The VFX. The vibrant colors. You have to watch it.

    • While I’m not familiar with the conflict between the Devas and the Asuras in Hindu mythology, I hope this story will once again use Baahubali’s character to explore dharma. An oversimplistic tale of good and evil would grossly misunderstand the franchise.
