  • Baahubali never takes an explicit stance on the existence of God/religion, allowing for multiple interpretations of the story.26 One interpretation is that it’s a quintessential Hindu tale of the triumph of good over evil. If God exists in the Baahubali universe, maybe he influenced its world such that good (Shiva) would ultimately triumph. A more secular interpretation is that Hinduism is merely the cultural context for the characters’ behavior.

  • Sivuni Aaana is so iconic that some Telugu people jokingly associate it with carrying heavy objects overhead. One of my favorite examples of this is the spoof “Bagbali.”

  • “Dheevara” is so iconic that some Telugu people jokingly associate it with jumping long distances or taking a leap of faith.

  • Each character in Baahubali has a unique symbol between their eyebrows. I wonder what these symbols mean.

Conclusion

There’s not much more for me to say. I’ve poured so many of my thoughts into writing regarding this beautiful piece of art. If you haven’t watched Baahubali before this article, I hope I convinced you to give it a try. If you haven’t watched it in a while, I hope I’ve convinced you to revisit it. And whether you deem it nothing more than Tollywood action slop or a masterpiece, I hope I’ve sparked some level of passion or rumination for this beloved franchise.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe to receive new posts and support my work.

1

All earnings statistics are sourced from here. Keep in mind that movie theater tickets are much cheaper in India than in the US. Also, Telugu movies are primarily watched in the Indian states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh and the Telugu diaspora. The Telugu community is collectively estimated to be about 100 million people. This is a more niche audience then you’re typical Hollywood blockbuster.

2

Its 2nd place spot was usurped by Dhurandhar: The Revenge some months ago. The highest grossing Indian film as of the time of writing is Dangal, likely due to its unprecedented box office success in China.

3

The director, S.S. Rajamouli, was a major fan of Hindu mythology since his childhood. Fascinatingly, despite these evident influences in his work, he’s an atheist.

4

I’m not a moral realist, so I use the terms “good” and “evil” here loosely.

5

An honorable mention of how Baahubali uplifted others: During the battle against the Kalakeyas, he gives his demoralized battalion a motivational speech. He essentially tells them that death is not losing one’s life, but losing courage.

6

I’ve been thinking about the moral patienthood of the Kalakeyas. Baahubali seems to readily accept their slaughter. I guess it’s not so crazy to retaliate against barbarians of wanton savagery.

7

While it’s arguably hypocritical for Baahubali—presumably a meat eater—to make an exception for the buffalo, I respect his willingness to defy tradition here. The history of moral attitudes towards animals in India is very complex and outside the scope of this article.

8

In Telugu, we have an idiom called “Ramudu Manchi Baludu” (రాముడు మంచి బాలుడు), literally translating to “Ram is a good boy.” It’s like calling someone a golden boy.

9

Bhallaladeva almost killed Baahubali by dropping the rope he was hanging on over a cliff.

10

I know this an oversimplified statement. I don’t feel like getting into all the nuances here.

11

I wonder how Baahubali and Bhallaladeva would have turned out if Bijaladeva raised the former and Sivagami raised the latter. Would their roles have reversed?

12

Some people have calculated the physics behind this. It’s physically impossible, as you’d expect. My dreams have been shattered.

13

Most of the contrivances are in the prequel.

14

As most Indian movies do.

15

This quality is also present in RRR. As I’ve said, Baahubali sprinted so that RRR could run.

16

Both literally and figuratively,

17

This further undermines Avantika’s combat proficiency.

18

There’s lots of evidence that Rajamouli had to pander to fans in the first film and had more creative autonomy in the sequel. First, the songs in the first film do little to progress the plot. The songs in the sequel are more diegetic and hence do more to progress the plot. Second, the songs in the first film follow more conventional Indian film song archetypes. There’s an item song (Manohari) and a song of the hero swooning over the heroine (Dheevara).

19

In fact, you could argue that her eventual loss of agency enhances the social commentary. It shows how insecure people in positions of power, like Bhallaladeva, deprive others of agency.

20

Colorism is discrimination on the basis of skin tone. It’s prevalent throughout India.

21

Children receive care without an expectation of reciprocation. Even with a parent’s inculcation, it can be difficult to feel grateful for what you’ve always had. The few children who feel and show genuine gratitude are usually neglected. In Baahubali’s case, although he wasn’t neglected, he probably recognized Sivagami’s kindness in adopting him (despite having no obligation to do so).

22

Fun fact: Vibuti has antiseptic properties

23

The Pandavas are the protagonists of the Mahabharata. They burnt an innocent low-caste family alive, a detail omitted from many modernizations of the urtext. I’m not sure whether the story’s authors were self-aware of the casteism in the story. Was it propaganda from the upper-caste elites or part of an effort to paint the Pandavas as morally complex characters?

24

Like the “tree catapults,” the use of chains as melee weapons was established when Shiva wields them in the first film.

25

Possible explanations include a lack of funding and/or failure to channel artistic talent.

26

I’ve heard some people interpret Shiva’s “second wind” (when he uses the Vibuti on a Shiva Lingam as a salve) as definitive proof of Hinduism’s legitimacy. I completely disagree. Moreover, this belief undermines the scene. The point of the scene should be that Shiva embraces his roots (his village worshiped Shiva, after all) to regain morale. Whether Shiva truly received a deus ex machina (both literally and figuratively) is moot.

item.title: Divine Knowledge
item.description: a surreal dream
item.content:encoded:
It was weird. I began to feel very euphoric. I laughed more than usual. Frequently. Uncontrollably. With my eyes wide open, like a demonic spirit had possessed me. I remained fully aware of the spirit’s influence over me. I had a choice: suppress the spirit or embrace it and thereby welcome an exotic conscious experience. I chose the latter.

An tingly energy coursed through my body, my brain as its hub. I felt compelled to sprint, dance, and unleash my madness. Out of caution and respect for my friends, I resigned myself to pacing. The spirit found other ways to surface. It began to feel less like a spirit and more like an amalgam of hidden aspects of myself—almost like a Jungian Id.

Various parts of my body—seemingly randomly—would go slightly numb. Only the numbness came with a restlessness; the spirit supercharged parts of my body. I flailed my supercharged left arm around to ease some of the excitement. Then my facial expressions shifted around, as if some puppeteer applied random noise to my facial muscles. My left cheek and the connected half of my mouth would stretch a bit to the side while my right half smiled normally. Sometimes both ends of my mouth would curl up unnaturally. Occasionally, such unnatural facial expressions caused me to laugh in that weird way again.

My friends wanted some quiet. I closed my eyes and slouched on the couch. I saw the burning red humans do when bright light shines on their closed eyes. I tingled. The spirit squirmed around in my body, attempting to leave. Instead, it merged with me. The burning red cooled to a soothing sandy brown. Streaks of glimmering light flitted and danced around. Then there was nothing but dazzling light. My mind ventured deeper into this light with an intense curiosity, as though it beckoned to me. The light faded. I was in an endless white void. In front of me was a large cube spinning on its yaw axis. The cube, sandy brown, glowed with familiar streaks of light.

I immediately recognized the cube. It was the unfathomably source of infinite knowledge. Truths limited to divine comprehension. Not forbidden nor blissful, but utterly mesmerizing. The cube was God itself. I felt like I was calling out to the cube. I implored it to bequeath me divine knowledge. My hand stretched farther and farther towards it. But my efforts were in vain. I faded out of this ethereal realm and back to reality. It was like I had woken up from a lucid dream, only I wasn’t truly asleep. Was the vision a chiefly subconscious construction or more so an attempt of my conscious mind to produce a story? I couldn’t tell. My brain’s creative limiters were removed. There was a world whose story I had to conclude before my brain returned to normal.

—I recommend that you begin listening to Beethoven’s “Moonlight Sonata”—

I closed my eyes again, returning to this surreal world. I clung to a canoe that churned in a turbulent, dark sea. Thunder illuminated the tenebrous clouds in the sky as a torrential downpour battered my raincoat. Ephemeral visions of writing on a notebook appeared in my head. Some interpretations of the visions became available in retrospect. Inside my dreamlike state, was I a writer immersing myself in the story of this man at sea? Was I a writer who was literally sucked into the world of the story? Was I a writer recounting his past experiences? Perhaps none of these interpretations were correct, yet they were my best attempt at coping with the metaphysical complexity that my dreamlike state induced.

The visions of writing faded. I was back to clinging for my life on the canoe. I flitted between viewing myself in first and third-person perspective in my dreamlike state hereafter. I noticed that my appearance was different from reality; all I can recall is that I was a black-haired White man. The ocean continued to buffet my boat. I shouted at the sky. I asked God why he couldn’t share divine knowledge with me. Why was the world so cruel? My screams and sorrows drowned against the endless ocean. It was futile. Or so I thought.

I suddenly found myself in an abstract realm. Around me was nothing but vibrant, iridescent fractals and kaleidoscopic imagery. I was in freefall, flailing around in this bottomless abyss of surrealism. My surroundings grew brighter and brighter, until I found myself free of this nightmare.

But perhaps there is no nightmare more chilling than enlightenment.

I found myself in a familiar, endless white void. My identifying bodily features (my hair, teeth, fingernails, facial features, etc.) were gone. I was reduced to a simple white form—a mannequin—only visible through the faint shadow bordering my figure. The man in front of me was of the same appearance, standing imposingly in front of me. I reflexively prostrated myself before him. He tapped my head, signaling me to stand up. This man exuded an aura no human could hope to replicate. I knew this man. He emanated the same essence as the cube of divine knowledge. The man was a humanoid manifestation of the cube. He was God.

The dialogue we exchanged is difficult to recall verbatim. It was poignant, melancholic, and profound. I pleaded with God once more to offer me divine knowledge. Not out of greed, morbid curiosity, or ego. I had a genuine determination to save my people. Our coastal town—the only verifiable civilization in our universe—was suffering. The town’s Gothic and Victorian structures stood as the last bastion against the endless night and storms. Our people tried our best to eke out a living. It brought us together. But chronic pain plagued us. A pain of spiritual, non-medical origin. The pain arrived in episodes that made us want to die. The episodes became more frequent and severe. My parents succumbed to the pain when I was little, committing suicide. I adopted a young orphan boy as my brother. While the entire town’s pain weighed on me, my brother’s pain particularly disturbed me. Our town’s best researchers discovered that there was only one person who could solve our problems: God.

And so, we return to my conversation with God. I doubt that God exists in our reality. But in this world of my imagination, he was certain to exist. I had to persuade him to help us. God refused repeatedly with a rueful look on his face. It was clear that he wanted to help. I insisted that God tell me the truth. I had to help my people. It’s what my parents (in my dreamlike world) would’ve wanted me to do.

God finally shared the divine knowledge I had sought for so long. The dreamlike world was merely one realm among many others. The area where I freefalled was a pocket of reality within my realm, of God’s creation. The realms were united under a single divine tree—the Yggdrasil. It existed in a black void: the Supreme Reality. Its roots are linked to the realms. Between the roots and their corresponding realms is an interstitial void, the white plane in which I now confronted God. God told me he wasn’t a unique figure. He, like other Gods, was delegated as the steward of a realm. That realm happened to be mine (in the dreamlike world).

But God wasn’t omnipotent. He made catastrophic blunders in his early stewardship of my realm. His blunders cursed us with eternal agony. In fact, he was in more pain than any of us. Much of his conscious sensation was the aggregate conscious experience of the sentient inhabitants of my realm. In other words, our curse of pain afflicted him several-fold. I yelled at him. I excoriated him for subjecting us all to this pain. Unfortunately, he revealed that there was only one way to end the pain: destroy our realm forever.

I demanded that he follow through; euthanasia was far better than an eternity of torture. God turned away once again with the same rueful look. I asked why he couldn’t let us die in peace. He insisted I wouldn’t understand. I screamed at him that he was foolish. He then laid out his rationale: he blundered so heavily in his stewardship of our realm that he insisted on repentance. By keeping our realm alive, he forced upon himself our eternal suffering. It was simultaneously selfish and selfless. Alas, I couldn’t thwart God. I soon faded from the interstitial realm in which we communed. My brother and fellow townsfolk were doomed to perdition.

—I recommend that you stop listening to Beethoven’s “Moonlight Sonata”—

I woke up. I had to save them. I had to go back into the “dream.” I shared my adventure with my friends. My life in the dismal, yet comforting coastal town. My expedition to find God. My communion with him. His betrayal of humanity. It all happened so fast. I waited for one of my friends to progress his own visions. Once he was ready, I closed my eyes again and the spirit merged with my body.

I was back on the canoe. The ocean looked as cruel as ever. I had to stop God. For the town. For my parents. Most of all, for my brother. I racked my brain for any way of meeting him again. I accessed the divine knowledge God imparted to me. I realized something. My realm “reset” repeatedly on a time loop. The outcome of each prior loop wasn’t what I’d hoped. I finally understood why I had such a unique affinity for God. It was horrifying.

I am God.

I was fated to become, by some divine machinations, the same man who doomed our world. But this iteration of the time loop was different. In previous iterations, I was left with no family after my parents committed suicide. I lost the compassion that now drove me. This iteration was different. Unlike before, I adopted a little boy who helped me heal from bereavement. My brother. His influence would help me break the cycle. A huge beam of light extended from me through the storm clouds. I rapidly flew up the beam, my exterior appearance crumbling to reveal my pure white form.

I was back in the interstitial realm, equipped with God’s powers. We clashed violently, our strikes generating astronomical explosions. We blitzed around space at infinite speeds. It all happened in the blink of an eye and no laws of our universe could describe our duel.

I eventually grabbed God’s throat, ready to finish him. He urged me to look down from where we floated in the air. Our battle somehow annihilated the boundaries of the interstitial realm. My realm—my home—was completely destroyed. I angrily closed my fingers around God’s throat. He faded into dust. Gone for good. I desperately focused energy into my hands. The town and the turbulent ocean gradually restored before my eyes. I flew back to the town to celebrate the results.

No one suffered from chronic pain anymore. But they didn’t celebrate the way I did. In fact, they didn’t recall ever suffering from chronic pain. It was as though our curse of pain never existed. I flew to my brother. He was all alone in an alleyway. I called out to him, but he didn’t respond. I tried to hug him, but my body passed through him. I was no longer a part of the material plane of this realm. Although I rid this world of their curse forever, I also rid them of their memories of me. I could no longer live here again with my people. I couldn’t celebrate my accomplishment, which they could never know. My brother would never meet me and grow up alone. Though bittersweet, it was a necessary sacrifice.

I flew through the interstitial realm and into the Supreme Realm for the first time. It was beautiful. A giant divine tree whose white glowed against the black void. More of my previously observed divine knowledge returned to me. I learned the final truth. When God (the one I usurped, not me) said that there were other Gods, he was only partially telling the truth. The “other” Gods were incarnations of me living as ordinary humans in the other realms linked to the Yggdrasil. These incarnations, these avatars of me, served as ways for me to gain wisdom. No amount of divine knowledge substitutes the experience of living life in a multitude of settings.

I would now incarnate in a new realm and lose my conscious memories until I could re-enter the Supreme Realm. I would truly leave behind what was recently the only life I had ever known. A necessary sacrifice. With the experiences I accumulate as avatars of myself, I would eventually have the wisdom to turn every realm into an everlasting utopia. And so, my Godly form entered a white orb—a universe—linked to a root of the Yggdrasil.

I was reborn on Earth as Adit Pakala.

But this was all like a dream. It wasn’t quite a hallucination. Indeed, I seemed to consciously and subconsciously construct the story. It was simultaneously a lived experience, a movie, and a retrospection.

The spirit has dissipated for now. I resume my “ordinary” behavior. Or perhaps I’ve changed. Perhaps the spirit and God and the realm of storms lives on with me.

item.title: Adventures in Quantum Mechanics
item.description: how I went insane
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic Status: I’m not an expert in physics. I’m far from the first person to identify the scientific and philosophical implications of quantum mechanics. This article is focused on my personal experience. I’ve repeatedly consulted expert sources in my writing process. Ideas are simplified where I thought appropriate.

Introduction

In the last 2-3 weeks, I embarked on a journey that pushed my cognitive limits and upended my worldview. I learned quantum mechanics (QM). You might wonder how I—someone with no physics background—justified this arduous commitment. I had a few different motivations.

First, I wanted to collect paradigms from fields outside of economics and mathematics (the two majors I’m taking in college). Historically, some of the most revolutionary ideas arrived by incorporating paradigms from one field into another. For example, development economics (my aspiring career field) borrows extensively from statistics, medical experiments, and political science. QM is about as paradigmatically divorced from development economics as a subfield1 of human knowledge can get. In theory, this separation was very promising. In practice, not so much.

Second, I was simply curious. I love learning, even when it doesn’t directly benefit my career. Thus, it’s usually regrettable when I “abandon” rigorous learning of a subject. QM was an opportunity to return to physics ever since I took AP Physics 1 in high school. Colloquial explanations of QM felt too vague to me to be rewarding. Maybe getting into the weeds would resolve my questions. It didn’t (kind of).

Finally, I thought it would be an agentic, personally enriching project.2 I’ve made an effort to broaden my life experiences during the past two years. It’s helped me grow tremendously as a person. Surely this project would do wonders for my growth. It did (kind of).

I’m gonna talk about the following things:

  1. My learning process

  2. Scientific takeaways

  3. Philosophical implications

  4. How it changed me

My Learning Process

I primarily learned from Introduction to Quantum Mechanics by David J. Griffiths (often referred to as “Griffiths”). This textbook seems to be a favorite among undergraduate physics students. I can see why. It contains useful analogies, mostly illuminating exercises, and a conversational style. It’s also the textbook of choice in the majority of QM courses taught at my university.

The book is divided into 12 chapters, each with about 5 sections. I elected to study chapters 1-3 (theoretical foundations), skim 4-5 (extensions to three dimensions and identical particles), and read 12 (the afterword). I read roughly one section daily, depending on the amount of content, and completed most of the exercises labeled “essential.” This occupied roughly 2-3 hours of my day for about two weeks. I’d often spent minutes rereading parts of the textbook because of how abstruse it could get. I consulted Claude and YouTube videos whenever a particular topic was especially perplexing. I did part of the exercises on my own and routinely asked Claude to verify my results. Sometimes I’d explain the steps of a problem and instruct Claude to perform the necessary computations for me.

If I could go back, I would’ve spent more time attempting a problem before asking Claude for hints. I also would’ve relied more heavily on supplementary material; exposure to different treatments of the same material is helpful. I would’ve consulted one of my best friends, who took a QM class last semester, for help. Finally, I would’ve chosen a different textbook than Griffiths.

Griffiths suffers heavily from a lack of formalization. His efforts to discuss QM casually do more to confuse than to elucidate. Indeed, the marriage of complex subject matter and a neglect of formality is dreadful.

It’s hard to know how much of my struggles to attribute to each of the following:

  1. The difficulty of learning QM

  2. My lack of a physics background (I leaned heavily on my math background)

  3. The style of Griffiths

I’ll elaborate on the second and third points for now. I’ve developed a complicated relationship with physicists.3

I began this journey equipped with knowledge of statistics, multivariable calculus, linear algebra, a bit of classical mechanics, and proof-based math.4 I would additionally recommend familiarity with Euler’s identity and methods of solving differential equations; I had to learn that ad hoc. My math background carried me. I found that knowledge of classical physics actually wasn’t that helpful because of how differently QM operates.

However, the dichotomy in how mathematicians and physicists think was insufferable. In particular, mathematicians place much more emphasis on formality. I love how math is derived from first principles reasoning. It’s for this reason that you often “know” whether you wrote a proof correctly. It’s beautiful. Physicists treat math as a tool rather than a foundation, regularly glossing over the implicit mathematical assumptions in their work. I’m sure physicists have good justification for the conventions of their field. Admittedly, formality’s a lot less crucial when results are empirically verifiable.

A concrete example of this dichotomy is in how mathematicians and physicists use notation. Mathematicians define notation rigorously, carefully stating their assumptions. New theorems are followed by a well-packaged bevy of propositions. In contrast, physicists use ambiguous, albeit concise, notation. New theorems are haphazardly followed by results that feel more like mathematical coincidences than artistry. What mathematicians elegantly think of as compositions of functions, physicists call “operators.” With how dense Griffiths could get, you’d think I’d welcome the notational shorthands of physics. On the contrary, this is precisely why I loathed them. Math reads like a well-defined code. Physics reads like English—an ill-defined, contextual language.

Scientific Takeaways

I had a lot of questions about QM at the beginning of this project. This list of questions grew, and my existing questions were rarely resolved. This is because QM feels less like tangible generalizations of physical phenomena and more like a mathematical puzzle that happens to comport.

Explanations of QM can feel circular. It’s sort of like explaining color to a blind person. You might say that color is a property that objects around us exhibit. When asked to elaborate, you add that it’s a reflection of a range of wavelengths of light. It’s something non-blind people can “perceive.” Now, if you’re really knowledgeable, you could explain more of the science behind color. But to a blind person, color would probably still feel like some abstract property of the universe that happens to comport. In QM, it’s like everyone’s blind and trying to explain color to each other.

Richard Feynman famously said, “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.” I see why now. It might be impossible to understand QM. We don’t have satisfying answers to its questions. It’s tempting to lament how little we know, but I’m honestly impressed at how much we know. Somehow real human beings discovered this stuff about a century ago.

I’m gonna try my best to summarize what I learned and where I stand on some of the scientific debates (not that my stance matters).

Incidentally, quantum particles (e.g., protons, electrons, quarks) behave “randomly.” Whether they’re truly “random” is complicated, like most questions in QM (I’ll delve into the philosophy of this “randomness” later and focus on the physics for it for now). Anyhow, the properties of a quantum particle—such as its position, momentum, and energy—are observed according to a probability distribution at that instant in time. This distribution is determined by the wave function. “What is the wave function?” you may ask. In short, we don’t really know5, but it encodes the state of a quantum particle.

Interpretations

Suppose we measure a quantum particle’s position. The position we observe is random, and subsequent measurements yield the same result. It's unclear whether its position was predetermined and/or is “truly” random. Einstein said that “God doesn’t play dice,” so what’s going on here?

There are three main interpretations for what happens when a quantum particle is measured:

  1. The realist interpretation is that the particle was already in that position before it was measured. Einstein was a notable proponent of this interpretation.

  2. The orthodox/Copenhagen interpretation is that the act of measurement induces the particle to assume its observed position. This interpretation is the consensus of most physicists.

  3. The agnostic interpretation is not to take a stance.

As I’ll explain soon, the agnostic interpretation was “ruled out.”6

The realist interpretation implies that QM is a “failed” theory in that we wouldn’t know why a particle was already in its exact position.

The Copenhagen interpretation is cursed in its own ways. First, it doesn’t specify what it means to “measure” a quantum particle. Indeed, there’s no satisfying answer to this question. Second, it implies that information can transmit faster than the speed of light (referred to as superluminal transmission). Suppose two particles, A and B, are propelled in opposite directions. With 1/2 probability, A is labeled7 1 and B is labeled -1. Equally likely is that A is labeled -1 and B is labeled 1. Now, say you observe particle A 10 light-years from where it was launched. You now know the label of B, a particle 20 light-years away. If the Copenhagen interpretation were true, then the act of measuring A instantaneously induced the label of a particle light-years away. It’s like pressing a remote that activates a TV with a signal faster than the speed of light.8 The idea that no “physical influence” should transmit superluminally is called locality. Realists assert that the particles somehow had their label before measurement (called the hidden variable theory).

So it seems we must choose which concession to make. Do we accept that QM is a failed theory? Or do we accept an ambiguous concept of measurement and the absurdity of superluminal transmission? It’s a difficult tradeoff that I’ll get into the philosophy of later.

You might think that the agnostic interpretation is safe from this debate. In most unresolved epistemic debates, an agnostic viewpoint is robust. Somehow, physicists “disproved” the agnostic interpretation in the sense that either the realist interpretation or the Copenhagen interpretation must be correct. This is called Bell’s Theorem. Essentially, if quantum particles have locality (i.e., measuring one particle can’t superluminally influence another) and hidden variables (i.e., they have their label for some inexplicable reason), there’s an upper bound on their correlation. However, experimentally, quantum particles are so highly correlated (entangled) that this upper bound is violated. In other words, the only way that quantum particles can behave as they do is if either locality is false or the hidden variable theory is false. This means that either the realist interpretation or the Copenhagen interpretation must be true.

Tunneling and Entanglement

In some states, the probability distribution of a quantum particle is positive even at its tail ends. It’s like how a normal distribution is positive at its extremes. This is why it’s theoretically possible for a human to have an IQ of 1000. Similarly, a quantum particle can theoretically “move” anywhere (given the right circumstances). This is how quantum tunneling works.

Another cool property of quantum particles is entanglement. Like most properties of quantum particles, it’s easier to think of entanglement as a mathematical implication than an intuitive aspect of our reality. Basically, all quantum particles interact with each other due to the overlap in their wave functions. This means that a particle in Texas can influence a particle in Antarctica. Though in practice, particles so far from each other have such an astronomically small influence on each other that their interaction is negligible.

The Link Between Classical and QM

I like to think that there’s always a way to traverse the ladder of emergent complexity. For example, let’s say you’re examining an individual’s behavior. That’s psychology. We can “descend” the ladder by examining the functioning of their neurons. That’s biology. These functions are really just chemical reactions. That’s chemistry. Finally, brain chemistry conforms to the laws of QM.

The link between classical and QM wasn’t so clear to me before. If I throw a ball, for instance, how can the ball’s motion be described as an aggregate of quantum phenomena? First, a result called Ehrenfest’s theorem shows that, on average, quantum particles behave the same as their classical counterparts. Second, if you aggregate the probability distributions for quantum particles, the distribution becomes narrower (I’m oversimplifying here). This is (partially) why the position of the ball is effectively deterministic. It’s like if you flipped a fair coin billions of times and multiplied some physical quantity by the percentage of heads. In practice, this percentage is almost exactly 50. This is a beautiful result.

No Clone Theorem

It’s impossible to “clone” a quantum particle. More precisely, it’s physically impossible to create an identical copy of a particular quantum state. The reason is that it’s mathematically impossible for some function that can clone individual quantum states to clone a combination of said states. Think of it like this: a six-sided die is placed under a cup. You don’t know which of its sides is facing up. You can orient another die to have one of its sides face up, but you can’t be certain that both dice are oriented the same way. You might think to observe the die from the cup. Unfortunately, the cup is magical. It’s possible that the cup detects that it’s being lifted and reorients the die inside. Regardless, the die exists in all six of its states prior to observation. Lifting the cup doesn’t really tell you how the die was oriented prior to its observation.

Interestingly, this theorem has applications in quantum cryptography.

What Schrodinger’s Cat Actually Means

Unfortunately, we don’t know what Schrodinger's cat actually means. What we do know is that it’s commonly misunderstood. Colloquially, we say that the cat was both dead and alive before its status was “measured.” Almost everyone who first hears of this thinks it’s ridiculous. I know I did. But I was willing to concede that I probably just didn’t understand the physics well enough. I’m proud to say that I’m finally vindicated. Erwin Schrodinger himself disagreed with the notion that the eponymous cat is both dead and alive before observation. The telos of the thought experiment isn’t to extrapolate quantum superposition to macroscopic systems; it’s to refute such an extrapolation to begin with.

Schrodinger’s cat elucidates the ambiguity as to what constitutes “measurement.” Suppose the cat did behave like a quantum particle. Was measurement the act of exposing the box to light? Was it the observer’s conscious ascertainment of its status? Was it some part of the mechanism that killed the cat? We don’t really know. There are a few theories for what actually constitutes measurement:

  1. Human consciousness (Wigner’s earlier belief)

  2. The use of the measurement apparatus itself (a simplification of Bohr’s belief)

  3. The existence of a permanent record left from measurement (Heisenberg’s belief)

There’s an argument that the cat isn’t superposed between life and death under any reasonable concept of measurement. In particular, decoherence is the belief that macroscopic systems are subject to “so much” measurement that it induces a deterministic state. The cat, a macroscopic system, is a composite of an astronomical quantity of quantum particles. Decoherence would suggest that, at a macroscopic scale, mere interactions with surrounding matter (air, fur, litter, etc.) constitute measurement. If you’ll recall, quantum particles remain in a fixed state after measurement (approximately). This means that the cat’s status is determined before the lid of the box is removed. That is, the cat is either dead or alive. Ergo, decoherence—if true—refutes the colloquial view that the cat is both dead and alive prior to observation.

Philosophical Takeaways

QM is one of the most philosophically rich subjects I’ve ever studied. It has profound implications for epistemology, metaphysics, probability theory, and religion. My foray into its technical details illuminated philosophical considerations I was otherwise unlikely to ever see.

Determinism

Is the universe physically deterministic? The Copenhagen interpretation is agnostic about this; it fails to specify whether the state of particles prior to measurement was random or deterministic. The realist interpretation similarly fails to explain why a particle is in a particular state to begin with.9 The realist and Copenhagen interpretations don’t really have an answer.

If we loosen our definition of the word “deterministic,” the conclusion is a bit different. A particle’s wave function—its state—specifies the probability distributions on its future behavior given a starting point in time. If we think of determinism as the notion that all possible futures conform to probabilistic laws, then quantum theory does imply determinism.

Imagine a monkey is trapped in a room where every second it will either press a red button or a blue button. Suppose you know the probability distribution of what the monkey will press next, given its history of button presses. For example, if the monkey last pressed the sequence red-blue-blue, we know the exact probabilities with which it will press each button. The sequence of future button presses is deterministic in the sense that we can have a perfect description of the probabilities of future sequences. Constrained randomness, if you like. However, it’s not deterministic in the sense that there’s still some level of randomness.

There are actually two interpretations of QM that imply determinism in a more conventional sense of the word. The Many Worlds Interpretation (MWI) essentially postulates that when measurement occurs, the universe branches into parallel realities containing each possible outcome. It’s like if you flipped a coin and the universe branched into two paths: one where it lands on heads and one where it lands on tails. Of course, a coin is a macroscopic object and therefore a faulty analogy (arguably). MWI isn’t actually as ridiculous as it sounds and has some implications we’ll touch on later. For now, just realize that it implies a deterministic universe, since there’s “no randomness”—every possibility occurs.

The Bohm Interpretation essentially postulates that the state of the universe is fully determined from some unknown initial state. It’s like a random seed. It implies that the perceived indeterminacy of quantum particles is just our ignorance of the initial state. This is my favorite interpretation as of writing. It’s simple, aesthetically pleasing, and has relatively straightforward philosophical conclusions. For example, it directly implies determinism. No agonizing philosophical argument required.10

We return to the original question. Is the universe deterministic? It seems QM introduces more questions than answers.

Unknowable Truths

Are all truths knowable? QM suggests to me that the answer is an emphatic “no.” It feels impossible to resolve some of its mysteries at a fundamental level. Though there’s no shortage of scientific mysteries, most of them offer some clues towards progress. QM is sort of like moral philosophy in that it leads us in circles around seemingly axiomatic—incontrovertible—beliefs. It’s like trying to argue that humans are morally obligated to help others. Unless you’re a moral realist, it’s ostensibly impossible to establish moral axioms on which to argue this.

A counterargument is that we’re unsure as to the scope of unknown information; we don’t know how much (or how little) we know. I’m inclined to reuse the analogy of a blind person attempting to understand color. Could the blind person ever understand color? Can the blind person establish how much they don’t know about color? Not to mention, there’s always the speculative possibility of a universal cure to blindness. In the scientific context, this could be an apparatus that enables observations hitherto unfathomable.

Axiomatic Truths

Every interpretation fails to explain its fundamental causes. For example, the Copenhagen interpretation fails to explain why measurement induces a particle’s state. It’s unknown whether all questions can be traced to irreducible axioms; can we take quantum phenomena for granted, or must there be an even more fundamental explanation?

Various fields of human knowledge handle this mystery in different ways. First, they can seek consistency of beliefs instead of establishing axioms. Philosophers often opt for this approach, some of them disagreeing that axioms can exist to begin with. Second, some fields can simply accept axioms that “feel intuitive” while acknowledging that such axioms are not necessarily true. Most modern mathematics is done this way. Finally, some fields never have to wrangle with axioms. Biologists, for instance, can find solace knowing that the physical and chemical explanations for their observations are beyond their purview. A biological system operates the way it does regardless of the quantum interactions at its most principal level.

Physics is an epistemic outlier in that it’s not content with any of the three aforementioned solutions. Its empirical nature arguably precludes us from thinking of QM as consistent beliefs. Moreover, what good are axioms that “feel intuitive” without proof? To make matters worse, physicists arguably can’t just dismiss the fundamental explanations for QM as outside their purview. After all, if physics can’t explain the apparent randomness of quantum particles, what can?

Physics is cursed to endlessly pursue explanations for phenomena that have none. Barring a revolutionary breakthrough, the alternative is to accept our universe’s most fundamental known properties as axiomatic.

Theism

Does God exist? Is our reality the “only” one (i.e., we’re not living in a simulation)? I hope you’ve realized by now that QM tends to make these questions tougher to answer—not easier.

The fine-tuning argument for theism seems less plausible to me under QM interpretations. QM is a mathematically consistent puzzle despite its persistent mysteries. It's tempting, then, to attribute this “lucky coincidence” to a greater power. However, I reckon that any such power would have intricacies far beyond those of human conceptions of God. Indeed, how else could such complicated, yet consistent phenomena have a unifying explanation?

Of course, this is all a rabbit hole of bottomless depth speculation. The conception of a greater power implicitly assumes that said power is unfettered by the rules of our reality.

It’s funny that the same quantum mechanical justification for God—the absence of a fundamental explanation—is also a justification for atheism. Think of it like this: if QM is so inscrutable, then isn’t it remarkable just how many secrets we’ve unraveled? Roughly a century of research has taught us increasingly fundamental explanations of the universe. Perhaps this should increase our credence in atheistic foundations of reality.

Does Anyone Know QM?

Does anyone know QM? There are certainly experts on humanity’s knowledge of QM. We’re able to solve relatively non-fundamental problems, such as the wave function of a free particle. But at what thoroughness of comprehension can we claim to “know” something?

QM certainly isn’t the only field where experts lack answers to crucial questions. Virtually every field of economics comes to mind. What’s fascinating here is how society confers “expert” status. It seems that experts are those proficient in the core components of their field during their time period. We wouldn’t call a pro soccer player a non-expert for being unable to explain the physics of a soccer ball. Their mastery of the actual game is what characterizes their expert status.11

Furthermore, we wouldn’t call Isaac Newton a non-expert because he never understood QM in any capacity. Likewise, we wouldn’t call modern physicists non-experts because there are unsolved mysteries in QM. I know this is obvious, but it’s not often I palpably feel just how much we don’t know about the universe.

Probability

It’s unclear what probability is. Mathematically, probability is well-defined. The real world doesn’t enjoy the same formalism. The two prevailing interpretations of probability are frequentism and Bayesianism. Frequentism asserts that probabilities represent the relative frequency of events across infinite trials. For example, if I flip a fair coin infinitely many times, it lands on heads and tails each half the time. Bayesianism asserts that probabilities represent our knowledge of a state. It’s how likely we think something is given our evidence. For example, if I flip a fair coin, my confidence that it’ll land on heads is 50% ex ante.

In practice, we use both interpretations. Frequentism is how we tend to think of random events that occur repeatedly and identically. Coin flips are repeatable and (effectively) identical. Bayesianism is how we tend to think of one-of-a-kind events. It’s like epistemic confidence. It’s like if I were to say that I’m 20% sure I’m sick.

The various interpretations of QM can be construed as conforming to either frequentism or Bayesianism. The Copenhagen interpretation is frequentist, assuming that the result of measurement is truly random. Experimentally, we would prepare an ensemble of quantum particles that are identical ex ante. This is because we can’t repeatedly measure the same particle—subsequent measurements yield the same result. It’s like having a collection of pennies that are either heads up or tails up. We don’t know. In theory, measurements across an infinite number of particles in the ensemble yield the probability distribution.

You can also construe the Copenhagen interpretation as Bayesian. It’s theoretically impossible to produce an ensemble of ex ante identical particles because the entire universe is entangled. Therefore, no two measurements can be treated like identical events. Frequentism can only hold if you treat approximately identical events (i.e., measurements of an ensemble of virtually identical, experimentally isolated particles) as identical. This makes Bayesianism an obvious alternative.

The realist interpretation can be construed as both frequentist and Bayesian. The aforementioned measurement of an infinite ensemble of identical particles would produce the probability distribution. But this is not frequentist in that there may be an indeterminate, non-random explanation for each particle’s state. To see why, suppose you flipped a fair coin one million times. Suppose that I’m secretly manipulating each coin flip to follow a pre-established sequence. The sequence contains heads and tails in roughly equal proportion, so it presents the illusion of randomness. In this sense, the Bohm interpretation also isn’t fully frequentist.

Bayesianism is easier to reconcile with the realist and Bohm interpretations. Given what we know about quantum particles, we have some probability distribution on their state.

The many-worlds interpretation is manifestly frequentist. As each possible outcome is realized in some branch, probabilities are just the relative frequency of the branches that correspond to a given outcome.

How QM Changed Me

The ~40 hours that went into writing this article have left me a changed man. I pushed my cognitive limits, updated myriad preconceptions, enriched my mental fortitude, and have now brought my ability to conceptualize and write to its limit.

As Avatar Roku once said:

It was bitter work, but the results were worth it.

*Queue epic sequence of me brandishing magical powers*

In all seriousness, I hardly scratched the surface of our current knowledge of QM. It’s not the kind of knowledge you can obtain from studying a single textbook. It likely requires years of serious study of theory, experimental methods, and the literature—all to be stuck with many of the same questions as the physicist LARPer writing this.

Updated Beliefs

The experience was ineffable. My updated scientific and philosophical views are the most tangible result of the project:

  • Of the five QM interpretations I listed, I’m most inclined towards the Copenhagen interpretation, followed by the Bohm interpretation.

  • I don’t think the wave function is "real,” but rather a practical mathematical tool.

  • I believe in decoherence and hence disagree that Schrodinger’s cat is both dead and alive before it’s observed.

  • My belief in the universe’s determinism remains the same: everything is an automaton of physical properties.

  • Some truths are unknowable. In that same vein, there are irreducible axioms—assumptions whose ultimate explanation is unknowable.

  • I have even less credence in any human concept of God. I now have more credence in unfathomable Gods and the simulation hypothesis.

  • No one is even close to knowing QM, though experts know a remarkable amount.

  • Bayesianism more accurately describes reality than frequentism.12 Frequentism is more of an approximation of reality.

  • I’m not sure whether true randomness exists.

I still believe that a scientific theory is immaterial if it’s not falsifiable (I mentioned this here). Philosopher Karl Popper proposed that falsifiability—the ability to prove a claim wrong—was what made a theory scientific to begin with. I find speculative scientific theories far more credible when there’s additionally a clear path to possibly falsify them. There are no such paths for the possible falsification of QM interpretations. No wonder the answers (provided they exist) have mercilessly eluded us. The lack of answers forced me to seriously reckon with these theories of unknown levels of falsifiability. I previously thought that this kind of rumination was reserved for economics—another field with questions lacking a clear path to falsifiability.

Physics Fatigue

I don’t have a strong physics background. I enjoyed AP Physics 1, the only physics class I’ve ever taken. I’ve had mixed experiences with popular physics media; it can be simultaneously fascinating and unsatisfying. That’s how I feel about physics in general. As a field of knowledge, it has an enviable scope, rigor, and level of generality. What development economics would give for a “law” or “principle.”

Meanwhile, physics sometimes glosses over formalization. Griffiths was especially bad about this. I also wish Griffiths had explained more about the experiments that led to the discoveries I learned about. It’s a luxury that I can treat years of arduous labor as a simple formula. Why not guide people through the process? Admittedly, I’m not familiar with alternatives to Griffiths. I’m not even sure that QM is a subject one can sufficiently understand with an undergraduate-level textbook. Yet, my stance is firm: I can’t confidently recommend Griffiths to anyone who wants to learn it.

A Unique Learning Experience

This project isn’t my first endeavor in self-study, but it’s unique in some interesting ways. First, it partially validated my choice not to pursue physics. Maybe I would’ve had a better time in an actual course or with a different textbook. Regardless, I don’t find physics as fascinating as economics.

Second, I didn’t enjoy the experience overall. Within a day or two, I no longer enjoyed the learning process. It was tedious, unrewarding, and exhausting. I stuck it out almost solely so that I could write this article. It’s rare for me to have such a negative experience with learning. I’m inclined to dismiss it as incompetence on my part. Maybe I hated it because I wasn’t good enough. But this is certainly not the first time I struggled to learn something. Usually, the struggle is far more enjoyable.

Third, I could never find satisfying answers to why the results of QM worked. My stubbornness to find physical intuition in the mathematical processes was rebuffed. Sometimes there was no intuition. It didn’t help that every analogy for the material was flimsy. I sometimes found myself blindly submitting to mathematical rigmaroles. Not a good feeling.

Fourth, QM has a strange relationship with the Dunning-Krueger effect. I’m at a relatively amateur level of knowledge where I feel like I know a “good amount,” even though I know that’s not true. This is consistent with the effect. The effect also proposes that individuals can attain a “slope of enlightenment,” whereby dedication yields a more justified feeling of mastery. In contrast, I’m not sure such a slope exists within QM. I imagine newly minted physics PhDs just indefinitely oscillate between various levels of feeling like they know nothing.

Fifth, QM has little to lend to the field of economics. This was largely expected. Physics and economics pretty different. One is rigorous. The other is faux-rigorous. One studies the universe at its most fundamental level. The other studies it at one of its least fundamental levels. However, mathematics and empiricism underpin both. It’s not so ludicrous to think that the paradigms of QM—the way quantum physicists think—could provide me insight. I did learn some tricks for simplifying computations. Physicists are great at that. I can also see potential insights into the distinction between ex ante, interim, and ex post expected utility (a crucial distinction in economic theory). A friend of mine noted an intersection between quantum computing and game theory called quantum game theory.13 There’s also a fringe subfield called econophysics that uses methods of statistical mechanics to model economic agents. I’ll have to look more into this. Nevertheless, I struggled to find meaningful extensions of QM to economics.

Finally, I’m beginning to internalize the idea that specialists are those willing to undertake an exasperating mental burden. Physicists are teased by such inscrutable enigmas. Biologists must contend with the sheer scope of biodiversity. Mathematicians the endlessly abstract. Artists the artistically ineffable. All fields have their unknowns. To allow oneself to fall so deep into an intellectual rabbit hole that you one day burrow at its darkest depths is both beautiful and accursed. I’m convinced that I have my own burden to undertake as an aspiring development economist. I must coexist with the suffering in the world that the scourge of poverty cruelly afflicts. Will it break me? Only time will tell.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe to receive new posts and support my work.

1

By subfield, I mean a field of study within a major field. For example, QM is a field of study within physics. I think of a subfield as the knowledge a university might offer as a handful of courses within a department.

2

Not to mention, a cool Substack article idea (I hope).

3

I’m generalizing from what little I know about the physics profession.

4

Griffiths doesn’t list statistics or proof-based math as prerequisites, though he notes the utility of differential equations techniques, some complex analysis, and some electrodynamics.

5

QM also forces us to think about what it means to “know” something. It’s a deep rabbit hole. Very deep.

6

I hope you’ve noticed how many quotation marks I use in this article. Turns out there’s a lot of uncertainty.

7

I’m simplifying here. Technically, the “label” is called spin.

8

I’m not familiar with relativity, but I’m told it explains all the issues that arise when the speed of light gets involved.

9

I suspect Einstein is inclined towards determinism. “God doesn’t play dice,” he said.

10

If the Bohm interpretation is true, then it’s unclear how the initial state was determined. In some sense, it’s an incomplete theory and therefore fails to establish determinism.

11

Relative skill also matters, of course. A soccer player beyond some arbitrary threshold of proficiency still may not make the cut. There’s unavoidably a lot of ambiguity in my definition of an expert.

12

While Bayesianism is subject to more phenomenological limitations, our priors on known quantum systems are well-established.

13

I suspect these games have a classical analogue. The “quantum” information component of them feels dubious and bastardizing.

item.title: On Child Prodigies
item.description: When I was a kid, my dad exposed me to media featuring child prodigies.
item.content:encoded:
When I was a kid, my dad exposed me to media featuring child prodigies. Whether it was a young teen who collaborated with IBM or the latest child inventor on Shark Tank, there was always a kid more agentic than me. It made me feel a little bad. Like I wasn’t living up to my potential. However, I would inevitably return from stories of the latest child prodigy feeling mostly indifferent.

As I got older, I began to see flaws in so much of what I was taught as a kid. I recall having always known that Santa wasn’t real. It wasn’t until later in elementary school that my PE teacher disillusioned us with the true history of Thanksgiving (turns out that the Wampanoags and the Puritans weren’t the best of friends). But child prodigies? Surely the sensational accounts of them were accurate. Surely.

It wasn’t so hard to believe that other people my age could be more accomplished. After all, I was a lazy kid who had witnessed firsthand the heterogeneity in individual genetics and childhood environment. Nonetheless, the mystique of child prodigies struggles to endure criticism. It’s a cliché. Child prodigies are groomed. Deprived of a fulfilling childhood. Charlatans. Doomed to failure in adulthood. Yet, they’re also extraordinarily talented. Wellsprings of potential. We may find ourselves thinking: “if they’re so skilled now, imagine how skilled they’ll be as adults.”

Indeed, the colloquial narrative surrounding these phenoms has embraced both the backlash and the sensationalism. I suspect that, as with most media narratives, the truth lies somewhere in the middle. Child prodigies are probably relatively talented individuals in a particular field, but are otherwise ordinary people. Of course, it’s more eye-catching when a bright elementary schooler promises the cure to cancer.

The exaltation of child prodigies is dehumanizing. To treat anyone, even tacitly, as superior establishes a rift in empathy. Their emotions go from an understood experience to something futile to relate to. For example, the hypothetical inability of a child prodigy to communicate with others can be distorted into a sign of inscrutable genius. Performance anxiety becomes “perfectionism.” A lack of personal desires becomes “dedication to mastery.”

On the other hand, the disparagement of child prodigies can be just as dehumanizing. Many people assume that child prodigies are miserable, isolated, frauds, and/or set up for failure. Perhaps the assumption is protective; opportunistic parents may think twice about overworking their kid if this is stigmatized. Or maybe it’s more self-protective; if there’s nothing positive about child prodigies, then I don’t have to feel bad about being “ordinary.” Regardless, it’s problematic to reduce the perception of a group of people to pity—just because they seem to suffer disproportionately from particular issues.

I still haven’t mentioned the teleological issues with the term “child prodigy.” What does it even mean? A child who exceeds some arbitrary threshold of mastery for a skill? If so, what about children who have a lower level of mastery across a greater variety of skills? What about children who are just below the definitional “threshold of mastery”? These kinds of social labels benefit from some practical purpose. For example, if someone is a “baby” (literally), we know to treat them differently from we treat an adult. If someone is a “medical doctor,” we know to take their words on medicine seriously. In contrast, if someone is a “child prodigy,” I’m not sure how useful it is to know that. Maybe it correlates with enough personality traits (e.g., introversion) to prove informative? Otherwise it’s seems like little more than sensationalism. I don’t see the term “child prodigy” as much more informative than “critical thinker” or “good communicator” or “cool.”

Despite all this polemic, I actually have a net positive perception of child prodigies.1 You see, my dad never showed me videos of child prodigies as a point of comparison and subsequent denigration (as some Asian parents unfortunately do). It wasn’t exactly about novelty to him either. Rather, he wanted to demonstrate what was possible for me—formerly a child—to achieve.

In my experience, society typically doesn’t take kids seriously. I’m sure it’s irritated many others as much as it did me. It’s one thing to have your words dismissed on merit. I’ll admit that kids, due to their lack of experience, can get a lot wrong. But to have your ideas dismissed unfairly due to your age is crushing. Experience comes in all kinds of forms—some of which are almost exclusively privy to kids. Furthermore, a wealth of years lived doesn’t equate to a wealth of wisdom. I think we’ve all met an adult whose wisdom falls short of their years, to put it charitably. All this is to say that kids are patronized too much. It’s—and this is my third time using this word—dehumanizing.

Child prodigies show kids who feel patronized that, with enough skill, they can perform at the level of the grown-ups who would belittle them. This is magical to me. People talk of the value of representation all the time: representing one’s country in the FIFA world cup, representing a minority in politics, representing global cultures in film, etc. Yet I’ve never heard people acknowledge the role that child prodigies can have in representing children. Just as prodigies may discourage children via social comparison, they may encourage children via representation.

As a kid who has felt unfairly patronized for so much of my life, I strive to treat kids with the seriousness I wish I had been given.2 Unfortunately, I’ve found this impractical. For example, when explaining concepts or answering a kid’s question, I try not to oversimplify. I don’t like dumbing things down because it produces the kinds of unsatisfactory explanations I got all the time as a kid. This sometimes leads the kid I’m talking to to want a simpler explanation. It’s probably some combination of faulty communication on my part and a discrepancy of preferences (i.e., not everyone wants more info).

I know this shouldn’t be surprising. Obviously, there are justifications for treating children differently from adults. I wouldn’t want toddlers to have a driver’s license, for instance. I also wouldn’t discuss dark subject matter with a kid. Obviously, parents shouldn’t groom their children into child prodigies. Even successful child prodigies rarely accomplished their best work before adulthood. But am I really so naïve for wanting people to take kids more seriously?

The summer before my senior year of high school, I attended a college admissions counseling boot camp. There, I discussed one of my internships with the college counselor, a former admissions officer for an Ivy League school. Without disclosing details, I claimed that a report I wrote was intended to inform investment decisions at some firm. While my minuscule contribution was likely unimplemented, I didn’t lie about anything. The counselor scoffed, advised me to remove the resume padding, and roughly said, “Yeah, if I were running a company, I wouldn’t use anything done by a high schooler.” I didn’t disagree with any of this. My claim was resume padding. I knew the report wasn’t anything substantial. And I had to agree with her: if I was running a company, it’s unlikely that a high schooler would make a substantial contribution to it.

I wasn’t hurt that she recognized my internship as unremarkable. I was hurt by this blanket insinuation that formal credentials and/or a few additional years of life experience were invariably the difference between meaningful work and child’s play. I felt some kind of unsolicited anger on behalf of high school students, as corny as that sounds. I’ll admit that nothing I did in high school was anywhere near professional caliber. Indeed, a lot of high school extracurriculars are just cash grabs and/or shell organizations designed to signal “impressiveness”. But I knew that there were high schoolers doing projects deserving of the level of respect conferred to adult pros.

Wanting to take a break from mega projects, I’ve penned what hopefully amounts to more than vague, shallow, anecdotal slop. I’m not sure exactly what the takeaway from this article is. Chances are, you’re already familiar with the intricacies of child prodigies and their depiction. Chances are, you agree overall with my trivial realizations about the treatment of children in society. If there’s one lesson I’d want readers to take away, it’s to see the beauty in precociousness. Namely, it demonstrates that people aren’t confined to labels.

Imagine a classroom where children, college students, working-age professionals, and retirees gathered to learn advanced knowledge for its own sake. Isn’t that cool? Children not fettered to the expectation that their ability is invariably inferior. Just people enjoying learning in its purest form.

1

This isn’t a claim that child prodigies are a net good for society. It’s a statement of my feelings—not my beliefs about facts. In fact, I believe that the popular conception of child prodigies (and talent more broadly) is a net bad.

2

Given that I’m twenty years old, I know I’m hardly an adult in the conventional sense. I’m also vague about what age group I mean by “kids,” though this is intentional.

item.title: Mafia
item.description: I’ve played my fair share of party games.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve played my fair share of party games. Although many lack originality, replayability, or conventional notions of good game design1, there’s something sublime about laughing with friends at whatever absurdity happened. I also cherish these games because I only get to play them in large groups.

One of my favorite party games is Mafia. The way players sit in a cozy circle and close their eyes as the game master narrates is magical. If you’re privileged enough that your group stays silent during the “nighttime phase”, a kind of suspense builds. Who will die? Will the healers save someone’s life? All is revealed at the dawn of the next day. Player counts dwindle night by night. To the mafia, it’s a matter of blending in and strategically eliminating opposing players. To the civilians (and allied roles), it’s a race to oust the mafia from little more than social behavior. Who can you trust? Who will get falsely executed? Only time will tell.

Disclaimer: If you’re not the kind of person who enjoys reading rules (I certainly am not), you might want to skim through parts of the “The Rules of Mafia” and “Design Choices” section.

The Rules of Mafia

I want to take a moment to clarify the house rules that I play with. I’ll justify these rules later. Feel free to skip this part if you don’t care. These rules are Claude’s revision of what I wrote.

One player is the narrator/game master and is not considered a player. Choose someone experienced with good storytelling ability.

Role Assignment

The narrator assigns each player a role, randomly and anonymously — typically using playing cards, where each rank corresponds to a role. For example: number cards = civilians/villagers, Jacks = mafia. The narrator deals cards face-down (e.g., four number cards and one Jack to each of five players).

The five roles:

  1. Mafia — selects players to kill each night.

  2. Healer — selects players to heal each night.

  3. Sheriff — investigates one player each night.

  4. Jester — wins if voted out of the game.

  5. Civilian — has no special abilities.

A common card mapping is Jack = Mafia, Queen = Healer, King = Sheriff, Joker = Jester, number cards = Civilian.

Each player must look at their own role without revealing it. Players may lie about their role at any time — they just can’t show or reveal their actual card.

The split is how many players are assigned to each role, written as four digits: mafia-healers-sheriffs-jesters. Any remaining players are civilians.

Example: In a 12-player game, a split of 2-2-2-1 means 2 mafia, 2 healers, 2 sheriffs, 1 jester, and the remaining 5 players are civilians.

Rule of thumb for choosing a split:

  • Mafia ≈ 25% of players, rounded down.

  • Healers and sheriffs: roughly one fewer than the mafia count each.

  • Jester: include 1 if there are at least 7 players.

  • Example: a 12-player game suits a 3-2-2-1 split.

These are starting guidelines, not fixed rules — adjust as you like.

Night Phase

The narrator tells all players to “go to sleep.” While asleep, players keep their eyes closed until told to wake. No verbal communication is allowed during the night, though gesturing or mouthing words silently is fine.

The night proceeds in this order:

  1. Jester wakes. The narrator notes who the jester is (this matters later), then the jester goes back to sleep.

  2. Mafia wakes. The mafia choose who to kill. They may target anyone except the narrator, including each other. They must unanimously agree on each target, pointing until the narrator confirms with a thumbs up. The mafia may choose as many targets as there are living mafia (e.g., 3 living mafia can select 3 targets). The mafia return to sleep.

  3. Healers wake. The healers must unanimously agree on who to heal by pointing (they may heal themselves). The healers may choose as many targets as there are living healers. A healed player survives even if the mafia targeted them. If the healers heal the same player more than two nights in a row, that player dies of overdose — the narrator warns the healers before this happens. The healers return to sleep.

  4. Sheriffs wake. The sheriffs must unanimously agree on who to investigate by pointing. Sheriffs may only investigate one player, even if there are two alive. The narrator responds with a thumbs up if the target is mafia or jester, and a thumbs down otherwise. A thumbs up doesn’t distinguish between mafia and jester, but a thumbs down definitively confirms innocence. The sheriffs return to sleep.

  5. Everyone wakes up.

Important: Players from different roles must never be awake at the same time (e.g., mafia and healers awake together would break the game’s anonymity).

Day Phase

Special protections:

  • Sheriffs have first-round immunity — they cannot die from a mafia kill on the first night. (Don’t forget this as narrator.) If a sheriff is both targeted by the mafia and healed on the first night, nothing special happens — they simply survive either way.

  • Jesters have a second life — the first time the mafia targets them, they survive automatically, whether or not they were also healed. This protection does not apply to being voted out — the jester wins immediately if voted out, regardless of whether they’ve used their second life.

The day proceeds as follows:

  1. Announce deaths. The narrator states which players died, without revealing how (e.g., overdose) or whether anyone survived a targeted kill. If the number of living mafia is now equal to or greater than the number of non-mafia players, the mafia win immediately.

  2. Discussion. Players confer, ideally under a time limit. No one may prevent another player from speaking (no talking over others, no stalling).

  3. Vote. The narrator points to each player in turn; players raise their hand for whoever they want to vote out. Players may vote for themselves but get only one vote.2 Players may raise their hands reactively (e.g., to blend in after seeing others vote). Thus, players can infer information from seeing “reactive voting”. Votes cannot be changed retroactively. Players shouldn’t exploit the voting order (e.g., if the group is split evenly between two suspects, the one voted on earlier in the cycle is more likely to lose). Whoever gets the most votes dies and their role is revealed. A tie means no one is voted out.

  4. Check win conditions.

    • If the jester is voted out, they win immediately and the game ends. (The jester can only win this way — being killed by the mafia doesn’t count.)

    • If the last living mafia is voted out, the “good guys” (everyone except mafia and jester) win.

    • If, after the vote, living mafia are equal to or greater than non-mafia players, the mafia win.

  5. Continue or end. If no win condition is met, return to the Night Phase.

Additional Notes

  • Dead players may stay and watch as spectators but cannot communicate anything — verbally or gesturally — to living players.

  • The narrator can add flavor by narrating each death as part of a story (e.g., framing the game as aristocrats dying one by one in a mansion, describing the manner of death). This is purely stylistic and must never reveal actual gameplay information.

  • Although the healers can attempt to infer a mafia player’s identity and overdose them, this is usually ill-advised.

Simulation

I wanted to compute the probability that each faction (mafia, jester, good guys) wins for balancing purposes. There are several perspectives regarding what makes for a well-balanced mafia split. You might believe that each of the three factions should win with roughly equal frequency. Maybe faction win rates should be in proportion to the number of players in each faction. For example, a jester in a 10 player game should win about 1/10 of the time. Or maybe it’s best to deliberately make some roles overpowered/underpowered; this is fun in its own way. I prefer to play with splits where the “most skilled” faction wins on average, whatever that means.

I wish I had data on the mafia games I’ve played. I also wish I could analytically obtain each faction’s win rate under a given split. Instead, I asked Claude to write a script using the aforementioned rules to simulate the game. You can access the code here. In principle, the simulation represents each faction’s win rate when the social deduction aspect of the game is completely removed (i.e., players kill, heal, investigate, and vote randomly). We would expect that the simulation provides an upper bound for the mafia/jester win rates and a lower bound for the good guy win rate, assuming players are equally skilled. The reason for this is that social deduction allows the good guys to suss out the mafia/jester’s identities.

In theory, the social aspect of the game could increase win rates for the mafia and jester. For example, the mafia can frame others and the jester can convince others to vote for them. However, from personal experience, group discussions are a net detriment to these players—especially the mafia. This seems even more true when players are equally skilled. Thus, my personal experience tells me that the win rates in the simulation are skewed against the good guys.

Here’s how the simulation works:

  • The user specifies the number of players, the split, and the number of iterations that the simulation will run.

  • The jester has a second life as usual. The sheriffs have first round immunity.

  • Mafia randomly select players besides themselves to kill.

  • Healers randomly select players to heal. They never overdose anyone.

  • Sheriffs randomly select players besides themselves to investigate. The user inputs an influence parameter from 0 to 1. The parameter basically skews the probability distribution towards players the sheriff received a thumbs up from (mafia or jester) and away from those they received a thumbs down from. For now, let’s discuss the results for when the parameter is 0; this means sheriff investigations are completely inconsequential. The details of how influence works are commented in the code.

  • Each round, a random player is voted out with equal probability. The game ends when one of the factions satisfies their win condition.

Here are the win rates for each faction in the default split by player count3:

Keep in mind that these win rates reflect the balance of the game when players play “randomly” and the sheriff is inconsequential. Also recall that the jester is not included in the default split when there are less than 7 players. The results have various implications for the balance of the game. If by balance we mean that each faction has a roughly equal win rate, then this only holds for 5 players. What’s going on here? A more visual representation helps to elucidate these results.

When increasing the player count from 5 to 6, the gap between the mafia and good guy win rates shrinks drastically. We can explain these kinds of shifts by breaking down how the default split changes. Here, the default split remains as 1-0-0-0. The mafia is simply outnumbered a bit more than they were earlier. This creates more opportunities for them to get voted out, as it takes longer for the mafia to eliminate enough players to win the game.

The mafia win rate tanks again when increasing from 6 to 7 players. This is almost certainly due to the introduction of the jester to the game. As expected, the mafia win rate rebounds when increasing to 8 players because the mafia count increases from 1 to 2. We see the effect of an increased mafia account again when increasing from 11 to 12 players.

So far, the results make intuitive sense. However, why does the win rate for the good guys plummet irrecoverably? I offer two potential explanations:

  1. The jester “absorbs” good guy wins. The good guys win by voting out all of the mafia. It’s much more probable that the jester is voted out before this happens.4

  2. The good guys can’t communicate with each other. Their votes amount the random guesses, which eliminate their allies more often than not.

Although the simulation is unbalanced by several standards, my personal experience would suggest that the win rates for 8-15 player games (under the default split) are about 25%, 25%, 50%, respectively. I’m not too confident of these estimates, but I am confident that the good guys win far more than in the simulation.

The primary motivation of the simulation was to answer whether Mafia players can make meaningful social deductions. Indeed, confirmation bias and overconfidence in one’s social abilities are rife in Mafia games. Yet, the simulation results are inconsistent with my personal experience. If you don’t want to take me on my word, feel free to gather your own data on the results of your mafia games. It’s plausible that playing the game in some groups, such as a group of strangers, would reproduce the results of the simulation. After all, I primarily play Mafia with the same pool of people.

Design Choices

My house roles are the result of many games of experimentation. Maybe there are some rules I haven’t considered. Perhaps my group plays the game idiosyncratically. Regardless, I want to provide some justification for the design choices.

The mafia count is a crucial component of the split. The game becomes lopsided with too many players and a long tightrope with too few. Naturally, the results vary by the skill level of the individual mafia players and their synergy. I prefer to err on the side of too few mafia because it makes the role more rewarding to win with for anyone who can pull it off. While a numbers disadvantage reduces the mafia’s kill count and reduces their “lives”, it makes it easier for them to blend in. A severely outnumbered mafia can effectively kill people during the day by cleverly claiming good guys.

The healer overdose rule may seem arbitrary. In fact, if the mafia truly killed people randomly, overdose is inconsequential.5 In practice, however, some players are killed more than others. The mafia tend to kill those that they’re most familiar with, such as a sibling. In groups of varying player skill, the mafia tend to kill relatively skilled players. Therefore, the healers are more likely to successfully “guess” the mafia target by persistently healing players perceived as the most skilled.
