Overdose guarantees that the mafia can kill such players during some night. Of course, the mafia won’t know who the healers will heal ex ante.

The jester serves a vital balancing role. They encourage the good guys to vote more thoughtfully due to the fear that a jester vote immediately ends the game. Moreover, it balances the strength of sheriff investigations. Recall that the sheriffs receive a thumbs up when investigating the jester or the mafia. If a sheriff uses a mere investigation to persuade the group to vote them out, they must acknowledge the risk of a jester win. In other words, the jester prevents the sheriff investigation from becoming overpowered.

The jester’s second life mitigates the likelihood that they lose because the mafia killed them by random chance. I’ve found that, without a second life, the jester is so uncommonly present in the late game that the fear of voting out a jester player nearly disappears. The sheriff’s first round immunity ensures that the sheriffs have at least one round to make use of the results of their investigation(s).

I’ve experimented with various alternate rules to mixed results (skip these if you don’t care):

  1. Sidebar conversations: This rule allows players to whisper to players adjacent to them. It’s fun in its own way, though it can allow players of the same role to communicate verbally without introducing much strategy otherwise.

  2. Private messages: This rule allows players to send written notes to each other. There are two variations here: 1) the recipient can’t show the note to anyone else. 2) the recipient can show the note to others. In either case, players are allowed to lie about the contents of the note.

  3. Multiple sheriff investigations: This rule allows the sheriffs to conduct multiple investigations. I found it overpowered because players would rely on sheriff investigations over social deduction.

  4. Role reveal: This rule allows individual mafia, healer, or sheriff players to forgo their action for the night. Instead, they decide to reveal their role by performing a specific gesture to the narrator. The narrator then temporarily wakes up a player of their choosing. The player who wakes up is now familiar with the role of the player who revealed themselves to them. Note that the reverse is not true. This means that, say, a healer who reveals themself to a player they deem innocent risks exposing their role to a mafia. Layers of strategy ensue. A healer in this scenario might “bait” the mafia to target them and subsequently heal themself. A mafia might reveal their role to a civilian; if the civilian is too aggressive towards them during the round, the mafia can frame the civilian as suspiciously quick to accuse others. The main reason I don’t play with role reveal often is that it inflates the length of an already long night phase.

  5. Alternate win conditions: One way to tweak the balance of the game is to modify the win conditions for some factions. Maybe the good guys win when they vote out all but one mafia. Maybe the mafia win when non-mafia players only outnumber them by 2 or less. I haven’t really tested these alternate win conditions.

  6. Random split: You can assign the split randomly according to some rules. This keeps players in the dark about how many players of each role are alive. It didn’t change the gameplay as much as I expected.

There are also no shortage of alternate roles to implement in the game (skip these if you don’t care):

  1. Double agent: If the number of players in a particular role dwindles “too rapidly” (by some specification), the double agent is inaugurated into that role. For example, say that there are 2 mafia and 1 of them is voted out during the first round. During the next night phase, the narrator will wake the double agent during the mafia phase to signal their new role. The double agent’s win condition depends on the role they inhabit by the end of the game. If the double agent never “substitutes” another player, they have the same win condition as the good guys. I designed the double agent as a counterbalance for horrendous players. In practice, it felt like players’ efforts became nullified.

  2. Jack of All Trades: The Jack of All Trades (JAT) has three actions in their “toolkit”: kill, heal, and investigate. After the sheriff phase of the night phase, the JAT may elect to use any combination of these three actions. Once they have used an action, they can’t use again for the rest of the game. I intended the JAT as a role with high skill expression. In reality, it came down to lots of arbitrary play.

  3. Mayor: The mayor has two votes, but their identity is known to all players at the beginning of the game. The mayor has a second life with the same rules as the jester’s second life. The mayor is intended to rally the good guys in eliminating the mafia. We paired this rule with role reveal so that healers and sheriffs could reveal themselves to the mayor. Since the mayor is known as innocent, they could thereby declare which players were innocent. The mayor shifted the focus of the game from social deduction to role gimmicks.

  4. Veteran: The veteran can choose to trap their house for one night. If the mafia target the veteran that night, one of them randomly dies, regardless of whether the veteran was healed. It’s funny as the veteran to taunt the mafia into killing you, only to get them back. Alas, the role extends the duration of the night phase without adding much meaningful strategy.

  5. Godfather: The Godfather is revealed as thumbs down when the sheriff investigates them. The Godfather chooses who the mafia kill. The role doesn’t meaningfully change the game and adds unnecessary noise to sheriff investigations.

  6. Alternate Mafia: What if the mafia didn’t know each other and/or they were on separate teams? This isn’t as fun as it sounds. Whereas it’s normally possible to deduce the mafia from how they talk about each other (e.g., vouching for each other), multiple mafia factions greatly weaken this possibility. It also introduces so much noise to voting discussions that it’s difficult to reach a consensus.

  7. Alternate Jester: If there are multiple jesters in the game, they can play in teams or alone. In the former case, jesters in the same team there are several possible win conditions you can use: 1) the first jester team to have all of their members voted out wins 2) the first jester team to have any of their members voted out wins 3) the first team to have some arbitrary proportion of their members voted out wins. You might consider tweaking or removing the jester’s second life when there are teams of jesters. In the latter case, where jesters play alone, the game ends when a jester is voted out. That jester wins. I find that having more than one jester introduces even more irritating noise to the game than having multiple teams of mafia.

Hopefully you’ve noticed the general design principles behind my house rules. I want Mafia games to emphasize social deduction over all else. The roles serve to complement the social aspects of the game—not supplant them. It’s also important not to introduce unnecessary noise or uncertainty to the game. All this is well and good in theory, but trying these ideas in actual games is the best way to test them.

Social Context

Mafia is a fundamentally social game. Practice can familiarize you with the intricacies of its rules, but the main skill progression is opaque. One of the biggest variables in a game is who is playing. It’s easy for group dynamics to set in. Some players are disproportionately associated with a given role. Confirmation biases run rampant; “I knew he was the mafia and no one listened!” many foolishly say. In games where players are distracted or lack information, voting becomes arbitrary. Kill patterns emerge as players identify the biggest threats to them. Healers attempt to adapt to these patterns.

Despite this, players can genuinely improve in their skill level. They often learn to suppress their “tells” after another player susses them out.6 The nature of the game is such that players identify each other’s mistakes afterwards. Unfortunately, the cycle of improvement creates an unsatisfying equilibrium where players struggle to deduce anything about each other from social behaviors. It’s sort of like rock paper scissors, which isn’t as random as people think. When you’re more inexperienced at the game, it’s easy to fall into patterns. You might cycle through a pseudorandom sequence of rock, paper, and scissors. You might throw scissors by default7 (a lot of you guys do this by the way). Repeated gameplay “smooths out” these patterns because players adapt to each other to the point where behavior is hardly predictable.8

This brings me to a bittersweet conclusion. I no longer enjoy Mafia as much as I used to, especially when playing with my usual group. We’ve optimized to the point that there are no low hanging fruit left.9 Games more random than ever before. It takes a high level of skill to eke out an advantage. It can feel almost…deterministic. Nihilistic. Like nothing I do during a game matters anymore. Maybe we only enjoy games—enjoy life experiences—for so long until they get old.10

Thank you for reading! Subscribe to receive more posts and support my work.

1

We might expect a game (e.g., tabletop games, video games, etc.) to have minimal or manipulable luck, for example. Principles of effective game design aren’t set in stone. Party games are especially notorious for disregarding them.

2

If the game has a huge number of players (~18+), you might consider multiple rounds of voting. This allows players to vote out multiple players each round.

3

These rates were obtained by running the simulation on the default split with 1000 iterations for each player count.

4

Interestingly, jester wins never exceed mafia wins in the graph, except with 7 players. I’ve found that this trend continues at arbitrarily high player counts under the default split. This is likely because it becomes increasingly unlikely that the jester is voted out as the player count increases.

5

You can think of this like the gambler’s fallacy. Suppose I flip a fair coin 100 times in a row. You must predict the outcome of each coin flip as either heads or tails. Suppose I impose an “overdose” rule that you can’t predict the same outcome more than two times in a row. This is inconsequential because switching your prediction between heads and tails doesn’t affect your accuracy.

6

This dovetails nicely with a tangential discussion about what your objective as a player should be. Should you view each game as independent or craft a meta-strategy that allows you to win as many as possible? If the latter is true, you might keep your strategies secret after the game is over. There’s also a question of what behavior to partake in outside of the game. For example, if you’re playing Mafia with a group of strangers, you might pretend to be dumb to deceive people. It’s fascinating to think about how the elements surrounding a gameplay experience constitute the game itself. It’s sort of like how you might value the presentation of a dish at a restaurant in addition to its taste.

7

I can’t remember when, but someone hypothesized to me that people who watch anime are substantially more likely to throw scissors in the first round of a rock paper scissors game. I want to say that this is true.

8

In fighting games, pro gameplay can come down to wheover can predict the other player’s actions just slightly better. In a fighting game, players throw so many punches and kicks that the differences add up. In contrast, in a Mafia game, players make too few consequential decisions (voting, killing, etc.) for miniscule differences in predictive ability to affect the outcome.

9

I chose not to write about strategies for the game because I want anyone reading this to have the joy of discovering strategies themself. I also got kind of lazy.

10

I’m realizing that my Substack articles habitually go from a niche topic to a sentimental conclusion. Is this cliche?

item.title: Some Interesting Things #2
item.description: why Substack is slop, how to live forever, and more
item.content:encoded:
0: On Substantive Writing

I find myself with ideas not substantive enough to warrant an article, yet novel1 enough to share. I try to write “project articles” like this one or this one from time to time. These are more time-intensive articles that involve some combination of transformative personal experience, research, and technical expertise. The effort is well worth it. They’re immensely rewarding, edifying, and distinctly personal. I intersperse project articles between “smaller” articles. These are articles where I explore some topic I haven’t seen discussed. This is article is such an article.

I want to avoid reducing this Substack to intellectual slop—the kind of writing that doesn’t change you or teach you or invigorate you. I suspect this is because many writers believe that they can produce excellent work in a vacuum. In contrast, my best articles are forged from novel life experiences2. Even the most abstract of writings benefits from the author’s conscious experiences.

It’s possible to draw inspiration in unexpectedly obscure ways. For example, when I wrote an article about population ethics, I recalled a video game I played called Haven. The game is about the life of a couple stranded on a far-off planet. It’s a cozy and surprisingly emotional. I remember reflecting on the value of the even the smallest human interactions in a vast universe. This prompted me to think about the moral value of a population in which there are few people who live blissfully. Think of it like this: is a world where two people live happily better than one where billions live “decent” lives? I couldn’t have thought about population ethics the way I did if I didn’t play that game.

All this is to argue that writing benefits enormously from the personal experiences of the author. This is probably why I’m short of ideas for project articles as of the time of writing. I haven’t had many novel experiences (that I want to share) within the past month. So for now, enjoy this comparatively lukewarm article; I hope I didn’t succumb to the same issues I pointed out.

1: How to Live Forever

Human immortality is a quintessential topic of speculative science, explored across numerous stories, cultures, and time periods. There’s even a field of study dedicated to it: gerontology.

About a year ago, one of my friends told me about a drug called salvia. Apparently, some of its users report hallucinating an entire 10 years of life, including memories of a raising a family who don’t exist. These hallucinations supposedly span a mere 5 minutes. Can you imagine experiencing 10 years of hallucinated life in 5 minutes? The veracity of these reports is irrelevant. My main takeaway was that our perceived lifespan matters far more than our actual lifespan.

It’s been said that time seems to speed up as we age. One hypothesis is that novel experiences, more common in childhood, slow our perception of time. This is consistent with my experience. In late July, I spent four days on a trip to the Bay Area in California. By the time I returned, I felt like I was gone for an entire month. I had an epiphany. It’s far more tractable to extend your perceived lifespan than to extend your actual lifespan. My California trip, for instance, effectively “extended” my lifespan by over 3 weeks.

Therefore, it’s plausible that novel opportunities can more tractably increase effective human lifespans than some medical advancements. Naturally, we’d expect a longer perceived lifespan to accompany a longer lifespan. The effect is thus complementary; a longer life allows for more novel experiences, which allows for an even longer perceived lifespan. At an individual level, this suggests that we should emphasize both good health and novel experiences. At a population level, our institutions should afford people the agency to pursue novel experiences. For example, if the global population was wealthier, we might travel more.

I know this is vague and (ironically) not that novel. After all, what even is a “novel” experience? Regardless, there were many times in my life when I didn’t consciously pursue novel experiences. Only now do I see benefits so large that they include an increase in perceived lifespan.

2: Astrology is Useful

A few months ago, I went with some friends to receive a tarot reading. These kinds of astrological services are more fruitful than I thought.

First, astrology is potentially predictive or revelatory. Astrologers can infer information about their clients, such as their mood, from basic human observation. Maybe some astrologers have a Sherlock Holmes-level of observation. During Tarot readings in particular, the astrologer can begin with vague claims and refine them using the client’s reaction. For example, if an astrologer says that you struggle to regulate your emotions, you might subconsciously nod in agreement. This allows them to probe deeper into that issue using increasingly precise claims.

Second, astrology can prompt introspection. If an astrologer makes a vague claim about you, like that “you really care about people,” this encourages you to question the statement. The astrologer doesn’t need to make any significant “divinations” about you to say something meaningful.

Ultimately, I doubt that astrological services are a worthwhile use of money. You don’t need to pay someone to read you or help you introspect. A good friend should suffice.

3: Gyms and Driving

Lifting weights and running have interesting properties as a form of skill development. The amount of weight you lift and your running pace are objective measures of your skill level. It’s generally unambiguous whether someone is stronger or faster than you.3 Other skills, such as writing, lack such measures. When I lift a weight at the gym, it’s relatively clear how well I performed. I could have botched my form, but otherwise the weight and the reps don’t lie.4

Also relatively unambiguous is how to progress and/or push yourself to your limits. In weightlifting, you’re generally encouraged to lift until or near failure. Failure is literally an integral part of the process. Whether your arms are twigs or logs, you struggle with the weight you lift. That’s poetic.

Driving a car has much less savory properties as a form of skill development. First and foremost, mistakes are punished heavily. You can die from a driving mistake. You can’t die from a writing mistake.5 Thus, drivers are strongly discouraged from pushing their skills to their limit, such as by speeding. You might say that all kinds of skills, including weightlifting and running, have safety guidelines. Though this is true, these skills still allow people to safely push themselves to their limits (e.g., lifting to failure with proper form).

Likewise, drivers don’t receive feedback on certain kinds of mistakes until it’s too late. For example, I don’t have any experience with car crashes. Although I learned how to deal with a car accident hypothetically, I lack practical experience. Unfortunately, car accidents don’t always leave the driver with the opportunity to receive feedback. A dead person can’t learn from their mistakes.

Despite how comfortable I’ve become with learning new skills, my attitude towards becoming a better driver is unenthusiastic. The risk of an accident doesn’t make for the most conducive learning environment. In life, I try to stay optimistic by establishing a “bottom line” whenever I fail. For example, if I bomb an exam, there’s always another exam. At the very least, I live to see another day. The bottom line in driving is less comforting. I guess no more than a few people can die, so that’s something.

Thank you for reading! Subscribe to receive more posts and support my work.

1

One of my heuristics for whether I should write about something on Substack is whether I’ve heard anyone discuss the topic before.

2

I’m not saying that I have more novel experiences than the average person. Rather, I’ve made it a point to seek these experiences. In the past year, the following experiences have culminated in at least one Substack article:

  • I joined a religious club at my university as an agnostic (atheist at the time of joining)

  • I learned a bit of quantum physics

  • I had a mystical experience

3

Okay, there are more nuances to this. For example, someone might sprint faster than you, while you’re the faster marathon runner. Nevertheless, you can make objective comparisons of running skill with running itself. You can make such objective comparisons in, say, basketball, but it would require a competitive environment far removed from the vagaries of the sport (e.g., teamwork, specialized roles, etc.).

4

We’re not going to turn this into a phenomenological argument that I could mis-perceive how much weight I lifted or how many reps I performed.

5

Okay, this also has more nuances to it. You might get killed if you write propaganda inside a totalitarian government. You get what I mean. It’s more appropriate to say that the cost of mistakes in writing is negligible in most circumstances.

item.title: The Cowboy and The Outlaw
item.description: Foreword
item.content:encoded:
Foreword

I experienced a revelatory period of altered consciousness during a dream. A story subconsciously manifested in my head. I’ve attempted to adapt my vision into a short story, with a dash of prose and a sprinkle of artistic liberties. The article I initially wanted to write seemed best split into two parts. This article, the first part, contains my adaptation. The second part will explore the interpretations of my dream, especially in relation to this question: are stories invented or discovered?

I used AI for cursory research on the American Wild West. However, the writing is entirely my own. Beware that the story contains descriptions of violence and suicidal ideation. I hope you enjoy.

The Cowboy and The Outlaw

The withered corn in the family garden crumbled to dust that slipped through the Cowboy’s fingers. He coughed on the obsidian-colored Particulate suspended in the gray sky. Covering his mouth with his red bandana, he walked back inside the house. The wooden planks on the porch creaked harshly underneath his boots. The rotting wooden walls could only protect his wife and daughter for so long.

He glanced behind himself, pretending that the carpenter was still alive to repair his house. Nothing remained but his dilapidated shack. Nothing in this town but everyone’s skeletons lying on the ground—ensnared in vile, black tendrils. That man got to them when he was out with his family.

The Outlaw.

He refused to so much as think of that wretch’s name. Sometimes he wished he was in town when everyone got massacred. He reckoned he could’ve taken that wretch down. And if the wretch’s bullet wound up in his heart—dark tendrils burrowing through his flesh until it enveloped him in Blight—would that have been so bad?

He shut the door behind himself with the same disappointment as common nowadays. “Papa!” his daughter exclaimed, running up to him. She was up to his belly button now, so the hug from her bone-thin arms strangled him a bit. She was about six or seven years old, though Daddy was beginning to count her age differently, as three months—the amount of time she had left. They had enough food in the kitchen to last them a while, but the air only got more dreadful to breathe each day as that monster corrupted the sky.

“Ma taught me how to subtact!” she beamed.

“Subtract, sweetheart,” his wife said. “Let’s give Papa a moment to breathe, okay?”

The little girl let go of him and started playing with one of her dolls in the corner of their house. It was covered in black splotches of what little Particulate seeped indoors.

“How many crops do we have left?” his wife asked, her face pale and gaunt.

“It’s not lookin’ good. Three cornstalks left. Not enough time to harvest.”

“We’re going to be alright then!” she smiled. Her eyes didn’t agree with her smile.

He took her emaciated hand in his. “We don’t got much time,” he whispered.

“We’ve got plenty of time! I’m gonna teach her multiplication tomorrow.”

“Honey, she’s not growin’ much. I can make the soil clean again.”

“Dear, I’m not having this conversation with you.”

“I need to venture out. To kill that bastard.”

“You need to stay with your family,” she hissed, grabbing his arm.

“There’s no one left. None, goddammit.”

“You have us! I never liked these folks to begin with!”

“I’m done with this.” He yanked his arm away and rummaged through the kitchen cupboards, tossing food and supplies into his knapsack. The sounds of his rummaging drowned out his wife’s pleas, which turned to screams. Once he was done, he turned to face the door, obstructed by an insistent mother.

“You’re not leaving, fool!” she screamed, crossing her arms.

His daughter tugged at his sleeve. “Papa, are you leaving?” she teared up, clenching her worn dress with her other hand.

He knelt and touched his forehead to his daughter’s. “Papa’s gonna make you strong and healthy. Just like me.” He marched towards his wife and shoved her to the ground. He tied the red bandana around his mouth. He shoved the door open, ready to run out, until he heard his daughter wailing. He realized he might never hear that voice again. Better to turn around and stay? No. Clenching his fists around his knapsack, he stepped out and slammed the door behind himself without looking back.

And so, the lone Cowboy set out on the barren road eastward, his only companions the sun, the moon, and the Blighted corpses along the ruined landscapes ahead.

It was arduous to walk across the world. The Cowboy sat down on a rock to rest his legs. The quaint campfire he built warmed him. It was nice not to worry about the wind anymore. The Particulate on the other hand, was dreadful to breathe; it clawed viciously at his lungs. A permanent reminder that there was hardly a respite left in the world. He looked up at the sky, hoping the stars had magically returned since they went missing. Alas, the full moon shined in solitude. What a shame. Stargazing was one of his favorite pastimes in his days as a wandering cowboy.

He cooked some black beans on a pan over the flames. They blended together with the black pollution. What we would give for bacon if the Blight hadn’t devoured the pigs. He slipped the beans underneath his bandana, coughing whenever the air entered his throat. Days of traveling eastward without a horse—they all withered away—was exhausting. He surveyed the land for anything eye-catching. Back in the day, these prairies flourished with birds and bison and lofty grass that glimmered in the golden sunlight. Now there were no chirping birds to hear or bison to be seen. Most of the grass had crumbled to dust, leaving cracked, barren rock. The few remaining patches of grass slumped, their once golden sheen tainted in an oily black.

There wasn’t much to see outside of his family’s cabin.

The next morning, he continued his journey past hills, marshes, and rivers. The few trees that hadn’t crumbled to dust had no leaves. It was like winter, yet even the pine trees had no needles. Would his daughter ever know what pine trees were supposed to look like? He drew his revolver from the holster that was always at his side, in case he encountered Him. He pointed it directly at a tree branch about the same distance from the ground that His heart would be. Imagining that devil at the other end filled with him rage. He felt his finger tremble around the trigger, tempted to pull it at the figment of his imagination. He calmed down and put the revolver back in its holster. The Cowboy only needed one bullet, since he had never missed a shot. However, he wanted to fire all six bullets into that fucker’s body.

He never got a good look at the fucker, but he imagined the guy to be the most hideous man imaginable. He remembered the exact day when the man robbed him of his world. The sky was already polluted and the stars missing. While everyone else was in town, he took his family out to fish nearby. He was reeling something in with his daughter, while his wife went to fetch some firewood from a thicket. Then the sky turned dark. The grass turned black and withered in a circle as the scourge of a man walked into town. The Cowboy could only discern a black outfit and hat. A young boy greeted the mysterious figure. The scourge shot a bullet through the boy’s skull. The townsfolk screamed, running as fast as they could. Some of the men tried to fire back at him to no avail. The scourge slaughtered with monstrously rapid, precise bullets whose Blight devoured everyone in sight.

The Cowboy held his daughter tight behind a boulder until well after they couldn’t hear any more gunshots. They walked for an hour until they found his wife huddled terrified behind a tree on the town outskirts. He took them back home, shielding his daughter’s eyes from the graveyard left behind: the bones of neighbors and friends ensnared in the tendrils that devoured their flesh. He never let his family leave the house again. He couldn’t let them see the corpses—the constant reminder that he wasn’t there to protect the town. The Cowboy never missed a shot, but what good is that when he’s not there to take the shot?

He continued his journey the next day to a black, contaminated river. The Cowboy tracked his target by following concentrations of the Blight. As easy as it was to follow this unambiguous trail, the surrounding sights of decay wore on him. “What if He’s immortal?” he mused. “I’m the best shot there is,” he reassured himself. Reassurances only mean so much when they come from oneself. He could always head back to the only people left to provide the reassurances. The only warmth left in this wasteland. If he died to Him, he would never experience it again. All he had to do was follow the trail back. He could enjoy whatever time he had left with them.

He stared into the raging river. His stomach grumbled from the absence of rations; he’d forgotten to eat. The rush of the river hypnotized him. Maybe if he fell inside, it could take him back home, he thought. Then, he hallucinated the devil in the water. Suddenly, he snatched a rock that appeared near the surface of the river. “I’ve got you now!” he screamed, mistaking the rock for his target. He pinned the rock to the ground, strangling it tightly like it was His neck. He eventually snapped back to reality, the hallucination of the target dissolving from his hands.

“There’s no corner of this world where I won’t murder you!” he screamed at the rock.

That night, he ate about triple the amount of beans, corn, and sunflower seeds that he had planned to ration. He hoped the extra food could stifle the melancholy of remembering his family. He’d stopped keeping track of the date through what felt like years of wandering. It didn’t feel worthwhile to estimate the date from the amount of rations he had left in his knapsack. He didn’t sleep well that night.

The next morning, he found an unpleasant change in scenery. The filth in the air was thicker than ever. The flora looked freshly decayed; their crumbled remnants hadn’t fully seeped into the cracked soil yet. The demon was nearby.

The Cowboy followed the trail of newly decayed grass. Soon, he encountered grass on the trail that hadn’t fully decayed. The wilted, black grass clung for its life as if to guide him to its killer. He coughed on the highest concentration of Particulate he had seen. It all pointed to a circle of cracked earth that warded away any surrounding verdure. The light of the full moon shined on a figure wearing a black cowboy hat. When the figure turned around, its black boots clacked harshly on the broken soil. It wore a suit so black that looking at it was like peering into an endless abyss. The shade from the hat obscured its visage. Faceless. It was truly a nightmare given form.

It was The Outlaw.

The Cowboy cautiously hovered his right hand over his holster. The nightmare hovered his hand over his own. Even his revolver was black. It couldn’t be seen. No matter. The Cowboy never missed a shot. He never lost a duel. His journey had proved that he would never yield. The victor of a duel was not the one with a faster or more accurate draw, but the one who could more accurately read the other’s very soul. The Cowboy could sure as hell feel his opponent’s soul. It was too odious to be called a soul. Nightmarish, empty, horrific, and far too dark. Indeed, it was a mass of pure evil.

It all came down to a single shot that would reunite him with his family and cure the world of the Blight. Would it bring everyone else back too? He drew his revolver, aimed for the heart, and pulled the trigger. It collapsed to the ground. The atmosphere gradually purified and the stars reappeared in the sky. What little grass remained around them regained its color, standing itself firmly upright.

The Cowboy approached the corpse. He returned his revolver back in its holster; he didn’t feel like shooting it another five times anymore. The world was regaining its beauty, yet he felt empty. He could still feel the corpse’s soul. It wasn’t completely dead. He knelt beside the body, red blood from its chest wound pooling underneath. A black bandana obscured the face. He gently removed the cloth, wondering what hideous visage lurked underneath.

It was his wife.

“You abandoned us,” she whispered, her face more pale and gaunt than ever. “The Blight grew stronger inside our own home.”

“Why?” he cried.

“Each day was pure agony. She died.”

As she closed her eyes, the flicker of her soul extinguished. The Cowboy knelt over her, collapsing into tears.

He eyed the revolver at his side. The barrel contained five bullets—more than enough. He stood up and pointed the revolver up his chin. Then he gazed at the beautiful stars in the sky, tears flowing down his cheek. His finger trembled around the trigger.

THE END

Thanks for reading! Subscribe to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: P-hacking in Empirical Research
item.description: Disclaimer: I am not a professional economist.
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: I am not a professional economist. Please let me know if I committed any factual inaccuracies.

“Studies have shown X,” some say. “Scientists say Y.” Unfortunately, empirical research isn’t a bastion of veracity. Researchers can apply questionable methodology, selectively report results, and fabricate data without getting caught. It’s commonly mentioned in the research ecosystem, yet the formal study of this—metascience—is hardly discussed. I want to share what a few papers have to say.

Background

First, let’s review some background information. The goal of empirical research is to produce informative statistics. For example, if I’m studying the height difference between men and women, I might collect a sample of the heights of 1,000 adult men and 1,000 adult women. I could compare the mean height of men and women in the sample to conclude that men are taller than women. Say the sample mean is 175 cm for men and 160 cm for women. This isn’t enough to conclude that men are taller than women. If the height difference was 1 cm instead of 15 cm, for instance, we might suspect that the difference is due to random chance.

Suppose you flip two fair coins 100 times each and one coin lands on heads 2 times more than the other (e.g., 51 heads vs. 49 heads). Does this mean that one coin is more predisposed towards heads than the other? Not necessarily. But what if we didn’t know that the coins are both fair? What if one coin landed on heads 20 times more than the other? That feels too extreme to attribute to random chance. This is the essence of statistical significance. It’s the idea that if a result (e.g., one coin landing on heads way more than the other) is sufficiently “extreme”, then it’s probably not due to random chance.

In the context of the aforementioned height comparison, there are statistical methods to assign a probability to how extreme the difference between male and female heights is. Informally, a p-value is the probability that a statistical result is at least as extreme as it is, assuming the result is due to random chance. We can obtain a p-value for the height difference—the probability that the difference in mean height between the male sample and the female sample is at least 15 cm. Note that this is only if the difference is due to random chance. An arbitrarily low p-value suggests that the statistic is not due to random chance. That is, men are actually taller than women.

P-hacking and publication bias

P-hacking is when researchers perform flawed data analyses to obtain statistically significant results (e.g., a low p-value). For example, let’s say that I’m estimating the effect of an individual’s level of education (high school diploma, bachelor’s degree, etc.) and their annual income. A good researcher would try to control for other factors that affect someone’s future income. For instance, they might control for parental income; individuals with wealthier parents tend to earn more income, regardless of whether they attend college. However, suppose that you’re intent on showing a statistically significant relationship between education and earnings. You could intentionally neglect to control for other variables to “inflate” your results.

P-hacking is difficult to catch because it can be more sophisticated than in my example. It can have serious consequences, especially when studies aren’t reproduced. In economics, a study’s statistical significance can determine its policy implications. An unscrupulous researcher’s decision to p-hack could cost lives. Fortunately, violations of research integrity bear severe professional consequences.1 You might wonder, then, why anyone would p-hack. Well, there’s a belief that statistically significant results are more likely to get published. This is called publication bias. It distorts scientific consensus via the over-representation of statistically significant results. Imagine if 99% of medical studies concluded that broccoli is healthy, while the other 1% said otherwise. If only that 1% of studies received publication, we might deem broccoli unhealthy. This is an extreme example, but you get the gist.

Intuitively, it’s intriguing to read that a policy has an effect; an ineffectual policy just doesn’t make headlines. Researchers, determined to publish their work, hope for significant results. Academics spend years in fields so specialized that they may not conceive of working on anything else. For a poor, overworked academic chasing prestige or tenure (a position of high pay and job security in academia), a publication can seem like the only light at the end of their proverbial tunnel. Research is costly and time-consuming. When an experiment doesn’t provide significant results, the desperate academic is left to grasp at straws. Or they could fudge the numbers.

Statistical significance is typically measured in terms of p-values. Think of a p-value as the probability that results would occur due to sheer random chance. For example, if I flip a fair coin 100 times, the probability that it lands on heads every time is astronomically low (1/2^100). If this happened, we’d have reason to think that something special is going on with the coin. Thus, a low p-value is an indicator that a phenomenon is not random. Lower p-values are considered more statistically significant. Accordingly, p-hackers try to reduce the p-values of their results.

We conventionally use .10, .05, and .01 as thresholds for p-values. The lowest threshold indicates the highest level of statistical significance. For the purposes of getting published, researchers care more about the threshold a p-value falls under than it’s exact value. That is, if my research yields a p-value of .01, I have no incentive to decrease it further. This gives us reason to believe that p-hackers would reduce the p-values of their results until they just barely fall under one of these thresholds.

Evidence of p-hacking and publication bias

“Unpacking P-Hacking and Publication Bias” by Brodeur et. al examines patterns of the eponymous phenomena.2 This particular paper uses data from the Journal of Human Resources (JHR), a leading empirical microeconomics journal. Submissions are reviewed by the head editor or a co-editor; journal editors are typically experienced in their subfield. The editor either rejects the paper or sends it to editors. The editor decides based on reviewer reports whether to reject the paper or grant revise and resubmit (R&R). The authors of a paper are expected to revise and resubmit it if it’s granted R&R. Resubmitted manuscripts are subsequently assigned to further review. This paper focuses on initial submissions to JHR from 2013 through 2018. I’m glossing over the rest of its methodology.

Suppose we plot a histogram of the p-values in a collection of empirical studies. This is called a p-curve. If p-hacking exists, we’d expect to see bunching—an unusual spike—in the histogram around the p-value thresholds. Indeed, this is what we observe below.

This histogram is constructed from the initial submissions to top 25 econ journals published in 2015 and 2018.3 Notice the small “spikes” around aforementioned p-value thresholds. We’d expect the distribution to be “smooth” in the absence of p-hacking or selective reporting (i.e. if researchers submit their results only when significant). The evidence strongly suggests some form of p-hacking or selective reporting.

If you’re wondering why the distribution is right-skewed (it’s “concentrated” on the left), it’s because statistically significant results tend toward lower probabilities. Say you test whether a coin is fair by flipping it 100 times. In this context, the p-value is the probability that the number of heads is at least as far from 50 as it is. If the coin lands on heads 60 times, the p-value is the probability that a fair coin would have a number heads greater than/equal to 60 or less than/equal to 40. Suppose the coin is not fair and its “true” probability of landing on heads is 80%. Then we’d tend to observe a number of heads far greater than 50. Thus, the p-values tends toward low values. Similarly, many of the studies submitted to journals are statistically significant. Given that they tend towards statistical significance, they will concentrate at low p-values.4

Guardrails against p-hacking

Ideally, the scrutiny of peer reviewed journals mitigates p-hacking. Does this hold up in practice? Kind of. R&R doesn’t reduce p-hacking.5 Specifically, there’s no evidence that the p-curve for initial submissions exhibits significantly more bunching than the p-curve for submissions that survive to an R&R decision. “Unpacking P-Hacking and Publication Bias” also found a negligible effect of the peer review process on p-hacking and selective reporting. I suspect that editors and reviewers in empirical research journals scrutinize submissions on criteria unrelated to suspicions of p-hacking. It’s unfeasible for them to comb through every minute detail of the methodology.

The economics profession has normalized the inclusion of replication packages—repositories of data, code, and notes that simplify the replication of research. Although this is a step in the right direction, there’s no guarantee that the data itself wasn’t fabricated. Indeed, it’s difficult to replicate the data collection itself. Logistically costly methods of data collection, such as large-scale field experiments, are especially tough to replicate. Sometimes we don’t have time to reproduce an experiment. For example, the kinds of experiments that might inform economic policy responses to AGI must adapt to meteoric advancements in AI. We don’t even have to speculate about AI to see the constraints on research replication. Crises like the Great Depression exerted an urgency on economic policy interventions.

There are successful methods of mitigating p-hacking and publication bias. Pre-registration is the registration of an empirical study before it’s conducted. A pre-analysis plan (PAP) is a specification of the methods of an empirical study before the study is performed. In principle, pre-registration and PAPs reduce p-hacking by imposing transparency in empirical research. To see why, suppose you plan to conduct an experiment on the effect of afterschool tutoring on the test grades of elementary school students. Keep in mind that researchers are incentivized to obtain statistically significant results. Suppose you find no statistically significant effect of the tutoring.

There are ways to manipulate the analysis ex post to obtain significant results. One such method is to keep dividing the sample into subgroups; none of the students showed significant improvements, but what about, say, black boys? You could claim that afterschool tutoring raises test scores for some particular subgroup without disclosing how ineffectual it was for other subgroups. A pre-registration and PAP limits the ability for researchers to perpetrate these kinds of analyses.6

Evidence suggests that pre-registration alone has no substantive effect on p-hacking and publication bias. However, when coupled with a PAP, it reduces p-hacking and publication bias. It’s important to note that pre-registration and PAP practices vary. A medical study, for instance, may demand different kinds of transparency than an economic study. Also, pre-registration and PAP aren’t enforceable in all contexts. Many empirical economics papers rely on a quasi-experimental design, meaning they infer results from existing data instead of conducting an experiment. Pre-registration and PAP assumes that the data and analysis can only be performed after a future date. Even if a quasi-experimental design required a pre-registration and PAP, the researchers could simply manipulate their data before submitting these plans.

So far, I’ve discussed guardrails that make p-hacking more difficult. A supplementary approach is to restructure the incentives in the research ecosystem to discourage p-hacking, publication bias, and selective reporting. This is much easier said than done. Especially in an age where LLMs make it easier than ever to produce and p-hack research. Remedies to the issue are outside the scope of this article because it would require a lot of explanation (institutional reform is complicated). I anticipate that as long as there’s a scarcity of careers and resources in the research ecosystem7, researchers will try to game the system. Nevertheless, existing guardrails are a step in the right direction.

Some have proposed changes to the criteria for hiring, tenure, promotions, publication, and funding. Perhaps more value should be placed on null (statistically insignificant) results; leave no stone unturned. We could relax expectations on research output. I find this unlikely, as much of research funding is contingent on output. Why would someone fund research otherwise? The small possibility of a breakthrough or a genuine appreciation for knowledge don’t pay back investments. An evolution in the editorial process seems plausible. This might include increasing the demand for robustness checks—essentially “proof” that your results endure under a slightly different methodology.

Why do p-hacking and publication bias exist?

While I’ve explained the reasons for p-hacking and publication bias informally, it would be great to have some evidence. Thankfully, the authors of “Unpacking P-Hacking and Publication Bias” anonymously surveyed researchers and journal editors across several journals about their experiences.

Researchers commonly reported:

  • Not submitting null results (30% of respondents)

  • Reporting only a subset of dependent variables (~50% of respondents). For example, say that I’m studying the effects of a school counselor on student mental well-being. Suppose the effects I’m studying are on anxiety, depression, and self-reported improvements in mental well-being. If I only find significant results for the third outcome, I can exclude the results for the first two. The program seems more effective if all of its measured outcomes demonstrated significant results.

  • Excluding or re-categorizing data ex post (17% of respondents). This is like the scenario where the author keeps dividing their sample into subgroups.

  • Modifying the original hypothesis to better fit the data (24% of respondents). In lay terms, this is like changing the goal post to make something look more impressive.

  • Selecting regressors based on the results (24% of respondents). This is what I explained about the relationship between education and future earnings. Failing to control for relevant variables can inflate the results.

Note that these percentages likely underestimate true behaviors due to social desirability bias.

Researchers perceive statistical significance as important to the evaluation of their work. To quote the paper: “on a scale from 1 to 10, with 10 being ‘very important,’ authors on average reported an 8 in response to the following question: ‘For studies that are claiming to identify an effect of x on y, how important do you think statistical significance is in influencing the editor’s/reviewer’s decision…?’

It turns out that the perceptions of researchers don’t align perfectly with reality. If publication bias was substantial, we’d expect the distribution of p-values of published papers to have much more bunching than that of the initial submissions. That is, editors and reviewers would systematically cull papers with null results. Instead, the paper found that submissions bunched around conventional p-value thresholds (.01, .05, and .10) are more likely to get desk rejected (rejected before being sent to reviewers). However, a paper that avoids desk rejection is more likely to receive a positive recommendation from a reviewer if its results are statistically significant. So journals exhibit “anti-publication bias” initially and publication bias for papers that enter the peer review process. In aggregate, these effects “cancel out” such that the distribution of p-values between initial submissions and published papers are roughly the same.

You might wonder how the results generalize beyond a single economics journal from 2013 to 2018. The surveys report similar researcher behaviors across journals, implying that p-hacking behaviors generalize. Whether publication bias generalizes is more of a mystery. Other studies corroborate many of these findings; we’ll skip over these for brevity’s sake.

Conclusion

By now you should understand the importance of metascience. It illuminates the disheartening truth that even our most trusted source of knowledge—academic research—is fallible. P-hacking and publication bias stem from the research ecosystem’s relatively intractable incentive structure. Yet, progress occurred through a proliferation of replications, pre-registrations, and PAPs.

There’s a more general takeaway. Life exerts pressures on us to think less rigorously about what we know. Sometimes it’s comforting not to look deeper into an uncertainty. Sometimes there are incentives to convince people of spurious or bombastic claims. It’s exceedingly unfeasible to thoroughly verify the knowledge we encounter.8 Nonetheless, we can become more educated in “how we know” in addition to “what we know”. The “how” teaches us patterns to help make our understanding of reality just a bit more right.9

Bonus: why null results are “better”

There’s a cool paper about the informativeness of null results. Suppose you have some prior probability distribution on a parameter. If corresponding sample statistic is insignificant, the posterior probability distribution is more informative than if it was significant. In particular, it has lower variance.

Think of it like this in lay terms:

  • If your result is statistically insignificant, you know there’s probably nothing special going on.

  • If your result is statistically significant, there may or may not be something special going on. You haven’t ruled anything out.

Alternatively, finding a significant effect of some phenomenon prompts further study. Null results rule out a “dead end”. This is encapsulated in the figure below for a sample size of n = 10.
