item.title: Are Stories True?
item.description: no
item.content:encoded:
Note: this article references two of my previous works: Divine Knowledge and The Cowboy and The Outlaw. It contains major spoilers for the stories contained in both.

Where We Last Left Off

In “Divine Knowledge,” I experienced a metaphysically complex, altered state of consciousness for the first time. While in this state of consciousness, I entered a dream-like state. Here, I simultaneously spectated and participated in a breathtaking story of a world suffering under God’s purview. I discovered that my protagonist’s world was actually part of a multiverse. In my dream, I was shown that our universe is part of this multiverse, though I don’t actually believe this is true. In my dream, I was told that I would continue to incarnate in each realm of the multiverse. My accumulated wisdom would prepare me to eventually assume a duty as God of the multiverse.

Over a month later, I experienced a similar altered state of consciousness, albeit with less potency. A surreal story manifested in my mind. I wasn’t sure to what extent the story emerged subconsciously as opposed to consciously; ordinarily, coming up with a story feels like a chiefly conscious process to me.

This feeling of consciously coming up with the story and having the story subconsciously come to me was present in both experiences. In “Divine Knowledge” (DK), I simultaneously felt like a first-person observer, a third-person observer, an active participant, and an author sculpting my dream in real time. In contrast, when manifesting the story for “The Cowboy and The Outlaw” (TCTO), I felt mostly like a third-person observer and only slightly like an author. Moreover, while writing “Divine Knowledge” felt like transcribing a story, writing “The Cowboy and The Outlaw” felt like an adaptation of an existing story. I took artistic liberties in imbuing the latter with prose, world-building, and character details.

It’s unclear to me whether TCTO occurs within the multiverse that subsumes DK. This may seem like a strange statement. After all, didn’t I create these stories? Surely I’m the arbiter of the ontology of my stories. I’m here to challenge that.

Invention vs. Discovery

Are stories invented or discovered?

I think we’d agree that invention implies that an idea isn’t fundamental, inherent, or natural to reality. In contrast, discovery is associated with fundamental, inherent, or natural phenomena. You might say that capitalism is an invention, while our understanding of the evolutionary behaviors that resulted in it are discoveries. Another example is that we might consider the laws of physics discoveries and the space shuttles designed from them as inventions. However, inventions aren’t necessarily built upon discoveries. Many would say that pure mathematics—math done without any “practical” telos—is invented. A compelling argument for this is that some abstract mathematical ideas don’t seem to have a physical manifestation. Moreover, there’s an argument that applied mathematics is invented. If calculus describes the laws of physics, is that because the math is a fundamental property of the universe or because it’s a useful descriptive tool?

It’s difficult to dichotomize invention and discovery. You can read some interesting arguments about the ontology of math here.

It might seem trivial that stories are invented, rather than discovered. It takes a mind to construct and articulate ideas. That doesn’t seem like a discovery. Further, some stories lack objective truth—a quality we might deem necessary for discovery—by many definitions. Perhaps only “true” stories, such as biographies, are discovered.1 What about fiction? Although I find fiction overwhelmingly invented, it has some components of discovery as well.

First, some stories are deliberately ambiguous. Sometimes even the author doesn’t know what “truly” happens in their own story. I’m going to use the video game Hollow Knight as an example. The game sees the player explore a ruined kingdom called Hallownest. The player is left to decipher evidence to piece together the game’s story. Some of the game’s mysteries remain unsolved, despite the extensive dedication of the fandom’s lore community. For all we know, some of these mysteries are fundamentally unsolvable. Heck, we don’t know if even the developers of the game know the answers. The developers have confirmed that the game’s multiple endings are equally canon.2 Nonetheless, the fandom treats Hollow Knight’s lore as discoveries—like real history— because Hallownest is immersive enough to feel like its own reality. Fictional worlds, like other abstract ideas in our world, arguably exist not only as their physical manifestation (ink on a page, the physical state of a digital screen, etc.), but in some abstract sense. More on this later.

Second, my writing process is consistent with stories as both inventions and discoveries. I don’t literally think of stories as some idiosyncratic entity our minds pluck from an abstract realm. Rather, it feels more appropriate to discuss stories as abstract realities that exist outside the author’s mind. As I write fiction, my initial “invented” ideas start to take shape on their own.3 Characters characterize themselves. The plot charts itself. I become a scribe for the abstract ideas and sensory details that emerge in my subconscious mind. I can go from a scribe to a omnipotent God as I wish, tweaking the narrative at my discretion. Even so, the story partially develops by itself.4 The role of the subconscious mind in writing is so profound that sometimes my understanding of my own story changes when I read it.

Again, I’m not arguing that stories are discovered in the sense of being some physical property of the universe. I’m explaining why they can feel discovered. They feel especially discovered in interactive storytelling (video games, role-playing, etc.) or in one’s own writing. This leads me back to DK and TCTO. There’s one context where stories feel entirely discovered: dreams.

The True Story?

If I had to assign a percentage split between the feelings of invention and discovery in my stories, it would be about 40-60. In my dreams, it’s usually around 1-99, since I rarely lucid dream. DK is about 10-90; I consciously filled in some vague ideas, but the rest came rushing in subconsciously. The vision that inspired TCTO is 20-80. My written adaptation is more like 40-60, as per usual.

I list these splits to question how much of these stories I can attribute to my own skill as opposed to luck. By luck, I mean the subconscious processes of writing I associate with the discovery of a story. It’s like when you come up with an unusually good idea. Our creative skills seem to trend upward over time, yet we don’t always hit a home run. I certainly don’t. Altered states of consciousness—whether it be dreams, meditation, emotional states, alcohol, and/or drugs—illuminate the wonders of the subconscious mind.

The dream that manifested TCTO felt too discovered/lucky to consider my work. The Substack article, on the other hand, included enough invention to qualify as mine.5 I say this because it has implications for the events of the story. It’s helpful to know the difference between what I experienced and what I added to the story.

Here are the details from the dream:

  • A scene of a cowboy and a black-clad desperado facing off at dusk. A black cloth covered the desperado’s face. The Old Western town around them was quiescent, not a person or blowing tumbleweed in sight.

  • I knew6 the Cowboy had no name. I knew the desperado’s name: The Outlaw

  • I can’t remember the exact order of events, but I recall the flashing back to the past before the duel concluded. The details were hazy. The world was dying in some way. The Cowboy chose, begrudgingly, to leave his family in pursuit of The Outlaw.

  • Flashing back to the duel, our protagonist defeated his nemesis with ease. It was anticlimactic.

  • He removed the Outlaw’s mask to reveal their identity: it was his wife.

I theorized about the possible explanations for the twist. It felt like an fundamentally, immutably discovered part of the story; I couldn’t just exclude it from the adaptation. After conferring with some friends (also ChatGPT and Claude) for possible explanations, here are some theories:

  1. There’s a time loop. The Cowboy abandoned his family, causing his wife to become The Outlaw. His wife tried to kill him out of resentment. I have a few issues with this theory. It’s both convoluted and a repeat of DK. It would also require hand-waving and/or the introduction of numerous potential plot holes. For example, why does his wife’s plan for revenge seem to bestow her magic powers that cause the Blight?

  2. The narrator and/or the Cowboy’s perception are unreliable. The Outlaw isn’t actually his wife. Maybe the Cowboy sees his wife’s face as a manifestation of guilt. ChatGPT and Claude were especially sympathetic to this theory.

  3. The Cowboy’s wife isn’t the true Outlaw. She simply disguised herself as him. My adaptation of the story strongly discredits this, as the Blight begins to disappear after her death. However, this is entirely plausible in the original story (the dream).

  4. There are multiple Outlaws. The Cowboy’s wife was merely one of them. My adaptation discredits this for the same reason. If there are multiple Outlaws, then it seems that only one of them caused the Blight.

  5. The Cowboy’s wife was genuinely the Outlaw. No time loop. This is my favorite interpretation, though it does introduce a potential plot hole. Namely, his wife’s motive for becoming the Outlaw is revenge, yet he only abandoned his family because of the Outlaw’s existence. This doesn’t explain why she became the Outlaw before he abandoned their family. Why did she kill the villagers? If she had control of the Blight, why did she unleash it? My adaptation fills in some details that we’ll cover in a bit.

The lack of a definitive explanation actually enhanced my enjoyment of the twist. It’s one of the main reasons I found the dream so compelling to begin with.7 My adaptation made some interpretations more credible than others via a series of creative decisions. I chose to rule out interpretation 3, since the Blight disappears after his wife’s death. Interpretation 3 felt too anticlimactic for me. Also, I wanted to add a cruel irony to the Cowboy’s victory in the duel: he succeeded in killing the Outlaw and restoring the world, but at the cost of his primary goal—to save his family.

Interpretation 4 fails to provide closure, as the existence of other Outlaws introduces another can of worms. I’m not that keen on continuing the story in a series about people affected by the Blight or some coalition working together to eradicate the Outlaws. There are plenty of stories about people coping with a decayed world.8 To me, the novelty of the article was a combination of factors: the vividness of my dream, the adaptation of my dream, the shocking twist, and the Cowboy’s decision to leave his family.

To believe in interpretation 1 requires prodigious speculation. It was somehow the first theory that came to me. I’m a big fan of a collection of tropes where the plot comes full circle in a disturbing way. It could be that the hero becomes the villain. Maybe the hero’s actions created the villain, such as by turning a character evil. Time loops, when adequately established, are an awesome way of doing this. My adaptation neither validates nor invalidates this interpretation in the same way that scientific discoveries don’t validate or invalidate the existence of unicorns. It’s with disappointment that I put this ridiculous theory to bed.

The uncertainty is really between interpretations 2 and 5. I find it difficult to rule out interpretation 2. I deliberately established that the Cowboy hallucinates. The interpretation is clean, introducing no plot holes that I can think of. It was actually too clean in my first draft of the article. Initially, I wrote that the Cowboy was with both is daughter and his wife when the Outlaw massacred their town (in the final version, his wife was nowhere to be seen).

This effectively ruled out interpretation 5. I wanted to keep interpretation 5 valid for a few reasons. First, I love the trope where the protagonist’s actions create the antagonist.9 Second, it adds some cruel ironies to the story. If the Cowboy never left his family, he wouldn’t have dueled his wife. If he didn’t kill her, he wouldn’t have discovered her identity. If he didn’t kill her, we don’t know what would’ve come of the world. Third, it adds some intrigue to his wife’s motives and magical abilities. Why did she massacre their town? If her existence is what produces the Blight, why does she continue to live? To me, it’s a good balance between intrigue and unexplained plot points that other interpretations lack.

Thus, I revised the story so that his wife is missing during the massacre. I also added a line of dialogue where she says “I never liked these folks to begin with!” It suggests a possible motive. It’s also compelling. The Cowboy misses the townsfolk so dearly that it intensifies his desire for revenge. His bereavement compels his decision to leave his family. In contrast, his wife ostensibly never liked them. Perhaps, in the past, the Cowboy neglected his family to spend time with them. Perhaps it was an attempt to relive his glory days as a gunslinger. By killing the townsfolk, she forced her husband to focus on their family, albeit in an apocalypse. Maybe she has a magical curse that ostracized her as a child. Maybe it gave her attachment issues, demonstrated in how controlling she is of her husband. Interpretation 5 is my favorite because it gives way to these fascinating theories.

Admittedly, this interpretation requires some suspension of disbelief. It’s unclear how the wife caught up to Cowboy, who by the time of their daughter’s alleged death was far away. It’s also unclear where she got her outfit and gun from. These details can easily be explained as the magic of someone who literally cursed the world.10

There are some more details I deliberately left ambiguous. I chose not to specify how the Cowboy and his wife met. I also left it slightly ambiguous whether the Cowboy shoots himself after the end of the story. Initially, I thought readers might wrack their brain over whether he ends his life. Instead, it seems almost certain that he shoots himself. In his perception, his wife and daughter are dead (neither is confirmed). It’s uncertain whether any fauna would re-emerge in his remaining years, let alone any humans. In other words, he has nothing left to live for.

The True Story

doesn’t exist.

A significant portion of this story was discovered (as opposed to invented). I see no reason to impose a definitive interpretation on the story. I’m not even sure I could. The original story was so compelling that I can’t bring myself to overwrite it; it would feel like a fundamentally different story.11

Is the author’s interpretation of their work the “true” interpretation? I disagree. I consider stories to exist beyond their physical presence (e.g., books) and their existence in the minds of their creators. Instrumentally, it’s more enjoyable to think of stories this way. Philosophically, to think otherwise admits peculiar properties of stories.

First, consider that stories are filtered through layers of translation. The creator translates their ideas to an artistic medium (text, pictures, etc.). The audience translates the medium into their own understanding, colored by their individual conscious experiences. Moreover, the author’s version of the story is by no means fixed. If stories only exist as an aggregate of ideas in the mind, then a different version of the story exists between the every reader, including the author.

Second, does the story continue to exist when the author dies? If you think stories only exist in the mind, you can rebut that the story lives on in the minds of readers. Even if the precise ideas that form the stories are filtered, maybe the understanding of the story remains similar enough. What if everyone who read a story died? Then maybe it exists only in its physical and/or digital12 records. What if these records also disappear? Perhaps it also partially exists in anyone who experienced the story without reading it, such as through a summary. It also may have left a lasting impact on the world, physically or otherwise (e.g., the Bible changed the world). At what point in this chain of questioning did the story cease to exist? It’s not a question with a definitive answer; I wouldn’t consider a story to exist once every summary, excerpt, retelling, and language translation of it is gone.13

Third, the author can consider some part of their story to exist without being physically/digitally written or thoroughly conceptualized. Suppose I write a sci-fi novel where an infinite number of idiosyncratic, life-containing planets inhabit the universe. How much would I have to write about or conceptualize a planet before it’s considered to exist (to the extent that the novel’s story exists)?14 A generous answer might be a description of the planet. I’d argue that claiming that there are infinitely many planets in the story isn’t enough for them to exist. Analogously, claiming that there are undiscovered species in oceans (in our world) doesn’t mean that they exist.

The argument that stories only exist physically and/or psychologically is only tenable under some peculiar intuitions. The view that stories also exist in some abstract way feels more intuitive. Granted, it belies our conventional intuitions of what it means for something to exist.

Conclusion

While stories are invented, they are also partially discovered. Their ambiguity, the writing process, and their abstract ontology complicate the determination of any “true” story. It’s so magical to me that creatives can act not only as creators, but as windows into ineffable ideas. That we may endlessly reinterpret stories, or even reality itself. That there is no end to some rabbit holes. That even an author may not know the truth of his own story.

Thank you for reading! Subscribe to receive new posts and support my work.

1

Even true stories are filtered through their teller. Sometimes they even turn out to be factually wrong.

2

In video games, there are sometimes multiple endings to the story. Often, one of these endings, referred to as the “true” ending, is the developer’s definitive vision for the story.

3

Among authors, this dichotomy is referred to as architects vs. gardeners (alternatively, plotters vs. pantsers). Architects heavily plan their story, while gardeners improvise. Notable examples of architects and gardeners include Brandon Sanderson and George R. R. Martin, respectively. In practice, all writers exhibit some combination of the two. For example, some might prefer to heavily plan the beginning and end of their story, while improvising the middle. Neither style is necessarily superior. For the 1% who cares, I’m more of a gardener; I plan out themes and major plot points, but the rest flows more organically.

4

Of course, the story doesn’t actually develop “by itself”—there are simply parts of it that come subconsciously. It’s sort of like saying that your lungs breathe by themselves.

5

I realize it’s strange to discredit someone’s work because their subconscious mind played a role in it. I’m writing this footnote during the revision of this article. I no longer discredit my story idea as luck.

6

When I say that I “knew”, I mean that this detail was so vivid that I had no uncertainties as to what I was perceiving.

7

The other reason was the Cowboy’s predicament. Should he leave his family for the chance to save the world, or enjoy a few more months with them? My subconscious mind probably took inspiration from Interstellar.

8

This is practically what defines the zombie genre.

9

According to interpretation 5, the Cowboy didn’t necessarily create the Outlaw, as she massacred the town well before he left his family. It’s more accurate to say that the Cowboy’s choice to leave his family—and the subsequent death of their daughter—motivated her to don her true identity once again. Vindictive, she tried and failed to defeat him in a duel.

10

Another “plot hole” is the question of why (under interpretation 5) she massacred the townsfolk when she did. Why not kill them earlier? Or even later? I don’t consider this a plot hole; maybe there was some event that brought her to her tipping point.

11

This brings up a question of how much a story can change before it’s no longer the same story. I’m not going to get into this here.

12

You could say that a digital record is a physical record because it’s an electrical phenomenon. Can the digital record be a physical record if computers stop working forever?

13

The Mahabharata has no definitive urtext. This, coupled with its complexity and salience, explain why so many disagreements around the story perpetuate. Some discussions, for instance, debate whether its protagonists are casteist. It’s cool that the question of whether a “true” version of a story exists has some practical application here. Was there ever a “true” version of the Mahabharata? If so, how historically accurate is it? If the answer to the former question is “yes”, then it has implications for the history of caste in India. If the answer to the latter is “yes”, then the Hindu Gods exist, confirming theism.

14

There’s a similar argument that mathematics exists beyond its physical representations. Some infinities, such as the infinitude of prime numbers, lack a physical representation.

item.title: Does UT Austin Weed Out Students?
item.description: analyzing UT Austin’s course grade data
item.content:encoded:
As a student at the University of Texas at Austin (UT), I spend some time thinking about our courses. Every semester, students scramble to register for courses with the easiest professors and most generous grade distributions. The effort is well worth it; a few hours of prudent optimization saves countless hours of stress in the coming semester. Have you ever regretted registering for a course or wished there was just one less item on your plate? Understanding the way institutional structures influence our day-to-day lives is fascinating. We don’t always have the data to draw such insights. Fortunately, UT has publicly available data on course grade distributions, enrollment statistics, and degrees conferred.

I’m restricting this analysis to UT, since cross-university comparisons are both difficult and outside the scope of this article. Although the raw data is hardly informative, we can draw some clever insights via real-world knowledge of the UT student experience. Here are just some of the questions we can answer:

Adit’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

  1. Does UT have administrative bloat?1

  2. What are the most competitive graduate programs at UT?

  3. Where do most students come from geographically?

  4. Does UT have grade inflation?

  5. Which majors have the highest/lowest course grade averages?

  6. How did COVID affect course grades?

  7. Does UT weed out students?

You can access a repository of my work here.

Data sourcing

The main dataset is the UT Course Grade Distributions. It contains the following information about course sections2:

  • Semester: Semesters are divided into Fall (late August-mid December), Spring (mid January-early May), and Summer (mid June-mid August). Summer courses are optional and offerings are often restricted to lower level courses, many of which are in a web-based format. The data ranges from Summer 2011 through Spring 2026.

  • Department/Program: This is simply the department or program that offers the course. This is also represented as a 1-3 character course prefix. For example, courses offered by the physics department are represented by the prefix “PHY”. Some prefixes don’t necessarily correspond to a particular department/program, though most do.

  • Course: This is a string which includes the course prefix, the course number, the course title, and the section number. The course title corresponds to a combination of the course prefix and its number. The course number is 3-digits and is sometimes followed by a letter. For example, ECO 420K corresponds to a course offered by the economics department of the title “Microeconomic Theory”. You can view the details of the numbering convention here.

  • Letter Grade: UT assigns final course grades as letter grades with a plus or minus. Additionally, some students can receive a final course grade of “Other”. This includes non-standard grades, such as when a student elects to take the course pass/fail or drops the course partway through the semester (called a q-drop).3

I typically exclude the summer semesters from semester/year grade averages. To compute a course’s grade average, I first convert letter grades to numbers according to UT’s 4.0 GPA scale.4 I sum these numbers and divide by the number of letter grades (the number of grades, excluding “Other”). Course sizes are determined by the number of final grades in a section, including “Other”.

There are about thousands of courses listed every semester, so sample size is rarely an issue. However, due to privacy, the data is excluded for courses that satisfy at least one of the following conditions:

1. The course is graduate level and there are less than 5 students of record.

2. The course is undergraduate level and there are less than 10 students of record.

3. All students received the same grade.

4. All students except one received the same grade.

5. None of the students received a letter grade.

Source: UT Course Grade Distributions

This will hamper our analysis of course size and course variety, but most of the analysis should remain the same. Small courses or those with homogeneous grade distributions are unreliable to begin with.

In addition to course grade distributions, we’ll examine admissions and enrollment statistics from graduate admissions. To my knowledge, this reports reliable statistics for every graduate program offered at UT in the 2021-2025 admissions cycles. It also includes average GPA, GRE scores, and GMAT scores for each cohort.

We’ll examine data on student demographics. This includes statistics on the student population by gender, race/ethnicity categories, undergraduate/graduate classification, age, part-time/full-time student status5, and college membership6. It also includes graduation rates, the geographic origin of students (by Texas county, UT state, and foreign country), and degrees conferred7.

UT at a glance

As of Fall 2025, UT’s student population is about 55,000. That makes us one of the largest public universities in the US and one of the largest in the world. In addition to the students, there are quite a few faculty and staff members.

There are about 19 students per faculty member and 4.5 per staff member as of 2024. If we include faculty as staff, the student-to-staff ratio is about 3.6:1. That’s lower than a national estimate of 5.2:1 at 4-year colleges, yet higher than the ~1.67:1 at Ivy League schools. Does UT have administrative bloat? Relatively speaking, no. In my experience, the size and diversity of the student body requires an administrative powerhouse. However, I’ve also seen convoluted administrative structures. I’ve met staff members at numerous levels of competency. It feels like there’s an “office” or “department” for everything. There were times when I had to email multiple different people to answer a basic question.

Nevertheless, the ratio of faculty to staff to students has hardly changed within the last decade, suggesting to me that little, if any, of the administrative bloat is recent. It does take a large staff to operate a university of over 50,000 students. My stance is that the issue with the staff isn’t how many of them there are. Instead, staff don’t always feel qualified and the information they provide is occasionally inconsistent.8

As expected, most of the students (~80%) are undergrads. There seems to be a slight decrease in the number of grad students relative to undergrads. Perhaps there’s a diminishing interest in attending grad school. There’s a similarly modest decline in the number of law students.

A more interesting trend, perhaps, is the widening gap in male-female college enrollment. Nationally, the gender gap has remained fairly constant in the last decade. Yet, it’s only widened at UT.

What’s going on? Here are some candidate explanations:

  1. More women are applying relative to men at UT specifically. I don’t know why this would be the case.

  2. There’s a gender gap in prospective majors. Men increasingly apply to competitive majors at UT relative to women. While I lack exact statistics, computer science, engineering, and business are known to be some of UT’s most competitive majors to get accepted to. These are fields that have historically shown more job growth and male interest. There’s a crude way of putting this: the men who do apply to college are increasingly choosing majors reluctant to make space for them.

Unfortunately, I don’t know of any detailed admissions data by major. However, there is evidence consistent with the second explanation. Namely, for the academic year 2024-2025, roughly the same number of men and women applied. The acceptance rates for men and women were about 23% and 31%, respectively.9 I’m inclined to believe that men disproportionately apply to the most competitive majors.

Where do students come from?

Under state law, 90% of first-year students must be Texas residents. When I ask someone where they’re from, I usually expect them to mention a city in the Texas triad: Dallas, Houston, or Austin. But these are sprawling metropolitan areas. What counties do UT students tend to come from?

It’s no secret that the most populous counties send the most students to UT. Perhaps more surprising is that adjusting for county population is fairly inconsequential. While it does reduce the disparities, UT students are still disproportionately from the Texas Triad. The most convincing explanation is agglomeration effects; cities concentrate academic and extracurricular opportunities.

What about the states that American UT students come from? Once again, states with high concentrations of opportunities tend to send more students to UT.

A more puzzling result is which countries UT international students come from.

A lot of them are from Canada and Mexico, likely due to geographic proximity. India, China, Brazil, and Nigeria don’t actually send that many students when you adjust for population size. Many of the countries with the most students per capita are noise: tiny populations with a handful of students. There are two countries whose representation in the UT student population isn’t easily explained: Taiwan and South Korea. I can’t say that I’ve met a lot of Taiwanese people10, but I have seen disproportionately many Koreans. The developed status of Korea isn’t enough to explain this phenomenon; other developed countries aren’t so heavily represented.

As expected, population strongly correlates with enrollment at the county, state, and nation levels.

The code repository contains tables listing counties, states, and nations from whom no students were enrolled in the 2024-2025 academic year. In general, the counties with zero enrollment had low populations. North Dakota is the only state which had zero enrollment. The 93 countries (according to 2025 World Bank classification) with zero enrollment were either minuscule in population or developing. Fun fact: there are no UT students from North Korea.

Graduate School

What are the most competitive graduate programs that UT has to offer?

The computer science and business programs are as competitive and popular as I expected. I was surprised to see how competitive the psychology programs are. A cursory search reveals that clinical psychology programs are generally extremely competitive. I remember hearing that many students major in psychology with the goal of becoming clinical psychologists, only for the vast majority to work outside of psychology.

As you’d expect, the largest graduate programs by enrollment are generally in computer science and business.

The data contains an interesting statistic called yield—the percentage of those admitted who enroll in a program. It tells us how likely someone is to attend given that they’re accepted. Interestingly, less selective programs (those with higher percentages) have a small correlation with higher yields. You’d expect it to be the opposite; surely those accepted to highly competitive programs are thrilled to take up the opportunity. I suspect that, actually, those accepted to more competitive programs at UT are more likely to receive acceptances elsewhere. It’s also worth noting that there’s high variance in yield among selective programs.

As expected, there’s a small correlation between GPA/GRE score with selectivity. More competitive programs tend to admit students with a higher GPA or GRE score on average. The relationship is weaker for GRE score, as many programs don’t require the GRE and/or value it less than GPA.

What courses are most popular?

What course prefixes offered the greatest number of distinct courses in the 2025-2026 academic year?

While there are 19 course prefixes that only offered one distinct course, many offered over 50. There isn’t really a unified pattern behind the prefixes with the most varied course offerings. They do tend to have a high amount of students.

What about course size? It looks like most courses are about 10-50 students, with the median class containing 22 students. This distribution is a bit unreliable, since it excludes sufficiently small classes and those where everyone obtained the same grade. The real distribution likely has more mass on the smaller course sizes; the mean and median are likely biased upwards.

The average course size has slightly increased over time.

What are the hardest majors/courses?

Grade averages are an imperfect proxy for course difficulty. An instructor might assign truckloads of work graded leniently. It’s also common for instructors to curve the class’ grade distribution. Nevertheless, it’s fun to see how grade averages stack up across majors. Note that grade averages are aggregated by prefix. Many prefixes encompass all of the courses of a specific major (e.g., “M” contains all classes offered by the math department). However, some prefixes don’t necessarily correspond to any major. Furthermore, students are often required to take courses outside of their major. Without further ado, enjoy this insanely tall bar graph.

Many of the prefixes at the top aren’t really associated with a major. Ensemble, for instance, isn’t offered as a major. Ensemble courses appear to be courses in music performance where the value of the course is in developing musical skills—not in obtaining a high grade. STEM11 majors do tend to be lower on the graph, but there’s considerable variation. The difference between a 3.4 and a 3.7 course grade average is roughly the difference between a B+ and an A-; it’s nothing crazy.

With my personal knowledge, I can explain why economics and engineering mechanics are at the bottom. UT Austin has a policy that students in the top 6% of their graduating class are guaranteed admission to the university. However, admission to a particular major is only guaranteed for a specific list of majors. Economics was one of those majors, but business wasn’t. This means that many who sought admission into UT’s prestigious and competitive business program chose economics as a backup option. I can tell you from personal experience that the two majors are very different. For one, the economics major is more quantitative than many expected. Essentially, economics courses are full of students who aren’t interested in economics.

Engineering mechanics isn’t a major. It contains notoriously difficult classes included in the degree plans of several engineering majors, such as statics and dynamics.

The overall distribution of UT course grades is heavily left-skewed, with more than half of grades being an A.

Now for a really interesting question: which courses have the highest/lowest grade averages?

Course titles of the top 10:

  1. UNIVERSITY ORCHESTRA

  2. INTRO TO CLINICAL PSYCH-WB

  3. LONGHORN PEP BAND

  4. ELEMENTS OF STAT MACH LEARNING

  5. JAZZ COMBOS

  6. LONGHORN BAND

  7. UNITED STATES IMMIGRATION

  8. INTRO TO ASIAN AMER STUDIES

  9. LEADERSHIP-MSS

  10. ORANGE CONCERT BAND

Course titles of the bottom 10:

  1. MATH MICROECON THRY ADV APP

  2. PSYCHOPHARMACOLOGY

  3. PHYSIOLOGY OF EXERCISE

  4. COMP ORGANIZATN AND ARCH

  5. CHEM REACTOR ANALYSIS AND DSGN

  6. FEEDBACK CONTROL SYSTEMS

  7. INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING

  8. DATA STRUCTURES

  9. DISCRETE MATH FOR COMPUTER SCI

  10. THE NATURAL ENVIRONMENT

The top 10 mostly consist of band courses and popular, low-level courses designed to be accessible. The bottom 10 seems to come down to a combination of conceptual difficulty, inadequate prerequisites, and difficult professors. Four of the bottom 10 courses are required in the computer science major. The course with the lowest grade average, ECO 420S, is one that I took in Fall 2025. The average would be even lower if people weren’t allowed to drop the course. There are a few reasons the course grade average was so low. First, this course is required for the BS in economics.12 Second, many students entering the course lack adequate mathematical preparation. It’s a class that rewards deeper mathematical knowledge over memorization. Third, the course is highly abstract and theoretical—a far departure from the interests and/or aptitudes of its average student. Finally, the professor likes to make the course challenging.

Does UT have grade inflation?

Let’s look at average course grade over time for some common course prefixes that we can reliably link to their respective major.

We see a general trend of grade inflation, especially outside of engineering. There’s also a spike in grades around the time of the COVID pandemic. It’s unclear how much of the post-COVID grade inflation is attributable to the release of LLMs, as opposed to increases in student ability and/or changes in the courses themselves.13 There are a few potential explanations for the COVID spike. First, as courses moved online, it became easier than ever to cheat on exams. Second, students probably had more free time, allowing them to invest more time into each course. Finally, it’s possible that courses were easier during COVID.

Before we look into potential explanations, I should note that the trend is somewhat noisy. Nonetheless, a whopping 71% of courses had higher grade averages during COVID.

To test the veracity of second and third candidate explanations, we can examine how web-based courses changed in grade average during COVID. In theory, web-based should observe a smaller COVID spike. Indeed this is what we see if we observe the mean course grades of web-based courses over time.14

You might think the spike is due to previously in-person courses becoming web-based during COVID. Indeed, COVID sharply increased the share of web-based courses, with the share remaining slightly higher afterwards.15

If we follow a pool of courses that remained web-based before and after COVID, we still see a COVID spike. Granted, the sample is small (n=27) and noisy.

All of this suggests to me a few things. First, none of the three explanations for the COVID spike can be ruled out. I believe that all of them hold in some capacity. Second, course grades have generally inflated, especially outside of engineering. I doubt that LLMs explain much of this, as the rate of grade inflation doesn’t appear significantly larger after the release of ChatGPT. This isn’t surprising. Exams, which account for the bulk of course grades, have largely remained in-person, precluding the opportunity to exploit LLMs. Moreover, homework, which is done outside of class, was typically graded generously to begin with.

What languages are most popular?

UT has a generous offering of foreign language courses, with 25 offered in the 25-26 academic year. There are nearly as many enrollments in Spanish courses as in every other language course combined. This makes sense, because Spanish is both practically useful in Texas (there’s a large Latin-American population here) and seen as the “default” language to learn. Anyone taking a foreign language course chiefly to satisfy their degree requirement would likely choose Spanish.

French is the runner-up, likely because it’s spoken in Canada. It’s also seen as the “second default” language. Japanese seems to take third place due to its significance in cultural exports (anime, video games, etc.). This would explain why it accounts for a greater share of language enrollment than Chinese16, despite having less speakers.

Does UT weed people out?

Students within a major are often required to take the same sequence of core courses before advancing to elective courses. This allows us to follow the same cohort of students within a major from the beginning of a sequence to the end. I’m going to examine the “attrition rate” for the computer science (CS) and economics (econ) majors.

Cohorts are defined based on the completion of the final course in a sequence. For instance, if the sequence is A → B → C, the Spring 2026 cohort took C during that semester. This means that they took B in Fall 2025 and A in Spring 2025. This approach to approximating a cohort assumes the following:

  1. Courses in the sequence are taken one after the other—not concurrently. In CS and econ, speaking from personal experience, students tend to enroll in the respective sequences in this order. It’s somewhat uncommon to take these core courses concurrently and/or to take a break in between them.

  2. All students in a cohort advance to the next course. In practice, a student who receives a lower grade than a C- might retake the course instead of switching majors, thus shifting to the subsequent cohort. If the tendency for students to retake courses was consistent across years, we can make stronger claims about the cohort trends. If retaking became less common over the years, subsequent cohorts would have lower proportions of students retaking the course. On the other hand, if retaking became more common, subsequent cohorts would have higher proportions of students retaking the course.17

  3. Students in a course took the previous course (excluding intro courses). It’s common for students to enter UT already having received credit for the introductory courses of their major’s core sequence. Beyond these courses, it’s safe to assume that someone in course C took course B. Prerequisites are strictly enforced.

The data doesn’t allow us to track students individual students across semesters. We could compare the number of students admitted to a major to the number of students who receive the corresponding degree four years later. Assuming we had these numbers, the latter approach fails to show us when people might leave a major. It could be that a specific course is where most of the attrition occurs. We should take caution in interpreting the attrition rates. It’s not the percent of people who start off in a major who drop out, transfer to another school, or switch majors. Rather, it’s the percentage change in the size of courses in the core sequence, assuming a typical schedule. Even if we knew the former quantity, we couldn’t interpret this as a “weed-out rate”. What truly counts as being weeded out? Someone might change their major for reasons unrelated to its difficulty.

Note that we don’t have an average attrition rate across majors because each major’s core sequence is so different. I chose to examine economics and CS because they’re popular majors with a relatively strict, linear core sequence.18

I’ll refer to the four courses on the horizontal axis, in order, as intro to programming, data structures, comp arch, and OS (Operating Systems), respectively. There’s a big enrollment jump from 312 to 314 for the fall cohorts because many people tested out of it via AP Computer Science: A. Anyone in a fall cohort completed OS in a fall semester, meaning they likely took 314 during their first semester instead of 312. In contrast, the course size for spring cohorts remains stable from 312 to 314 because these students likely didn’t test out of 312.

After 314, we see a general, steady decline in enrollment. On average, course size decreases 18.5% from 314 to 439. Additionally, the fall cohorts—those that likely “skipped” 312—are larger. This affirms the belief that the field of computer science normalizes precociousness; the majority of CS majors don’t take the intro course. I reiterate that we shouldn’t interpret the decline as a weed-out rate. There are students who took a break (gap semesters are not uncommon in computer science) and/or retook a course. Regardless, we can interpret the attrition as students switching majors and/or being behind schedule.

The grade trends are also fascinating. Keep in mind that if multiple professors taught the same course during a semester, the grade distributions from the sections are aggregated. Every cohort received a better average grade in OS than in comp arch. The Spring cohorts all performed worse than their Fall counterparts. The gap is especially pronounced for the Fall 2025 and Spring 2026 cohorts. Let’s keep in mind that most of the Spring cohorts didn’t skip 312. To me, this suggests that those who entered the UT CS program with a head-start retained an academic advantage. Finally, grades in each course have generally decreased over the years. I’m unsure of whether this has more to do with changes in the courses or in the cohorts themselves.

We see different trends for cohorts in economics. I’ll refer to the courses in the sequence below, in order, as intro micro, intro macro, eco stats, (math) micro theory, metrics, and macro theory. The reason 420K and 420S are stacked on top of each other is that students in the BA Economics degree plan can enroll in either one, while those in the BS Economics degree plan must enroll in 420S. 420S is a more mathematically rigorous version of 420K. Students can test out of intro micro and/or intro macro. They may choose to take metrics concurrently with 420K/S or 320L.

There’s a sharp decline from intro micro to intro macro because intro micro is commonly taken by non-majors. There’s a smaller drop from intro macro to eco stats because a subset of non-majors takes intro-macro. Moreover, anyone who tests out of intro micro via AP exams tends to also test out of intro macro. In other words, if an econ major skipped intro micro, they probably also skipped intro macro. The drop-off is steeper for the spring cohorts.19 For some reason, enrollment in intro micro for the Spring cohorts and not the Fall cohorts is increasing. Enrollment remains roughly stable afterwards, as the remaining courses in the sequence consist almost exclusively of econ majors. Enrollment dips around 420K/420S simply because cohorts split into two course types. On average across the cohorts, there’s a 14.2% decrease in enrollment from ECO 329 to ECO 320L.

Except for the Fall 2023 and Spring 2024 cohorts, grades consistently tank around micro theory, especially for those in the mathematical version. The gap in average course grade between 420K and 420S has only increased with time. We see the more recent cohorts underperform in 420S specifically. In my experience, the course has seemed to get curved less generously over time. An interesting observation is that the grade average for ECO 420S was especially bad in Spring 2024 and Fall 2024, with averages of around a C and C-, respectively. In Fall 2025 and Spring 2026 pooled, it was 2.27 (about a C+).

If econ does weed people out, it’s not primarily through any one course. I can infer that this is because many who struggle with 420S simply switch from the BS to the BA degree plan, allowing them to take the comparatively easier 420K.

The philosophy of data science

I want to appreciate what it’s possible to glean from an under-discussed public dataset like this:

  1. The nation’s gender gap in college enrollment is steady, yet at UT it’s ballooning.

  2. Texan students disproportionately come from urban areas.

  3. American students disproportionately come from developed states.

  4. Disproportionately many international students are from Taiwan and South Korea.

  5. Graduate programs in psychology are insanely competitive.

  6. Different majors and fields of study aren’t so different in terms of average grade.

  7. UT is experiencing increases in average grade, which one might classify as grade inflation.20

  8. Course grades spiked during COVID. The increase doesn’t seem entirely driven by a newfound ability to cheat.

  9. Spanish is by far the most popular language offered.

  10. CS and econ seem to weed some people out. It’s unclear exactly why. There is considerable average course grade variation by semester. Ostensibly, students with an head-start in programming ability perform better.

Let’s take a step back to understand what we did at a more philosophical level. Data reifies complex characteristics of the human condition. Information like a person’s income, the gender composition of an occupation, and the grade averages for a course encapsulate lived experiences. An egregious grade distribution is more than numbers on a page; it’s real people whose academic choices may have upended months of their emotional state.

In data science, especially in economics, it’s commonplace to analyze data for which one lacks real-world familiarity. It’s one thing to see poverty statistics on a spreadsheet, for instance, and another to have witnessed or experienced the phenomenon in-person. Having real-world familiarity with the data we analyze can equip us with more robust hypotheses or set us on a more reliable path. I hope this analysis has demonstrated how much additional mileage you can get out of synthesizing quantitative and qualitative insights.

On the other hand, it can be valuable to simplify these subjective experiences into numbers. To treat outcomes as some stochastic machine whose odds we can manipulate. To see this in action, say you wanted to build a tech startup. A more “intrinsic” approach is to work harder. A more “extrinsic” approach is to embed yourself in an environment that statistically improves your odds of making it big. If a statistical analysis tells you that living in one census tract improves your odds on average, that’s a consideration worth making. It can feel weird to treat aspects of our outcomes as uncontrollable. We’re used to treating our outcomes as the result of more direct actions. Reasoning about the statistical effects of external factors allows us to swing the dice in our favor.

In the context of this course grades at UT, a low mean course grade doesn’t preclude you from obtaining an A. The intrinsic outlook is to work hard in the class. A valuable perspective. Meanwhile, the extrinsic outlook is to reason about what kind of course schedule might influence you to be the best person you can be.

Appendix

This appendix contains additional tables and figures.

It’s possible for a particular course to have multiple sections during a semester, even under the same professor. For example, a calculus course with Dr. X could have sections that meet from 8am-9am and 10am-11am, respectively.

In lay terms, the difference between a 0.0 and a 2.0 is not the same as the difference between a 2.0 and a 4.0. In fact, the vast majority of grades lie in the 2.0-4.0 range.

I’m not a big fan of the term “STEM” for a few reasons.

First, the fields of mathematics, the natural sciences, and engineering are vastly different. Even the term “natural sciences” encompasses biology, chemistry, and physics. The diversity of fields within STEM is indicative of how different students within each field are. Biology students and physics students are, in my experience, different animals.

Second, in many communities, STEM is seen as the default career path. For example, among Asian-Americans, knowing that someone is majoring in STEM doesn’t reveal much about them.

Finally, it compartmentalizes career paths. Human knowledge overlaps heavily, even within STEM. Some examples of careers that straddle the line between STEM and “non-STEM” include economists, patent lawyers, tech policy, managerial positions, and sci-fi authors.

There are spikes during the summer semesters because web-based courses tend to have higher grade averages during the summer. As shown in the appendix, this is not true more generally of summer courses. I suspect this is because some courses are only offered as web-based during the summer. These courses tend to have relatively high grade averages, which artificially drives up course grade averages. These courses also tend to be large, hence why weighting by course size shows larger “summer spikes”.

15

You can also see big shift towards web-based courses during the summer term. I think COVID convinced UT that summer courses could be made web-based for convenience.

16

Spring cohorts took their first econ class in Fall two years prior. Fall cohorts took their first econ class in Spring two years prior. It looks like intro micro is generally much more popular to take in the Fall.

20

I’m not making a statement on how detrimental/beneficial grade inflation is. All we know is that average course grades are increasing at a steady rate.

item.title: Economic Growth Won’t Solve Everything
item.description: miscellaneous thoughts on development economics
item.content:encoded:
The chief objective of the field of development economics (dev econ) is to investigate an important question:

How can we make poor people in the developing world better off?

It’s a difficult question to answer. I find it compelling because poverty is more than someone having a light wallet. Poverty is a pattern of human suffering that emerges from material deprivation.

In the developed world, we have the luxury of decoupling money from happiness. When someone here is unhappy, we don’t tell them that money is the solution. For instance, in the United States, happiness seems to plateau after about $75,000 a year of income.1 Some of us are told that “money can’t buy happiness” or to resist materialism. Even our stories decouple money from happiness. Characters in realistic fiction set in the developed world often suffer from issues unrelated to their wealth.2

At the lowest levels of wealth, money and happiness are more strongly intertwined. It can mean the difference between a baby’s death and its survival. This would suggest that economic growth alleviates most poverty-induced suffering. Indeed, we have cause for celebration. Global poverty has rapidly fallen by many measures, though the level of growth varies.

We have also seen significant reductions in mortality, likely due to improvements in nutrition, sanitation, and medicine. It’s difficult to identify how much of the improvement in human welfare is attributable to economic growth. As my professor says, “good things tend to go together and bad things tend to go together”. For example, children who have worse material conditions might also have greater exposure to pollution, infectious diseases, and malnutrition.

Micro vs. Macro

It doesn’t take an economist to realize that economic growth improves well-being. However, the design of policies that accelerate economic growth is intractable. There are too many variables for us to find a silver bullet. To some, it’s futile. Development economists responded with the “credibility revolution”, a shift towards studying smaller scale issues with more empirically rigorous methods. The tradeoff between tractable, small-scale change and uncertain, large-scale change is one hotly debated even outside of economics.

Understanding smaller scale ideas like the effect of a de-worming program on educational outcomes is valuable. It bumps the needle. A “small” scale improvement in material welfare could mean that hundreds more children survive to adulthood. Randomized Control Trials (RCTs) are now viewed by many as the gold standard.3 RCTs involve randomly assigning people into a treatment and control group, then comparing the groups’ respective outcomes. For example, suppose you want to test the effect of after school tutoring on students’ grades. If you simply compared one kid who didn’t receive tutoring to a kid who did, you couldn’t claim the difference as causal; the kids could have all kinds of differences (gender, socioeconomic status, etc.) that influence their grades. Instead, if we randomly assigned 100 kids to the tutoring program and 100 kids not to participate, the two groups would be “similar enough” on average. Observing a difference across large samples allows us to infer a causal effect of the tutoring program on students’ grades.

While RCTs are a powerful tool for evaluating policies, they are costly to run and struggle to generalize to other settings. For example, the effect of after school tutoring in Ghana might be different from that in Nigeria. Critics argue that global poverty is fundamentally a structural issue, which RCTs can’t solve. Indeed, RCTs aren’t intended to solve poverty at a structural level. Yet, there are calls to study poverty at a more macroeconomic scale. Macroeconomic (macro) research has the potential for much larger scale welfare improvements at the cost of empirical rigor and tractability. Microeconomic (micro) research has reliably produced smaller scale welfare improvements without answering fundamental questions of what makes poor countries poor.

Most of my dev econ knowledge is in micro research. This typically consists of using statistical methods and/or field experiments to analyze some particular social scientific phenomenon. Examples include social mobility, pollution, malnutrition, and immigration. With the right skill and funding, it’s possible to greatly scale this kind of research. In contrast, macro research uses theoretical models to understand national and international phenomena, such as inflation, employment, trade, and economic growth. I remain skeptical that macro research is conducive to increased economic growth. Nonetheless, there are compelling arguments that economic growth is both necessary and sufficient for major improvements in human welfare.4

I’m left with a dilemma. I want to alleviate global poverty by pursuing research through a dev econ PhD. I find micro research more rewarding because of its tractability and relatively certain theory of change. Moreover, when done thoughtfully, it involves understanding people at their most fundamental level. Yet, I keep speculating about whether a macroeconomic silver bullet for poverty exists. Even if there is one—which I highly doubt—it’s plausible that we nearly eradicate poverty before its discovery.5

Will AI Replace Economists?

To complicate my career choices, there are more ways to tackle poverty than micro or macro research. Politics, other social sciences, and technological development help fill the gaps in mainstream dev econ. The value of micro dev econ research is uncertain. The 2026 job market for economists was brutal. Only one of the econ PhD students at my school received a tenure track placement at a US university that year.

The potential capabilities of AI do me no favors. Will AI replace economists? AI has accelerated much of my research workflow—especially coding. However, AI would require the social abilities of a human to fully replace development economists. Fieldwork plays a vital role in dev econ research. My professor says (roughly) that “the best way to learn something is to get on a bike in some foreign country.” I don’t see AI replacing this process anytime soon. If you don’t believe me, I encourage you to read Where India Goes by Dean Spears and Diane Coffey. To automate the kind of work detailed in this book, AI would have to:

  • Talk to locals in developing countries

  • Synthesize academic literature with fieldwork to produce quality research ideas

  • Compile relevant qualitative and quantitative analyses into incisive writing

  • Communicate policy-relevant findings to bureaucrats

I’m not so prideful as to assume AI will never become this capable. However, if AI can replace development economists, it can replace virtually every occupation.6

Nevertheless, if AI delivers unprecedented economic growth, it could eradicate poverty within my lifetime.7 Would this render development economists obsolete? I anticipate that an eradication poverty will simply raise the standards for poverty.8 For instance, before the early 1900s, American children suffered from iodine deficiencies. A nutritional deficiency once common in the developed world is now considered material deprivation. If AI-induced growth keeps raising the proverbial goalpost, you’ll hear no complaints from me.

But if AI can accelerate economic growth, what counter-factual benefits will development economists actually deliver? To repeat the words of my professor: “good things tend to go together and bad things tend to go together”. A better reframing of the question is this: what kinds of welfare deficiencies does economic growth struggle to address?

Through a combination of astute fieldwork, thoughtful experimental design, historical context, and good ‘ol fashioned economics, we can investigate this question via a single subject: poop.

Open Defecation

Typical, material dimensions of welfare can’t fully account for human welfare. Colloquially, “money doesn’t buy happiness.” Many of us can point out examples of miserable rich people and happy poor people. I’m not surprised that individual characteristics influence happiness. When studying developing populations, it’s tempting to attribute negative outcomes (infant mortality, financial insecurity, crime, etc.) to poverty. Fair enough. But what happens when a socioeconomically disadvantaged population actually has better outcomes?

In India, Muslims are socioeconomically disadvantaged relative to Hindus. Yet, Muslim babies have lower rates of infant mortality than Hindu babies. Evidence points to the practice of open defecation—defecating outdoors without a latrine or toilet. Open defecation is far more common in India, particularly rural North India, than in other developing countries. Moreover, Hindus in India are much more likely to open defecate than their Muslim counterparts. The practice persists despite continual investment into digging latrines in rural North Indian villages. In many cases, Hindu villagers open defecate despite latrine accessibility.

The explanation, detailed in Where India Goes, lies in caste. Primarily, once latrines become full, someone must empty them. This heavily stigmatized duty was once relegated to Dalits, the lowest caste in India. The refusal of Dalits to perpetuate their role in rural sanitation has discouraged latrine use among Hindus. Muslims, who lack the same Hindu, casteist beliefs, are 21 percentage points less likely to open defecate.

Open defecation exposes babies to fecal pathogens both in utero and after birth. For example, an airborne pathogen from someone’s poop can impair the mother’s ability to absorb nutrients, posing a major infant mortality risk. These pathogens can come from the feces of anyone in a village. In general, sanitation affects people at the neighborhood-level. Thus, one’s own excretory practices matter less for health outcomes than those of their neighbors.

Muslims tend to live around other Muslims, just as Hindus tend to live around other Hindus. This means that Muslims, whose neighbors are less likely to open defecate, face less disease burden from open defecation. Indeed, Hindu babies in areas with a higher proportion of Muslims face lower infant mortality risk. Open defecation rates offer a potential explanation for why Indian children are shorter than their counterparts from Sub-Saharan Africa.9 In African villages, which have lower rates of open defecation, the sanitation environment is far different.

Rates of open defecation are on the decline. The most plausible way that Hindus in rural North India stop open defecating is that they gain access to a flushable toilet. For the aforementioned reason and more, a latrine remains insufficient; caste-related beliefs seem highly intractable. Nonetheless, it seems that economic growth was both necessary and sufficient to decrease open defecation. It was necessary in the sense that the plausibly effective alternative, mass construction of flushable toilets, was too expensive. It was sufficient in the sense that richer people, newly equipped with flushable toilets, have no reason to revert to open defecation.

Is growth sufficient?

If economic growth is so great, can we abstain from researching microeconomic issues?10 Even if growth eliminates open defecation within the next few decades, I doubt it’ll erase the entrenched legacy of caste in India. Perhaps economic growth is so powerful that it outweighs persistent inequalities. An underlying question of what makes for a great world is whether non-decreasing inequity is worth other forms of progress. More specifically, is the world better off if people are individually better off, but inequality increases?11 Inequality, decadence, and other aesthetic preferences could eventually outweigh material, population-level pareto improvements.

You might say that I’m straw-manning the argument for growth. The goal, after all, is inclusive growth. Well, that’s hard to define in practice. Growth yields enormous human welfare benefits, albeit with limitations. I believe that patching the holes in growth is an interdisciplinary, microeconomic endeavor. I doubt that a macroeconomic policy could address casteism, for instance. I’m not saying that we shouldn’t prioritize growth. I’m just saying that stipulations for growth (sustainability, inclusivity, etc.) demand micro research. For example, clean air, a microeconomic issue, is not guaranteed by economic growth.

Perhaps the most convincing evidence that growth is insufficient concerns life expectancy. The global life expectancy increased rapidly from 1930s onward. The global population exploded for the first time in human history. It’s unclear how much of the mortality decline is attributable to economic growth relative to improvements in public health. According to one estimate, less than 16% of the 12.2 year increase in life expectancy from the 1930s to the 1960s is due to income growth. In fact, at every level of national income per capita, estimated life expectancy was higher in the 1960s than in the 1930s. Evidence for the role of public health in the mortality decline includes (but is far from limited to) the effects of vaccines, pasteurization, treatment of water, washing hands, and nutritional fortification. You could argue that growth was instrumental to developing these innovations. However, I’d argue that optimizing for growth alone is parochial.

There is a role for non-growth economics research in improving public health, accelerating innovation, and investigating non-traditional dimensions of human welfare. Growth might dwarf and partially subsume these improvements. Nevertheless, we should interrogate the counterfactual impact of development economists on economic growth. Just because growth is larger scale doesn’t mean that economists who research it make larger contributions to human welfare.

Conclusion

To ask development economists to prioritize growth above all else is to impose a lofty goal: the eradication of poverty. At it’s strongest, this goal entails optimizing the betterment of the world. Did most of the field give up too early in researching growth? I can’t say with my current level of understanding. Ultimately, I still lean towards Pritchett; growth should remain a major focus of development economics.

At higher levels of development, the effect of growth on happiness is dubious. There may come a point where every locality, let alone country, is so developed that growth is no longer effective for increasing human welfare. Perhaps development economists will hang up their hats and join anthropologists in more humanistic research.

It’s crazy to imagine a world where poverty is eradicated. One where I high-five my colleagues that our life’s work is complete. The day may never come. Until then, we have work to do.

To say that growth is necessary also seems trivial. Suppose that instead, major welfare improvements occurred without any growth. This ostensibly necessitates greater availability in resources (labor, capital, technology, etc.). How could these windfalls not appear in measures of economic growth? It would make no sense. The claim that sustainable, inclusive growth is necessary and sufficient for large scale human welfare improvements is only valuable to the extent that it can dismiss some poverty interventions as myopic.

We should think of this as the scale at which issues are studied in addition to the scale of the issues themselves. The economic impacts of data center construction, a microeconomic issue, could massively shape the trajectory of AI progress. Inflation, a macroeconomic issue, is rooted in microeconomic behaviors. An analogy is that biology is “larger scale” than physics. We tend to study biology at a larger physical scale, yet both can be used to understand so much of our reality.
